lessons.title: V3·DB1 — Query shapes, tracking, and the N+1 you ship by accident
lessons.summary: Eight problems about the gap between a LINQ expression that compiles and the SQL it becomes. Deferred execution, client evaluation, the two flavours of N+1, cartesian explosion, identity resolution, keyset paging and set-based writes. Most gates here count SQL commands as strictly as they check the body.

# V3·DB1 — Query shapes, tracking, and the N+1 you ship by accident

`d13_efcore_tracking` taught you what the change tracker remembers. This sector
is about the other half of the same machine: what the provider *sends*. A LINQ
query is not code that runs. It is an expression tree that EF Core translates,
and the distance between "this compiles" and "this issues one sensible SELECT"
is where almost all Entity Framework performance incidents live.

None of the bugs in this sector are exotic. Every one of them ships from real
teams every week, passes code review, passes the integration test on a seeded
database of twelve rows, and then falls over the first time a branch has four
thousand books. That is the shape of the problem: **query bugs are invisible at
small scale and quadratic at large scale.** The only defence is to look at the
SQL, so several gates here grade the number of commands the endpoint issues.

Everything is under `/v3db01/...`. The entities, DTOs and the `V3Db01Db`
context live in `src/Api/V3DB01_QueryShapes/Model.cs` — given code, read it
first. The domain is a small library system: `Branch` has many `Book`, a `Book`
has many `Copy` and many `Review`, a `Copy` has many `Loan`, and a `Loan`
points at a `Member`. `Book` carries a `Withdrawn` flag and the model declares
a **global query filter** that hides withdrawn books; that filter is going to
matter twice.

Each exercise owns one file, so nothing you do here can break another exercise.

## Exercise 1 — deferred execution is the whole point

Edit `src/Api/V3DB01_QueryShapes/Ex1.cs`. `GET /v3db01/books?city={city}`
answers **200** with a list of `BookRow` — `id`, `title`, `author`,
`copyCount` — for every book in a branch in that city, ordered by title A–Z.

The shipped version calls `ToListAsync()` on `db.Books` and then filters,
sorts and counts in C#. It returns the right answer. It also drags the entire
`Books` table across the wire on every request. Make the whole query run in
the database, in exactly **one** command, and make sure it never materialises
a `Book` entity at all.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db01_query_shapes ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — the filter that could not be translated

Edit `src/Api/V3DB01_QueryShapes/Ex2.cs`. `GET /v3db01/search?term={term}`
answers **200** with matching `BookRow`s, ordered by title; **400** when
`term` is blank or shorter than two characters. The match is
case-insensitive and substring-based over the title.

The shipped version does the matching with a compiled regular expression
inside the `Where`. That is not translatable, and the version of EF Core you
are running will not quietly fall back to the client — it throws. Express the
same predicate in something the provider can turn into SQL, and keep it to one
command that returns only matching rows.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db01_query_shapes ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — N+1, the loop flavour

Edit `src/Api/V3DB01_QueryShapes/Ex3.cs`. `GET /v3db01/branches/{id}/shelf`
answers **404** for an unknown branch, otherwise **200** with a `ShelfReport`:
the branch name, and a `books` list of `ShelfRow` (`title`, `copyCount`,
`onLoanCount`) ordered by title.

The shipped version loads the books, then inside a `foreach` reads
`book.Copies.Count`. On a branch with 300 books that is 301 queries and it
looks completely innocent in the diff. The gate allows **at most two**
commands.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db01_query_shapes ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — one query is not always the cheap one

Edit `src/Api/V3DB01_QueryShapes/Ex4.cs`. `GET /v3db01/books/{id}/detail`
answers **404** for an unknown book, otherwise **200** with a `BookDetail`
carrying the title, every copy's barcode (ascending), and every review's stars
and body (newest first).

The shipped version `Include`s both collections in one query, which makes the
database produce `copies × reviews` rows and hands EF the job of stitching
them back together. With 12 copies and 40 reviews that is 480 rows to move
5 kilobytes of data. Ask for the two collections in separate round trips
instead. Three commands are allowed; the response shape must not change.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db01_query_shapes ex4
```

## Exercise 5 — identity resolution, and why your JSON tripled in size

Edit `src/Api/V3DB01_QueryShapes/Ex5.cs`. `GET /v3db01/catalogue` answers
**200** with a `CatalogueReport`: a `books` list of `CatalogueRow` (`title`
plus the owning branch's `name`) ordered by title, and `branchInstances` — the
number of *distinct `Branch` object references* in the loaded graph.

The gate seeds two branches and eight books. With plain `AsNoTracking`, the
answer is 8: every row builds its own `Branch`. Make it **2**, without
tracking anything, without a second query, and without deduplicating by hand.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db01_query_shapes ex5
```

## Exercise 6 — filtered includes

Edit `src/Api/V3DB01_QueryShapes/Ex6.cs`. `GET /v3db01/members/{id}/current`
answers **404** for an unknown member, otherwise **200** with a
`MemberLoans`: the member's name and their **open** loans only — those with
no `ReturnedAt` — newest first, each as a `LoanRow` (`loanId`, `barcode`,
`title`, `takenAt`).

The shipped version includes every loan the member has ever had and filters
the returned ones out in C#. For a member with nine years of history that is
most of the table for a list of two. Push the filter into the include, and
keep it to one command.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db01_query_shapes ex6
```

## Exercise 7 — set-based writes, and the filter that hides your own rows

Edit `src/Api/V3DB01_QueryShapes/Ex7.cs`. `POST /v3db01/authors/{author}/
withdraw` marks every one of that author's books withdrawn and answers **200**
with a `WithdrawReport` (`withdrawn` — how many rows this call changed —
and `totalWithdrawnForAuthor`). **404** when the author has no un-withdrawn
books; **at most three** commands, and no entity may be loaded to do the
update.

The trap is the second number. `Book` has a global query filter on
`Withdrawn == false`, so the obvious follow-up count reports **zero** every
time, no matter how many rows you just changed.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db01_query_shapes ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — paging that does not degrade on page 900

Edit `src/Api/V3DB01_QueryShapes/Ex8.cs`. `GET /v3db01/loans?size={n}&after=
{cursor}` answers **200** with a `LoanPage`: up to `n` `LoanRow`s ordered by
`takenAt` descending then `loanId` descending, plus `nextCursor` — the cursor
that fetches the following page, or `null` on the last page. **400** when
`size` is outside 1–50 or the cursor is malformed.

The cursor format is `"{ticks}_{loanId}"`; `V3Db01Cursor.TryParse` and
`V3Db01Cursor.Format` are given. `Skip` is banned — the gate fails the
exercise if the generated SQL contains an OFFSET. One command per page, and
you must decide whether there is a next page without a second count query.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db01_query_shapes ex8
```

## Challenge — one query, three aggregates, and a tag you can grep for

Edit `src/Api/V3DB01_QueryShapes/Challenge.cs`. `GET /v3db01/report` answers
**200** with a list of `BranchReport` — branch `name`, `openLoans` (loans on
its copies with no `ReturnedAt`), and `topTitles`: the three titles with the
most loans of all time, ties broken by title A–Z — ordered by `openLoans`
descending then `name` A–Z.

Constraints the gate enforces: **exactly one** SQL command, no grouping or
sorting done in C#, and the command text must carry the tag
`v3db01-report` so an on-call engineer can find it in the slow-query log.

Correlated subqueries inside a projection are the tool. The part that catches
people is that `Take(3)` inside a projection is legal and that the whole
`topTitles` sequence has to be built server-side.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db01_query_shapes challenge
```

## Review

`review1` is not part of finishing this sector; the scheduler brings it back
later. Edit `src/Api/V3DB01_QueryShapes/Review1.cs`:
`GET /v3db01/books/{id}/availability` answers **410 Gone** for a withdrawn
book, **404** when no such book exists at all, and otherwise **200** with an
`Availability` (`title`, `hasFreeCopy`, `openLoans`) — in exactly one
command, with no entity materialised.

# Reading - dotnet/v3db01_query_shapes

## Notes

Every problem in this sector is one question asked eight ways: **what SQL does
this expression tree become, and how many times is it sent?** The LINQ you
write is a description, not an execution. `db.Books.Where(...)` allocates an
`IQueryable<Book>` and sends nothing. The provider only builds and executes
SQL when something forces enumeration — `ToListAsync`, `FirstOrDefaultAsync`,
`CountAsync`, `AnyAsync`, a `foreach`, or an `await` on an async enumerable.

**Composition is free; enumeration is not.** That is the rule the whole
sector rests on. Adding `.Where()`, `.OrderBy()`, `.Select()` and `.Take()`
to a query costs nothing because you are editing a tree. The moment you call
`ToListAsync()` you have frozen the shape, and anything you do afterwards
happens in your process on rows you have already paid to move.

**The boundary between server and client is the terminal operator.** Before
it, you are writing SQL in C#. After it, you are writing C#. `ex1` is exactly
this: the shipped version's `.Where` is a `List<Book>.Where`, not a
`IQueryable<Book>.Where`, and the compiler is perfectly happy about it because
both extension methods exist and `List<T>` implements `IEnumerable<T>`.

**Untranslatable predicates throw.** EF Core 3.0 removed automatic client
evaluation of `Where` for exactly the reason in `ex2`: silently pulling the
table down and filtering in memory turned a typo into an outage. You now get
`InvalidOperationException: The LINQ expression ... could not be translated`.
That is a good error. Read it, and either express the predicate in something
translatable or call `AsEnumerable()` deliberately so the switch is visible.

**There are two N+1s.** The loop flavour (`ex3`) is a `foreach` over parents
touching a navigation property, where each touch is a round trip — under lazy
loading proxies it is completely invisible in the source. The include flavour
is subtler: `Include` on two sibling collections in one query produces the
cross product, which is `ex4`. One is too many queries; the other is one query
that is too big. Both are fixed by deciding what shape you actually want.

**Projections are the general answer.** `Select` into a DTO means no entity is
constructed, nothing is tracked, only the columns you named cross the wire,
and the aggregate happens in the database. Almost every read endpoint in a
real system should end in a projection. `Include` is for when you are about to
*modify* the graph.

## ex1 - deferred execution and the extension method you did not mean

The shipped code's mistake is one call in the wrong place. `ToListAsync()`
before the `Where` changes which `Where` binds: `Queryable.Where(this
IQueryable<T>, Expression<Func<T,bool>>)` becomes `Enumerable.Where(this
IEnumerable<T>, Func<T,bool>)`. Identical syntax, completely different
machine. Nothing warns you.

The model answer never leaves `IQueryable`. `Select(b => new BookRow(b.Id,
b.Title, b.Author, b.Copies.Count()))` translates the count into a correlated
subquery, so a table with a million books answers with the twelve rows the
city has. Note that the projection also means the global query filter on
`Withdrawn` is still applied — filters are part of the query, not of
materialisation.

## ex2 - translatable predicates

`Regex.IsMatch` has no SQL equivalent, so the translator gives up and throws.
`string.Contains`, `StartsWith` and `EndsWith` do translate, to `LIKE` with
the appropriate wildcards. `EF.Functions.Like(b.Title, $"%{term}%")` is the
explicit spelling and is worth preferring when you care about which pattern
lands in the SQL.

Case sensitivity is a database property, not a LINQ one. On a case-insensitive
collation `Contains` is already case-insensitive; calling `ToLower()` on both
sides "to be safe" is how you make the column index unusable. Know your
collation instead.

The `term.Length < 2` guard is not decoration. `%a%` on a large table is a
full scan and a denial-of-service vector; short-term search is a product
decision that belongs in the handler.

## ex3 - the loop N+1

The fix is to ask for the aggregate rather than the objects. Projecting
`b.Copies.Count()` and `b.Copies.SelectMany(c => c.Loans).Count(l =>
l.ReturnedAt == null)` gives two correlated subqueries in one command; the
branch lookup for the 404 is the second command the gate allows.

The reason this bug survives review is that the loop reads like it is looking
at data already in memory. It is, right up until the navigation property is
untouched, at which point either lazy loading fires a query or — with lazy
loading off, which is the default — you silently read an empty collection and
report `copyCount: 0` for everything. That second failure mode is worse,
because it is a wrong answer rather than a slow one.

## ex4 - cartesian explosion and split queries

A single query with two collection `Include`s joins both collections to the
root, so the database returns `copies × reviews` rows and every scalar of the
book is repeated in each of them. EF de-duplicates correctly; the cost is on
the wire and in the database's join.

`AsSplitQuery()` issues one command per collection, correlated by the root's
key. The trade is real: split queries are not atomic with each other, so a
concurrent write between them can produce a graph that never existed in the
database. Inside a serializable transaction that is not a concern; on a hot
read path it usually is not one either. `QuerySplittingBehavior` can be set
per query or as a context-wide default in `UseSqlServer(o =>
o.UseQuerySplittingBehavior(...))`.

Projection avoids the whole question, which is why the reference answer for
this one is worth comparing against the `AsSplitQuery` version.

## ex5 - identity resolution

`AsNoTracking` skips the change tracker, and the identity map lives *in* the
change tracker. Without it there is nothing to say "I have already built the
`Branch` with id 3", so every row constructs a fresh one. Serialise that and
the branch's fields appear once per book.

`AsNoTrackingWithIdentityResolution()` keeps a lightweight identity map for
the duration of the query only, and throws it away afterwards. You get shared
references without paying for tracking snapshots. It is the right default for
any read that returns a graph rather than a flat list.

The honest alternative is not to return the graph: project the branch name
into the row and the question disappears. Both answers are correct; knowing
that they are different answers is the point.

## ex6 - filtered include

`Include(m => m.Loans.Where(l => l.ReturnedAt == null).OrderByDescending(l =>
l.TakenAt))` filters and orders inside the include, so the SQL only returns
the open loans. The rules worth remembering: only `Where`, `OrderBy`,
`ThenBy`, `Skip` and `Take` are allowed there; the same navigation may only
be filtered one way per query; and the loaded collection is now *incomplete* —
if the entity is tracked and you call `SaveChanges`, EF does not conclude that
the missing loans were deleted, but any code that reads `member.Loans.Count`
downstream is reading a filtered count and will be wrong.

That last point is why filtered includes belong on read paths that end
immediately in a DTO.

## ex7 - ExecuteUpdate and IgnoreQueryFilters

`ExecuteUpdateAsync` compiles to a single `UPDATE ... WHERE` and returns the
affected row count, which is both your write and your existence check.
Nothing is loaded, nothing is tracked, and — importantly — nothing in the
change tracker is updated either, which is the `d13` lesson restated.

The subtle half is the global query filter. `db.Books` means "books where not
withdrawn", everywhere, including in the `Where` of your `ExecuteUpdate` (which
is what makes the call idempotent) and including in the count you run
afterwards, which is what makes it return zero. `IgnoreQueryFilters()` is the
escape hatch, and it is all-or-nothing for the query it is applied to.

## ex8 - keyset paging

`Skip(page * size)` makes the database produce and discard every preceding
row: page 1 is instant, page 900 is a table scan. Keyset paging says "give me
the rows after this position in this order", which is an index seek at any
depth: `Where(l => l.TakenAt < t || (l.TakenAt == t && l.Id < id))`.

The composite comparison is required because `TakenAt` is not unique; the tie
break on the key is what makes the order total and the cursor unambiguous. The
"is there a next page" trick is to `Take(size + 1)` and check whether you got
the extra row, which costs nothing compared with a second `COUNT(*)`.

Keyset paging cannot jump to an arbitrary page number, and that is its only
real drawback. For an infinite scroll or an API cursor it is strictly better.

## challenge - correlated subqueries in a projection

Everything in `BranchReport` is expressible as a subquery over the branch:
`b.Books.SelectMany(x => x.Copies).SelectMany(c => c.Loans).Count(l =>
l.ReturnedAt == null)` for the open loans, and an ordered `Take(3)` projection
for the titles. EF translates the inner sequence into a lateral join, so the
whole report is one command.

`TagWith("v3db01-report")` prepends a SQL comment to the generated command.
It survives into the database's query store and every slow-query log, which
turns "which of our four hundred SELECTs is this" into a text search. Tag
anything expensive.

## review1 - Any, and the three outcomes

`AnyAsync` stops at the first matching row; `CountAsync() > 0` counts them
all. On an unindexed large table that is the difference between a seek and a
scan, and there is no case where the count version is better.

The three-way answer — 404, 410, 200 — needs one query that ignores the
global filter, because "withdrawn" and "does not exist" are different facts
and the filter erases the distinction. Project the withdrawn flag into the
result and branch on it in C#: one round trip, three outcomes.

## Further reading

- [Efficient querying](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/performance/efficient-querying) — projections, pagination, tracking and the N+1 discussion.
- [Single vs. split queries](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/querying/single-split-queries) — cartesian explosion, `AsSplitQuery`, and the consistency trade.
- [Tracking vs. no-tracking queries](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/querying/tracking) — identity resolution and when to ask for it.
- [Client vs. server evaluation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/querying/client-eval) — what throws, and how to opt into client evaluation deliberately.
- [ExecuteUpdate and ExecuteDelete](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/saving/execute-insert-update-delete) — set-based writes and their relationship with the change tracker.
- [Global query filters](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/querying/filters) — soft delete, multi-tenancy, and `IgnoreQueryFilters`.

# V3·DB1 — Query shapes, tracking, and the N+1 you ship by accident

The deep version of this sector. Everything below assumes you have read the
briefing and want the mechanism rather than the instruction.

## The pipeline, end to end

When you write `db.Books.Where(b => b.Author == author).Select(b => b.Title)`,
nothing database-shaped happens. `DbSet<Book>` implements `IQueryable<Book>`,
which carries two things: an `Expression` and an `IQueryProvider`. Each LINQ
operator wraps the existing expression in a new `MethodCallExpression` and
hands it back. You are building a syntax tree.

Enumeration triggers the provider. EF Core then:

1. **Normalises** the tree — evaluating any subexpression that does not depend
   on a query parameter (this is why a captured local variable becomes a SQL
   parameter, and why `DateTime.Now` inside a query is evaluated once on the
   client rather than becoming `GETDATE()`).
2. **Translates** it to a provider-agnostic `SelectExpression`, then to SQL.
   Anything it cannot translate raises `InvalidOperationException`.
3. **Caches** the plan keyed by the shape of the tree. Two calls that differ
   only in parameter values reuse the plan; two calls that differ structurally
   do not, which is why building predicates with `if` branches can quietly
   fill the query cache.
4. **Executes**, and runs a generated *shaper* over the `DbDataReader` to
   build your objects.

The shaper is where tracking, identity resolution and include-fixup happen.
It is worth knowing that the shaper is compiled once per query shape, not
interpreted per row.

## Projection versus Include

```csharp
// Include: full entities, tracked, every mapped column, graph fixup.
var book = await db.Books
    .Include(b => b.Copies)
    .FirstOrDefaultAsync(b => b.Id == id);

// Projection: exactly these columns, no entity, no tracking, no fixup.
var row = await db.Books
    .Where(b => b.Id == id)
    .Select(b => new BookDetail(b.Title, b.Copies.Count()))
    .FirstOrDefaultAsync();
```

The decision rule is boring and reliable: **if the request will write, load
entities; if the request will render, project.** Include on a read path costs
you every column of every row (including the 40 KB `Body` you did not want),
a tracking snapshot per entity, and the fixup pass.

A projection also survives schema growth better. Adding a column to `Book`
changes what `Include` transfers and does not change what `Select` transfers.

## The two N+1s, with SQL

Loop flavour:

```csharp
var books = await db.Books.Where(b => b.BranchId == id).ToListAsync();
foreach (var book in books)
    total += book.Copies.Count;   // lazy load: one SELECT each
```

```
SELECT ... FROM Books WHERE BranchId = @id
SELECT ... FROM Copies WHERE BookId = 1
SELECT ... FROM Copies WHERE BookId = 2
...
```

Include flavour:

```csharp
var book = await db.Books
    .Include(b => b.Copies)
    .Include(b => b.Reviews)
    .FirstAsync(b => b.Id == id);
```

```
SELECT b.*, c.*, r.*
FROM Books b
LEFT JOIN Copies c ON ...
LEFT JOIN Reviews r ON ...
WHERE b.Id = @id           -- copies × reviews rows
```

Twelve copies and forty reviews is 480 rows, each carrying the whole book row.
Add a third collection and it multiplies again. `AsSplitQuery()` turns it into
three commands with the correct row counts.

## Identity resolution

```csharp
var a = await db.Books.AsNoTracking().ToListAsync();
// a[0].Branch and a[1].Branch are different objects with equal data

var b = await db.Books.AsNoTrackingWithIdentityResolution().ToListAsync();
// b[0].Branch and b[1].Branch are the same reference
```

Tracked queries always resolve identity, because the change tracker *is* the
identity map. The no-tracking variant that resolves identity keeps a private
map for the query and discards it. Cost: one dictionary. Benefit: no
duplicated subgraphs in your JSON, and no possibility of two "copies" of one
row disagreeing after you mutate one.

## Common mistakes

- **`ToList()` then `Where`.** The commonest and the most expensive. Search
  your codebase for `ToListAsync()` followed by LINQ on the next line.
- **`Count() > 0` instead of `Any()`.** Also `Count()` when you wanted
  `Count(predicate)`, which loads nothing but scans everything.
- **`ToLower()`/`ToUpper()` in a predicate.** Kills index usage. Fix the
  collation or use `EF.Functions.Like`.
- **`Include` on a read endpoint.** Then wondering why the payload is 4 MB.
- **Ignoring the global query filter.** Soft-deleted rows are invisible until
  the day you need to count them, and then they are still invisible.
- **`Skip`-based paging on a growing table.** Fine on page 1, a scan on page
  900, and it silently duplicates or skips rows when the underlying data
  changes between requests.
- **A `DateTime.UtcNow` inside the query expecting `GETUTCDATE()`.** It is
  evaluated on the client and parameterised, which is usually what you want
  but is not what you said.
- **Assuming `AsNoTracking` makes the query faster.** It removes snapshot and
  fixup cost, which is real but small next to transferring columns you did not
  need.

## Interview answer

> *"How would you find and fix an N+1 in an EF Core service?"*

Say this: first, prove it. Turn on `Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database
.Command` at Information level, or attach a `DbCommandInterceptor`, and count
commands per request — an assertion on command count in an integration test is
how you stop it coming back. Then classify: many small queries means a
navigation touched in a loop, and the fix is a projection with correlated
aggregates or a single `Include`; one enormous query means sibling collection
includes producing a cross product, and the fix is `AsSplitQuery` or, better,
projecting only the fields the response needs. Mention that you would tag the
expensive query with `TagWith` so the next person finds it in the slow-query
log, and that lazy-loading proxies are the version of this bug that does not
appear in the source at all.

That answer covers detection, classification, two fixes, a regression test and
an operational hook. Most candidates say "use Include".

## Check yourself

1. What exactly does `db.Books.Where(...)` return, and how many round trips
   has it cost?
2. Why does moving `ToListAsync()` one line earlier change the meaning of the
   code that follows it, with no compiler warning?
3. Give one predicate that translates and one that throws, and explain the
   difference in terms of the expression tree.
4. In what situation is `AsSplitQuery` the wrong answer?
5. What does `AsNoTrackingWithIdentityResolution` keep, and for how long?
6. Two collection includes on one root produce how many rows, given `m` and
   `n` children?
7. Why does `ExecuteUpdate` leave already-tracked entities stale, and what
   should you do about it?
8. Your global query filter hides soft-deleted rows. Which three places does
   it silently apply that surprise people?
9. Write the keyset predicate for a descending sort on a non-unique column.
10. How do you know whether there is a next page without a second query?
11. Why is `Count() > 0` worse than `Any()` even when the table is small?
12. When is a compiled query (`EF.CompileAsyncQuery`) worth the ceremony?
13. What does `TagWith` change about the generated SQL, and where does it
    show up?
14. Your endpoint returns the right JSON and issues 340 queries. Which test
    would have caught it?

# Reading - dotnet/v3db01_query_shapes

## Why the abstraction leaks on purpose

Entity Framework is often described as a leaky abstraction, usually as a
complaint. It is more useful to read the leaks as deliberate. An ORM that
successfully hid the database would have to make the performance decisions for
you, and there is no universally right answer to "should this be one query or
three". So EF Core exposes the seams — `AsSplitQuery`, `AsNoTracking`,
`IgnoreQueryFilters`, `TagWith`, `ExecuteUpdate` — and expects you to know
what you are asking for. Every one of those methods exists because a team hit
a wall that the default could not have avoided.

The history matters for one of them in particular. EF Core 1.x and 2.x would
*silently* evaluate an untranslatable `Where` on the client: the provider
translated as much as it could, pulled the intermediate result into memory and
finished the job with LINQ to Objects. It logged a warning. Nobody read the
warning. The failure mode was an endpoint that worked perfectly in
development, where the table had 200 rows, and pulled 40 million rows in
production. EF Core 3.0 made it a hard error, which broke a great deal of code
and was unambiguously the right decision. The only client evaluation left is
in the final `Select`, where it is explicit and bounded.

## What translation actually does

The translator walks your expression tree and tries to map each node to a SQL
construct. It is not a general-purpose compiler; it is a pattern matcher with
a large but finite table of known methods. `string.Contains` is in the table.
`Regex.IsMatch` is not. `DateTime.AddDays` is (on most providers).
`MyHelper.Normalise` never will be, because the translator cannot see inside a
compiled method body — it only has the `MethodCallExpression` node naming it.

This is why the standard advice "extract the predicate into a helper" breaks
queries. `Where(b => IsRecent(b))` fails; `Where(IsRecent())` where the helper
returns `Expression<Func<Book,bool>>` works, because now you are handing over
a tree rather than a delegate. That distinction — `Func<T,bool>` versus
`Expression<Func<T,bool>>` — is the single most useful thing to understand
about writing reusable query fragments, and it is what libraries like
LinqKit exist to paper over.

Parameterisation deserves a note too. A captured variable becomes a SQL
parameter, which is good: the plan is reused and the value cannot be an
injection. A constant written inline becomes a literal in some cases, which is
worse for plan reuse. And a value that varies structurally — `if (x)
query = query.Where(...)` — produces a genuinely different tree and therefore
a different cache entry. A handful of optional filters is fine. Twenty
optional filters is 2²⁰ possible plans and a query cache that never hits;
`EnableServiceProviderCaching` and the query cache size are both things you
can end up tuning because of a "flexible search" endpoint.

## The cost model

It helps to have rough numbers in your head.

- **Round trips dominate at small sizes.** A query that returns 10 rows costs
  a network round trip plus a plan lookup — call it half a millisecond on a
  local network, five on a cross-AZ one. Three hundred of them is a second and
  a half of doing nothing.
- **Bytes dominate at large sizes.** A cartesian explosion does not add round
  trips; it adds rows. Twelve copies × forty reviews × a 2 KB book row is a
  megabyte to answer a request whose useful payload is four kilobytes.
- **Tracking dominates at large row counts in memory.** Every tracked entity
  gets a snapshot — a second copy of its scalar properties — and every
  `SaveChanges` walks all of them. Loading 50,000 tracked entities to render a
  report is measurable in both allocation and time; the same query with
  `AsNoTracking` is meaningfully cheaper, and with a projection cheaper again.
- **Materialisation dominates for wide rows.** The shaper is compiled, so it
  is fast, but it still constructs an object per row and a string per text
  column. `Select`ing three columns instead of thirty is the cheapest
  optimisation available in the entire framework.

The order to attack a slow endpoint in: reduce round trips, then reduce
columns, then reduce rows, then think about indexes, then think about
caching. People usually start at caching.

## Compiled queries, and when they matter

`EF.CompileAsyncQuery` skips the tree-shape lookup and translation cache
probe by handing you a delegate that goes straight to execution:

```csharp
private static readonly Func<V3Db01Db, int, Task<Book?>> ByIdQuery =
    EF.CompileAsyncQuery((V3Db01Db db, int id) =>
        db.Books.FirstOrDefault(b => b.Id == id));
```

The saving is the cache probe, which is on the order of tens of microseconds.
That is irrelevant next to a 3 ms query and highly relevant in a hot loop
running a million times — a background reconciliation job, say. Use it there
and nowhere else; the ceremony (a static field, an explicit context parameter,
no dynamic composition) is real.

## Streaming versus buffering

`ToListAsync()` buffers: the whole result is in memory before your code sees
row one, and the connection is released. `AsAsyncEnumerable()` streams: rows
arrive as you consume them and the connection stays open for the duration.

Streaming is right when the result is large and you are writing it out
somewhere — a CSV export, a message queue. It is wrong when you are going to
issue other queries while consuming, because the connection is busy, and it is
wrong when the consumer is slow, because you are holding a database connection
open at the speed of your slowest client. The default should stay
`ToListAsync`; reach for streaming with a reason.

## Where the query filter bites

Global query filters (`modelBuilder.Entity<Book>().HasQueryFilter(b =>
!b.Withdrawn)`) are the cleanest implementation of soft delete and
multi-tenancy available, and they have three sharp edges.

First, they apply to *navigations* too, so a `Branch` you load will have its
withdrawn books missing from `branch.Books` with no indication. Second, they
apply to the `Where` of an `ExecuteUpdate` or `ExecuteDelete`, which is
usually what you want and occasionally hides rows you meant to fix. Third,
`IgnoreQueryFilters()` is all-or-nothing per query: with several filters
defined you cannot switch off one of them, so a multi-tenant filter plus a
soft-delete filter means "show me deleted rows" also means "show me every
tenant's rows". That is a genuine footgun and the reason some teams keep
tenancy out of query filters and in an explicitly applied extension method.

## When not to use any of this

Reporting is the honest boundary. Once a query has four levels of grouping,
window functions and a pivot, the LINQ that produces it will be longer, harder
to read and slower than the SQL. Put it in a view or a `FromSql` call against
a keyless entity type and stop fighting. EF is excellent at "load, change and
save an object graph" and very good at "project a shape for an API response".
It is not a query generator for analysts.

The same applies to bulk work. `ExecuteUpdate` and `ExecuteDelete` cover
set-based single-table changes; beyond that — merging a million rows, copying
between tables — use the database's own tools. Loading a million entities to
change one column is the mistake this whole sector is about, and the fact that
it is *possible* is exactly why the abstraction has to leak.

## Exercise 1 — deferred execution is the whole point

Edit `src/Api/V3DB01_QueryShapes/Ex1.cs`. Implement `ListBooks` so that
`GET /v3db01/books?city={city}` answers **200** with a JSON array of
`BookRow` — `id`, `title`, `author`, `copyCount` — covering every book whose
branch is in `city`, ordered by title A–Z. An unknown city is an empty array,
not a 404.

For the seeded data, `GET /v3db01/books?city=Leeds` answers:

```json
[
  {"id":3,"title":"Ariadne","author":"Saint","copyCount":2},
  {"id":1,"title":"Piranesi","author":"Clarke","copyCount":4}
]
```

The shipped version materialises the whole table first and then filters. Two
constraints from the gate: exactly **one** SQL command, and **no `Book`
entity may be materialised** — the change tracker must be empty afterwards.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db01_query_shapes ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Look at where `ToListAsync()` sits relative to the `Where`. Everything before
it is a description of SQL; everything after it is C# running over rows you
have already paid to fetch. The compiler cannot tell you which `Where` you
called because both exist.

## Hint 2

An `IQueryable` can be composed freely before you enumerate it:

```csharp
var q = db.Copies.Where(c => c.Condition == "good");
q = q.OrderBy(c => c.Barcode);
var rows = await q.Select(c => new { c.Id, c.Barcode }).ToListAsync();
```

One command, and the anonymous type means no `Copy` is ever constructed.

## Hint 3

Filter on the navigation (`b.Branch.City == city`), order, then `Select` into
`BookRow`, and only then await the terminal operator. The count you need is
expressible inside the projection — decide whether you write it as
`b.Copies.Count()` or as a subquery over `db.Copies`; both translate, one is
shorter.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the gate's second constraint rather than the first. "No `Book`
entity is materialised" rules out every solution that ends in a list of
entities, however efficient — including `Include`. That leaves exactly one
family of answers.

## Hint 2

A projection into a DTO is never tracked, because there is no entity to
track. That is not a flag you set; it falls out of the fact that `BookRow` is
not an entity type. So the shape of the answer is fixed:

```csharp
.Select(x => new SomeRow(/* … */))
```

and the only question is what goes before the `Select`.

## Hint 3

Filtering by a related table's column does not need a `Join` — EF turns
`b.Branch.City == city` into one for you. Order before you project or after;
both translate, and it is worth running the gate with `TagWith` attached once
to read the SQL either way.

## Exercise 2 — the filter that could not be translated

Edit `src/Api/V3DB01_QueryShapes/Ex2.cs`. Implement `Search` so that
`GET /v3db01/search?term={term}` answers **200** with the matching `BookRow`s
ordered by title, and **400** when `term` is null, whitespace, or shorter than
two characters after trimming.

Matching is a case-insensitive substring test against the title:
`term=ria` matches both `Piranesi` and `Ariadne`; `term=ARIA` matches
`Ariadne`.

The shipped version uses `Regex.IsMatch` inside the `Where`, which the
translator cannot handle — run the gate once and read the exception, it is a
good one. Replace it with a predicate the provider can turn into SQL. The gate
requires one command, and asserts that the command returns only matching rows
rather than filtering afterwards.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db01_query_shapes ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The translator is a pattern matcher over a table of known methods, not a
compiler. It cannot see inside `Regex.IsMatch`; all it has is a node saying
"call this method". A handful of `string` methods *are* in the table, and one
of them is exactly a substring test.

## Hint 2

Both of these translate to `LIKE`:

```csharp
db.Members.Where(m => m.Email.EndsWith("@example.com"))
db.Members.Where(m => EF.Functions.Like(m.Email, "%@example.com"))
```

The second spells out the pattern, which matters when you care about which
wildcards reach the database.

## Hint 3

Guard first — trim, check the length, return `TypedResults.BadRequest` — then
one query with a translatable predicate, an `OrderBy` and the projection from
ex1. Resist adding `ToLower()` on both sides; think about whose job case
folding is, and what it does to an index.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ignore the regex entirely and ask a different question: if you were writing
this by hand in SQL, what would the `WHERE` clause say? Write that clause down
first. Now find the LINQ that produces it.

## Hint 2

The exception message names the exact expression it gave up on. That is the
fastest debugging loop available here: change one thing, run, read. Note also
that the gate's `ARIA` case passes on a case-insensitive collation without any
help from you — the seeded database uses one.

## Hint 3

Two guards, one query. The 400 has three triggers (null, whitespace, too
short) and `string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace` plus a length check on the trimmed
value covers all three. Then decide between `Contains` and
`EF.Functions.Like`; either passes, and one of them tells the next reader
exactly what SQL to expect.

## Exercise 3 — N+1, the loop flavour

Edit `src/Api/V3DB01_QueryShapes/Ex3.cs`. Implement `Shelf` so that
`GET /v3db01/branches/{id}/shelf` answers **404** for an unknown branch and
otherwise **200** with a `ShelfReport`:

```json
{
  "branch": "Leeds Central",

    {"title":"Ariadne","copyCount":2,"onLoanCount":1},
    {"title":"Piranesi","copyCount":4,"onLoanCount":0}
  ]

```

`onLoanCount` is the number of loans on that book's copies with no
`ReturnedAt`. Books are ordered by title A–Z.

The shipped version loads the books and then reads `book.Copies.Count` inside
a `foreach`. The gate allows **at most two** SQL commands for the success

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db01_query_shapes ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The `foreach` looks like it is reading data that is already in memory. It is
not: `book.Copies` was never loaded, so each read either fires a query or —
with lazy loading off, which is the default here — hands you an empty
collection and a confidently wrong `0`.

## Hint 2

An aggregate over a navigation belongs inside the projection, where it becomes
a correlated subquery:

```csharp
.Select(m => new
{
    m.Name,
    Open = m.Loans.Count(l => l.ReturnedAt == null),
})
```

That is one command regardless of how many members there are.

## Hint 3

You need the branch name and the 404, which is one command, and the rows,
which is the second. Going two levels deep — from a book to its copies to
their loans — is a `SelectMany` inside the projection, or a nested `Sum` over
the copies. Both translate; pick the one you would want to read in six
months.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Count the commands before you write anything. Write down, in English, the
minimum number of times the database must be asked something to produce this
response. The answer is two, and knowing that tells you the shape.

## Hint 2

The 404 does not need its own existence query if the first command already
fetches the branch name — `FirstOrDefaultAsync` on a projection of the branch
gives you both facts at once:

```csharp
var name = await db.Branches
    .Where(x => x.Id == id)
    .Select(x => x.Name)
    .FirstOrDefaultAsync();
if (name is null) return TypedResults.NotFound();
```

## Hint 3

For the second command, start from `db.Books.Where(b => b.BranchId == id)` and
project. The nested count has two spellings —
`b.Copies.SelectMany(c => c.Loans).Count(l => l.ReturnedAt == null)` and

generate different SQL. Try both and look.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — one query is not always the cheap one

Edit `src/Api/V3DB01_QueryShapes/Ex4.cs`. Implement `Detail` so that
`GET /v3db01/books/{id}/detail` answers **404** for an unknown book and
otherwise **200** with a `BookDetail`:

```json
{
  "title": "Piranesi",
  "barcodes": ["LC-0001","LC-0002","LC-0003","LC-0004"],
  "reviews": [{"stars":5,"body":"Extraordinary."},{"stars":4,"body":"Odd and good."}]
}
```

Barcodes ascend; reviews are newest first by `PostedAt`.

The shipped version `Include`s `Copies` and `Reviews` in one query. Read the
SQL it generates and count the rows: with 4 copies and 2 reviews the database
returns 8 rows, and the multiplication does not stop there. Fix it so the
database is asked for the two collections separately.

The gate allows **at most three** commands and asserts that no single command
returns more rows than the larger collection has members.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db01_query_shapes ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two collection `Include`s on one root become two `LEFT JOIN`s, and a join of
`m` rows against `n` rows is `m × n` rows. EF stitches them back correctly;
the cost is entirely on the wire and in the join.

## Hint 2

There is a per-query switch that turns one command with joins into one command
per collection, correlated by the root key:

```csharp
var order = await db.Orders
    .Include(o => o.Lines)
    .Include(o => o.Payments)
    .AsSplitQuery()
    .FirstOrDefaultAsync(o => o.Id == id);
```

Three commands, `1 + m + n` rows.

## Hint 3

Either answer passes: `AsSplitQuery` with includes, or a projection whose
sub-selects EF issues separately. If you take the include route remember that
ordering inside an include is its own syntax; if you take the projection route
remember that a projected `Select` on a collection is ordered where you say so
and nowhere else.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask what the response actually needs: four strings and two small objects.
Nothing in it requires a `Copy` or a `Review` to exist as an object. That
observation makes the include question optional rather than central.

## Hint 2

A projection can contain collections, and each one becomes its own correlated
sub-select:

```csharp
.Select(o => new
{
    o.Reference,
    Lines = o.Lines.OrderBy(l => l.Sku).Select(l => l.Sku).ToList(),
})
```

No `Include`, no joins between siblings, no cross product.

## Hint 3

Whichever route you take, the 404 and the payload should come from the same
command — `FirstOrDefaultAsync` over the projection gives you `null` for
"no such book" without a separate existence check. Then decide where the two
orderings live.

## Exercise 5 — identity resolution, and why your JSON tripled in size

Edit `src/Api/V3DB01_QueryShapes/Ex5.cs`. Implement `Catalogue` so that
`GET /v3db01/catalogue` answers **200** with a `CatalogueReport`:

```json
{
  "branchInstances": 2,
  "books": [
    {"title":"Ariadne","branch":"Leeds Central"},
    {"title":"Piranesi","branch":"Leeds Central"},
    {"title":"Small Things Like These","branch":"Bristol Harbour"}
  ]
}
```

Books are ordered by title. `branchInstances` is the number of **distinct
object references** among the loaded books' `Branch` navigations — count them
with a `ReferenceEqualityComparer`-backed set, which `V3Db01Graph.CountBranches`
already does for you; pass it the loaded books.

Because you must hand `CountBranches` real entities, this is the one exercise
in the sector where a projection is not the answer. The gate seeds eight books
across two branches and requires `branchInstances` to be **2**, the change
tracker to be **empty**, and exactly **one** SQL command.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db01_query_shapes ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three constraints look contradictory: shared references, nothing tracked, one
query. They are not — one API gives you all three, and it is not the
`AsNoTracking` you already know.

## Hint 2

The identity map that makes two rows for branch 3 produce one `Branch` object
normally lives in the change tracker. A tracked query resolves identity for
free; `AsNoTracking` throws the map away along with everything else. There is
a third option that keeps the map for the duration of the query only.

## Hint 3

`Include` the branch so the navigation is populated, add the no-tracking
variant that resolves identity, order by title, and build both parts of the
report from the one loaded list. `CountBranches` takes the books; the rows are
a plain `Select` in memory over data you already have.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Run it once with plain `AsNoTracking()` and look at `branchInstances`. It will
be 8. That number is not a bug in your code — it is exactly what
"no change tracker" means, and understanding why is the whole exercise.

## Hint 2

Compare these three lines and predict the `branchInstances` for each before
running any of them:

```csharp
await db.Books.Include(b => b.Branch).ToListAsync();
await db.Books.Include(b => b.Branch).AsNoTracking().ToListAsync();
await db.Books.Include(b => b.Branch).AsNoTrackingWithIdentityResolution().ToListAsync();
```

Two of them give 2. Only one of them also leaves the tracker empty.

## Hint 3

Once the list is loaded the rest is ordinary C#: `V3Db01Graph.CountBranches(books)`
for the number, and a `Select` over the same list for the rows. Decide whether
you order in the database or in memory — one of those keeps the command count
honest and the other is a habit worth not forming.

Write the SQL you want first. It is a single select joining loans to copies to

## Exercise 7 — set-based writes, and the filter that hides your own rows

Edit `src/Api/V3DB01_QueryShapes/Ex7.cs`. Implement `Withdraw` so that
`POST /v3db01/authors/{author}/withdraw` marks every one of that author's
books `Withdrawn` and answers:

- **404** when the author currently has no un-withdrawn books;
- **200** otherwise, with a `WithdrawReport`:

```json
{"withdrawn":3,"totalWithdrawnForAuthor":5}
```

`withdrawn` is how many rows *this call* changed. `totalWithdrawnForAuthor` is
how many of that author's books are withdrawn now, including ones withdrawn
before this call.

Constraints: **at most three** commands, and no `Book` entity may be loaded or

```

```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two facts, one write. The write can tell you the first fact for free, and the
second fact needs you to ask a question the model has been quietly rewriting
for you on every query in this sector.

## Hint 2

A set-based update returns its row count:

```csharp
int changed = await db.Copies
    .Where(c => c.Condition == "poor")
    .ExecuteUpdateAsync(s => s.SetProperty(c => c.Condition, "withdrawn"));
```

That count is also your 404 signal — no separate existence check needed.

The count afterwards must see withdrawn rows, which the global filter hides.
There is a single method that switches filters off for one query; it is
all-or-nothing, which is fine here because `Book` has only the one filter.
Order matters: update first, then count.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Run the shipped version and stare at `totalWithdrawnForAuthor: 0` after a
successful withdrawal of three books. Nothing in your handler is wrong. The
lie is in the model, and it is applying to every `db.Books` in the file.

## Hint 2

Global query filters are appended to the `WHERE` of every query over that
entity type — including the `Where` of an `ExecuteUpdate`, which here is
actually useful: it stops you rewriting rows that are already withdrawn, so
the endpoint is naturally idempotent and `withdrawn` is honest on a second

## Hint 3

Three commands are allowed and you only need two: the update, and the count.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — paging that does not degrade on page 900

Edit `src/Api/V3DB01_QueryShapes/Ex8.cs`. Implement `Page` so that
`GET /v3db01/loans?size={n}&after={cursor}` answers **200** with a
`LoanPage`:

```json
{
  "loans": [ /* LoanRow, newest first */ ],
  "nextCursor": "638912736000000000_18"
}
```

Rules:

- Order is `takenAt` descending, then `loanId` descending.
- `size` must be 1–50 inclusive; anything else is **400**.
- `after` is optional. When present it must parse with
  `V3Db01Cursor.TryParse(string, out DateTime takenAt, out int loanId)`;
  a malformed cursor is **400**.
- `nextCursor` is `V3Db01Cursor.Format(lastRow)` when more rows exist, and
  `null` on the last page.

Constraints: **one** command per request, `Skip` is banned — the gate fails if
the generated SQL contains `OFFSET` — and you may not run a second query to
decide whether there is a next page.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db01_query_shapes ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`Skip(n)` asks the database to produce `n` rows and throw them away. Keyset
paging asks a different question: "the rows that come *after* this position in
this order". With an index on the sort columns that is a seek at any depth.

## Hint 2

With a two-column sort the predicate needs both columns, because the first one
is not unique:

```csharp
q = q.Where(x => x.Score < score || (x.Score == score && x.Id < id));
```

Strictly less on the leading column, or equal-and-strictly-less on the tie
break. Getting this wrong loses rows or repeats them.

## Hint 3

Ask for `size + 1` rows. If you get them, there is another page and the extra
row is not part of this one — trim it, and build the cursor from the last row
you are actually returning. If you get `size` or fewer, `nextCursor` is
`null`. That is the whole "is there more" mechanism, and it costs nothing.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Build the query in stages and only enumerate at the end. Start with the sort,
conditionally add the cursor predicate, then take. The optional `after`
parameter is the reason composition matters here: two shapes, one enumeration.

## Hint 2

Think about what makes a cursor *correct* rather than merely functional. It
has to encode a total order — a position no two rows share — otherwise a page
boundary that lands in the middle of a group of equal `takenAt` values either
drops rows or repeats them. That is why the cursor carries two values.

## Hint 3

Sequence: validate `size`; parse `after` if present, 400 if it will not parse;
`OrderByDescending(l => l.TakenAt).ThenByDescending(l => l.Id)`; add the
keyset `Where` when you have a cursor; `Take(size + 1)`; project; then decide
in C# whether to trim and what `nextCursor` is. The projection can go before
or after the `Take` — one of those makes `Format` easier to call.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — one query, three aggregates, and a tag you can grep for

Edit `src/Api/V3DB01_QueryShapes/Challenge.cs`. Implement `Report` so that
`GET /v3db01/report` answers **200** with a list of `BranchReport`:

```json
[
  {"name":"Leeds Central","openLoans":7,"topTitles":["Piranesi","Ariadne","Trust"]},
  {"name":"Bristol Harbour","openLoans":2,"topTitles":["Small Things Like These"]}
]
```

- `openLoans` — loans on copies of that branch's books with no `ReturnedAt`.
- `topTitles` — the three titles with the most loans of all time in that
  branch, ties broken by title A–Z. A branch with fewer than three books
  returns fewer than three titles.
- Branches are ordered by `openLoans` descending, then `name` A–Z.

The gate enforces three things:

1. **Exactly one** SQL command.
2. No grouping, sorting or `Take` performed in C# — the response must be
   correct if you serialise the query result directly.
3. The generated command text contains the tag `v3db01-report`.

Honest difficulty note: the aggregates are the easy half. The part that
catches people is that an ordered `Take(3)` over a projected collection is
legal inside a projection, and that the outer ordering has to reference the
same subquery you projected.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db01_query_shapes challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Everything in a `BranchReport` is a question about one branch, so everything
belongs inside one projection over `db.Branches`. Nothing here needs a
`GroupBy`; correlated subqueries do the whole job and read better.

## Hint 2

Walking two levels down inside a projection is `SelectMany`:

```csharp
.Select(b => new
{
    b.Name,
    Open = b.Books.SelectMany(x => x.Copies)
                  .SelectMany(c => c.Loans)
                  .Count(l => l.ReturnedAt == null),
})
```

EF turns that into a lateral join, still one command.

## Hint 3

For `topTitles`, order the branch's books by `x.Copies.SelectMany(c =>
c.Loans).Count()` descending then `x.Title`, `Take(3)`, and `Select(x =>
x.Title)`. For the outer sort you cannot order by the projected property name
before it exists — repeat the expression, or project into an intermediate and
sort that. One of those is one command and one is a mistake; find out which.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Do this in three passes, running the gate between each. Pass one: names only,
with the tag attached, and confirm you see one command. Pass two: add
`openLoans` and the outer ordering. Pass three: add `topTitles`. Debugging
three correlated subqueries at once is not a good time.

## Hint 2

`TagWith` is a query operator like any other and can go anywhere in the chain:

```csharp
db.Loans.TagWith("nightly-reconcile").Where(/* … */)
```

It prepends a `-- nightly-reconcile` comment to the SQL, which is what makes
the command findable in a slow-query log. It changes nothing else.

## Hint 3

The constraint "no sorting in C#" is the one to design around. If your final
statement is `rows.OrderByDescending(...)` you have failed it even though the
JSON is right. Keep the `OrderByDescending` on the `IQueryable`, before
`ToListAsync`, and accept that the open-loans expression will appear twice —
or hoist it by projecting first and sorting the projection, which is still one
command because the whole thing is still an expression tree.

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.prompt:
## Review 1 — three outcomes, one command

Edit `src/Api/V3DB01_QueryShapes/Review1.cs`. Implement `Availability` so that
`GET /v3db01/books/{id}/availability` answers:

- **404** when no book with that id exists at all;
- **410 Gone** when the book exists but is withdrawn;
- **200** otherwise, with an `Availability`:

```json
{"title":"Piranesi","hasFreeCopy":true,"openLoans":2}
```

`hasFreeCopy` is whether at least one copy of the book has no open loan.
`openLoans` counts the book's loans with no `ReturnedAt`.

Constraints: **one** SQL command, no entity materialised, and the existence
test must not scan more than it needs to. The interesting part is that the
global query filter erases the difference between "withdrawn" and "does not
exist" — and you need both.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db01_query_shapes review1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three outcomes from one query means the query has to return enough to
distinguish them. `null` gives you one outcome; the other two have to be a
field in the row.

## Hint 2

Suppressing the filter changes what `null` means:

```csharp
var row = await db.Books
    .IgnoreQueryFilters()
    .Where(b => b.Id == id)
    .Select(b => new { b.Title, b.Withdrawn })
    .FirstOrDefaultAsync();
```

Now `null` really is "no such row", and `Withdrawn` tells you the rest.

## Hint 3

Project title, the withdrawn flag, the open-loan count and the free-copy test
in one go, then branch in C#. For the free-copy test prefer the operator that
stops at the first match over the one that counts everything — and note that
"has a copy with no open loan" is an `Any` over copies containing an `All` or
a negated `Any` over loans.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Write down the three outcomes as three predicates over one hypothetical row,
before touching LINQ. If you cannot express "withdrawn" as a value in that
row, your query is not fetching enough.

## Hint 2

`Any()` short-circuits; `Count() > 0` does not. On a copy with 4,000
historical loans that is a seek versus a scan, and there is no situation where
the counting version is the better one. The same choice appears twice in this
handler — once for the free copy and once, if you write it carelessly, for the
open-loan count, which genuinely does need a count.

## Hint 3

`FirstOrDefaultAsync` over a projection that ignores query filters gives you
all three cases: `null` → 404, `Withdrawn` → `TypedResults.StatusCode(410)`,
otherwise 200 with the rest of the row. Decide whether you build the
`Availability` inside the projection or afterwards — one of those makes the
410 branch slightly awkward.

lessons.title: V3·DB2 — Mapping, owned types, value converters and inheritance
lessons.summary: Eight problems about the model, not the query: fluent configuration, owned types and the optional-owned null trap, value converters for strongly typed ids and JSON columns, the ValueComparer bug that silently drops your writes, discriminator-based inheritance, shadow properties and backing fields.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·DB2 — Mapping, owned types, value converters and inheritance

`v3db01_query_shapes` was about what EF sends. This sector is about what EF
*believes*, which is a different and older source of production incidents. The
model — the set of entity types, properties, keys, conversions and
relationships EF builds at startup — is inferred from your classes by
convention, then adjusted by whatever configuration you supply. Get an
inference wrong and nothing fails loudly. You get a nullable column where you
wanted a constraint, a `decimal(18,2)` where you wanted four decimal places, an
address that comes back `null` because every one of its fields happened to be
empty, or a list of tags you mutate and save and which is simply never
written.

That last one is the reason this sector exists. **A change EF does not detect
is a change that does not happen**, and there is no exception, no log line and
no failing test unless you wrote one.

Everything is under `/v3db02/...`. The entities, DTOs and the per-exercise
contexts live in `src/Api/V3DB02_MappingConversions/Model.cs` — given code,
read it first. The domain is billing: a `Customer` with a billing `Address`, an
`Invoice` with `Money` amounts and a `Tags` list, invoice `Line` items, and a
`PaymentMethod` hierarchy with `CardMethod`, `TransferMethod` and
`WalletMethod` subclasses.

Each exercise owns a private context — `Ex1Db`, `Ex2Db` and so on — whose
`OnModelCreating` calls `Ex1Model.Configure(modelBuilder)`. **You write that
static method**, in the same file as the endpoint. The gate creates the
schema from your model with `EnsureCreated` on a fresh SQLite database, so a
mapping mistake shows up as a wrong column, a wrong constraint, or a
round-trip that loses data.

Several gates read the model back rather than the data: `db.Model` is a
queryable object, and asking it what it believes is the fastest way to check
whether your configuration did what you meant.

## Exercise 1 — say it in the fluent API

Edit `src/Api/V3DB02_MappingConversions/Ex1.cs`. Configure `Invoice` so that:
`Reference` is required, at most 20 characters, and carries a **unique** index
named `IX_Invoice_Reference`; `Notes` is optional with no length limit; the
table is named `invoices`; and `Total` is `decimal(12,4)`.

`GET /v3db02/model/invoice` answers **200** with an `InvoiceMapping` built by
reading `db.Model` — table name, the reference column's max length and
nullability, its index name and uniqueness, and the total's column type. The
handler that reads the model is already written; your job is the
configuration.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db02_mapping_conversions ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — owned types share the table

Edit `src/Api/V3DB02_MappingConversions/Ex2.cs`. `Customer` has a `Billing`
property of type `Address` (`Line1`, `City`, `Postcode`). Map it as an owned
type stored in the customer's own table, with columns named
`billing_line1`, `billing_city`, `billing_postcode`, all required.

`POST /v3db02/customers` stores a customer and answers **201**;
`GET /v3db02/customers/{id}` answers **200** with the customer and its
address, or **404**. `GET /v3db02/model/customer` answers **200** with the
list of column names in the customers table, ascending — that is what the gate
checks first, because a passing round trip proves nothing about where the data
landed.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db02_mapping_conversions ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — the optional owned type that vanishes

Edit `src/Api/V3DB02_MappingConversions/Ex3.cs`. Same `Address`, now on
`Supplier.Registered`, and this time every column is **nullable** because the
address is optional in the domain.

Store a supplier whose address is `("", "", "")` — three empty strings, which
is a perfectly valid address as far as the domain is concerned — and read it
back. As shipped, `Registered` comes back `null` and the endpoint throws a
`NullReferenceException`.

`GET /v3db02/suppliers/{id}` must answer **200** with the supplier and the
address exactly as stored, and `GET /v3db02/suppliers/{id}/registered-null`
must answer **200** with `{"isNull":false}`. Fix the mapping, not the
handler.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db02_mapping_conversions ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — strongly typed ids

Edit `src/Api/V3DB02_MappingConversions/Ex4.cs`. `Account.Id` is an
`AccountId` — a readonly record struct wrapping an `int`. Configure a value
converter so it persists as a plain integer column, and make the key
generated by the database on insert.

`POST /v3db02/accounts` creates an account and answers **201** with the
assigned id; `GET /v3db02/accounts/{id:int}` answers **200** or **404**, and
must find the row with a translated `Where` — `a.Id == new AccountId(id)` —
not by loading everything.

The gate asserts the column's provider type is `int`, that the round trip
works, and that the lookup issues one command.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db02_mapping_conversions ex4
```

## Exercise 5 — the comparer, and the write that never happened

Edit `src/Api/V3DB02_MappingConversions/Ex5.cs`. `Invoice.Tags` is a
`List<string>`. Store it as a single JSON text column with a value converter
(`V3Db02Json.Serialise` / `Deserialise` are given).

`POST /v3db02/invoices/{id}/tags` appends a tag to the loaded invoice's list
and saves, answering **200** with the full tag list; **404** for an unknown
invoice; **409** when the tag is already present.

With only a converter, the append is never written: the snapshot and the
current value are the *same list object*, so change detection compares it with
itself and finds nothing. Supply the missing piece so mutation is detected.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db02_mapping_conversions ex5
```

## Exercise 6 — enums as text, and instants that stay UTC

Edit `src/Api/V3DB02_MappingConversions/Ex6.cs`. Configure `Payment.Status`
(an enum) to persist as its **name**, not its number, and `Payment.SettledAt`
(a `DateTime`) so that whatever `Kind` it arrives with, it is stored as UTC
and comes back with `Kind == DateTimeKind.Utc`.

`POST /v3db02/payments` stores a payment; `GET /v3db02/payments/{id}` answers
**200** with `status` as a string and `settledAtKind` as `"Utc"`, or **404**.
The gate posts a `DateTime` with `Kind == Local` and one with
`Kind == Unspecified` and requires both to survive as the same instant in UTC.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db02_mapping_conversions ex6
```

## Exercise 7 — one table, three kinds of payment method

Edit `src/Api/V3DB02_MappingConversions/Ex7.cs`. Map `PaymentMethod` and its
three subclasses as **table-per-hierarchy** in a table called
`payment_methods`, with a discriminator column named `kind` holding
`"card"`, `"transfer"` and `"wallet"`.

`POST /v3db02/methods` creates one of the three from a `MethodRequest`
(**400** for an unrecognised kind); `GET /v3db02/methods/cards` answers
**200** with only the card methods, fetched with a subtype query rather than
by loading everything and filtering; `GET /v3db02/model/methods` answers
**200** with the discriminator column name and its three values, ascending.

Subclass-only properties must be nullable columns in the shared table — think
about why that is forced on you, and what it costs.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db02_mapping_conversions ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — shadow properties and a collection nobody can corrupt

Edit `src/Api/V3DB02_MappingConversions/Ex8.cs`. `Basket` exposes
`IReadOnlyCollection<Line> Lines` over a private `_lines` field and an
`AddLine` method; there is no setter and no public `List<Line>`. Map the
collection through its backing field, and add a **shadow property**
`LastTouchedUtc` (a `DateTime`) that `Ex8Db.SaveChangesAsync` stamps on every
added or modified basket — the override is given, it just needs the property
to exist.

`POST /v3db02/baskets/{id}/lines` adds a line and answers **200** with the
line count; `GET /v3db02/baskets/{id}/touched` answers **200** with the shadow
value read via `EF.Property`, or **404**. Nothing may add a public setter to
`Basket`.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db02_mapping_conversions ex8
```

## Challenge — an aggregate that maps itself correctly

Edit `src/Api/V3DB02_MappingConversions/Challenge.cs`. Configure `Order` as a
single aggregate:

- `Order.Id` is an `OrderId` record struct, converted to `Guid`.
- `Order.Total` is a `Money` (`decimal Amount`, `string Currency`) mapped as
  an owned type into columns `total_amount` `decimal(18,4)` and
  `total_currency` `char(3)`, both required.
- `Order.Lines` is owned by the order but stored in its own table
  `order_lines`, keyed by `(OrderId, LineNo)`, with `Money` again inside each
  line.
- `Order.Status` persists as text, and the whole aggregate loads in **one**
  command.

`POST /v3db02/orders` creates an order and answers **201**;
`GET /v3db02/orders/{id}` answers **200** with the whole aggregate or **404**.
`GET /v3db02/model/orders` reports the two table names and the line table's
key columns.

The part that catches people: an owned collection needs a key, and the default
one EF invents for you is a shadow property you cannot address.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db02_mapping_conversions challenge
```

## Review

`review1` is not part of finishing this sector; the scheduler brings it back
later. Edit `src/Api/V3DB02_MappingConversions/Review1.cs`: map `Money` on
`Quote.Price` as a **complex type** rather than an owned type, and report
through `GET /v3db02/model/quote` what that changes — whether it can be null,
whether it has its own entity type, and what its columns are called. Be able
to say when you would pick each.
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - dotnet/v3db02_mapping_conversions

## Notes

**The model is built once, at startup, and cached.** `OnModelCreating` runs
the first time the context type is used in a process; the result is an
immutable `IModel` shared by every instance. That is why model building can be
expensive without mattering, why you cannot make mapping decisions per
request, and why `db.Model` is a perfectly reasonable thing to read in a
handler — you are reading a cached object, not doing work.

**Convention comes first, configuration second.** EF applies its conventions
to your CLR types, then runs your fluent configuration over the result. So
every configuration call is an *override*, and if a convention already did
what you wanted, your call is a no-op you should still write, because the
convention can change and the intent should be visible.

**Data annotations versus the fluent API.** Annotations are fine for a model
you own end to end. The fluent API wins the moment the entity classes are
shared with something that should not know about EF — a domain library, a
contract assembly — and it is the only place some things can be said at all:
composite keys, owned types, discriminator values, converters, comparers,
filtered indexes. Put configuration in `IEntityTypeConfiguration<T>` classes
and call `ApplyConfigurationsFromAssembly`; a 900-line `OnModelCreating` is a
smell with a known cure.

**Owned types are not entities.** An owned type has no identity of its own; it
is *part of* the owner. By default it is stored in the owner's table with
prefixed column names (table splitting), and it can never be loaded, tracked
or queried independently. That is a modelling statement, not a storage
optimisation: an `Address` has no meaning apart from the customer it belongs
to.

**Value converters change what is stored; they do not change semantics for
free.** `HasConversion` gives EF a pair of expressions, model-to-provider and
back. They are applied on read and on write, and — importantly — inside
translated queries, so `Where(a => a.Id == someId)` works. What a converter
does *not* give you is change detection for a mutable object, because EF's
default comparer for a converted type is reference equality. That is `ex5`.

**Inheritance is three strategies with three cost profiles.** TPH: one table,
a discriminator, subclass properties nullable, no joins, cheapest to query,
weakest at the constraint level. TPT: a table per type joined on the key,
clean constraints, a join per level on every query. TPC (EF 7+): a table per
concrete type, no joins and no nulls, but the key must be unique across
tables so database-generated identity is awkward. TPH is the default and is
right most of the time.

## ex1 - configuration as documentation

`IsRequired`, `HasMaxLength`, `HasColumnType`, `ToTable`, `HasIndex(...)
.IsUnique().HasDatabaseName(...)` are the vocabulary. What matters more than
the calls is that they are the *only* record of intent: a `string Reference`
with no configuration is `nvarchar(max)`, nullable in older conventions and
non-nullable under nullable reference types, and indexed not at all. None of
those defaults is wrong; all of them are accidental.

Reading it back through `db.Model.FindEntityType(typeof(Invoice))` is worth
doing once by hand. `GetTableName()`, `FindProperty("Reference")!
.GetMaxLength()`, `.IsNullable`, `GetIndexes()` — the metadata API is stable
and it is how you would write a startup assertion that a critical column never
silently becomes nullable.

## ex2 - table splitting

`builder.OwnsOne(c => c.Billing, a => { a.Property(x => x.Line1)
.HasColumnName("billing_line1").IsRequired(); ... })`. The columns live in
`customers`; there is no `addresses` table and no join. `Include` is neither
needed nor allowed — an owned reference is loaded with its owner always.

The gate checks the column names before it checks the round trip, because a
round trip passes even when EF has quietly created a second table with a
shadow foreign key, which is what happens if you configure it as a separate
entity by accident.

## ex3 - the optional-owned null trap

EF distinguishes "this owned value is absent" from "this owned value has
default fields" by checking whether **every** mapped column is null. There is
nowhere else to put the flag — table splitting means there is no separate row
whose existence could carry it. So an `Address("", "", "")` where every column
is nullable and the empty strings are stored as… empty strings, is fine; the
failure is when your properties are nullable and the value is genuinely all
nulls.

Two fixes, both legitimate. Mark the owned navigation required
(`.Navigation(c => c.Registered).IsRequired()`), which makes at least one
column non-nullable and the value always present. Or make one column non-
nullable so the presence flag has something to key on. The one thing not to
do is defend against `null` in every handler.

## ex4 - strongly typed ids

`HasConversion(id => id.Value, value => new AccountId(value))` is the whole
mechanism. The payoff is that `GetAccount(CustomerId id)` cannot be called
with an `AccountId`, which removes an entire class of bug that integer keys
invite.

Two details bite. First, a converted key is not, by default, understood as
database-generated; `ValueGeneratedOnAdd()` plus a converter works, but the
temporary-value handling means the id you read *before* `SaveChanges` is not
the real one. Second, `FindAsync` needs the model-side value, so you pass
`new AccountId(42)`, not `42` — a detail that produces a confusing exception
if you get it wrong.

## ex5 - ValueComparer, and the silent lost update

Change detection snapshots each property on load. For an ordinary `string` or
`int`, the snapshot is a copy and `!=` on the copy tells the truth. For a
converted `List<string>`, the snapshot is a *reference to the same list*, and
the default comparer is reference equality — so after `invoice.Tags.Add("x")`
the snapshot and the current value are equal, because they are the same
object. `SaveChanges` writes nothing and returns 0.

`SetValueComparer(new ValueComparer<List<string>>(
(a, b) => a!.SequenceEqual(b!),
v => v.Aggregate(0, (h, s) => HashCode.Combine(h, s.GetHashCode())),
v => v.ToList()))` supplies the three functions EF needs: equality, a hash,
and — the important one — a **snapshot function that deep-copies**. With a
real copy in the snapshot, the sequence comparison detects the append.

The alternative that avoids the whole problem is to make the property
immutable: replace the list rather than mutate it. Reference equality then
tells the truth by construction. EF 8's `ToJson()` mapping and `HasConversion`
with a comparer both work; knowing why the comparer is needed is the point.

## ex6 - converters for enums and instants

`HasConversion<string>()` on an enum stores the name. It costs a wider column
and a conversion; it buys a database you can read, and a value that survives
someone reordering the enum members. Almost always worth it.

The UTC converter is the standard one: `new ValueConverter<DateTime,
DateTime>(v => v.ToUniversalTime(), v => DateTime.SpecifyKind(v,
DateTimeKind.Utc))`. Note the asymmetry — going out, normalise; coming back,
*label*, because the database has no notion of kind and would otherwise hand
you `Unspecified`, which silently becomes local time the first time somebody
formats it. `DateTimeOffset` avoids this and is the better type where the
provider supports it.

## ex7 - TPH

`HasDiscriminator<string>("kind").HasValue<CardMethod>("card")...` names the
column and the values. Without it you get a `Discriminator` column holding
CLR type names, which works and turns any rename into a data migration.

Subclass properties must be nullable in the shared table because a transfer
row has no card expiry. That is TPH's real cost: you cannot put a `NOT NULL`
constraint on a property that is required *for one subtype*. If those
constraints matter, TPT gives them to you at the price of a join per query;
TPC gives them with no join at the price of key generation and of queries over
the base type becoming a `UNION ALL`.

`db.Set<PaymentMethod>().OfType<CardMethod>()` becomes `WHERE kind = 'card'`,
which is the query you want. `Where(m => m is CardMethod)` translates the same
way. Loading everything and filtering with `is` in C# does not.

## ex8 - shadow properties and backing fields

`builder.Property<DateTime>("LastTouchedUtc")` declares a property with no CLR
counterpart. It is in the model, in the table, and in the change tracker;
you read and write it with `EF.Property<DateTime>(entity, "LastTouchedUtc")`
or through the entry. Audit stamps are the canonical use: the domain class
stays clean and `SaveChanges` fills them in.

The backing field half is about encapsulation. `builder.Metadata
.FindNavigation(nameof(Basket.Lines))!.SetPropertyAccessMode(
PropertyAccessMode.Field)` tells EF to write `_lines` directly rather than go
through the read-only property, which lets the aggregate keep its invariants —
there is simply no public way to add a `Line` except `AddLine`, and EF is
happy anyway because it never uses the public surface.

## challenge - the owned collection's key

`OwnsMany(o => o.Lines, l => { l.ToTable("order_lines"); l.WithOwner()
.HasForeignKey("OrderId"); l.HasKey("OrderId", nameof(Line.LineNo)); ... })`.
Left alone, EF invents a shadow `Id` and makes it the key, which works until
you need to address a line or a migration renumbers them. Declaring the
composite key of owner plus line number says what the domain means.

Owned collections always load with their owner — they are part of the
aggregate — so the "one command" requirement is satisfied automatically. Money
inside a line is an owned type inside an owned type, which is legal and reads
exactly as you would hope.

## review1 - complex types

EF 8 added `ComplexProperty`, which is what owned types should have been for
value objects. A complex type has no key, no identity, cannot be null, is
never tracked separately, and cannot be the target of a navigation — it is
genuinely part of the owner, which is exactly what `Money` is. Owned types,
by contrast, are entity types with a hidden key, which is why they can be
null, why they can live in their own table, and why the `ex3` trap exists at
all.

Rule of thumb: value object with no independent lifetime → complex type;
something that is conceptually a child row → owned entity; something another
aggregate can reference → a real entity.

## Further reading

- [Creating and configuring a model](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/modeling/) — conventions, the fluent API and `IEntityTypeConfiguration<T>`.
- [Owned entity types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/modeling/owned-entities) — table splitting, optional owned navigations and owned collections.
- [Value conversions](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/modeling/value-conversions) — converter expressions, built-in converters and provider types.
- [Value comparers](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/modeling/value-comparers) — snapshotting, mutable values and the lost-update failure.
