- [Inheritance](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/modeling/inheritance) — TPH, TPT and TPC, with their query shapes.
- [Shadow and indexer properties](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/modeling/shadow-properties) — declaring them and reading them with `EF.Property`.
lessons.fullReadme:
# V3·DB2 — Mapping, owned types, value converters and inheritance

The deep version. The briefing tells you what to build; this tells you what
the model builder is doing while you do it.

## How the model gets built

`OnModelCreating` is not where the model is created. By the time it runs, EF
has already walked your `DbSet` properties, discovered reachable types,
inferred keys from `Id`/`<Type>Id` naming, inferred relationships from
navigation properties and foreign key names, inferred nullability from nullable
reference type annotations, and applied a long list of `IConvention`
implementations. Your fluent calls then edit that result, and afterwards a
second pass of conventions runs to fill in anything your edits implied.

This ordering explains several confusing behaviours. Configuring one side of a
relationship reconfigures the other. Declaring an owned type removes it from
the set of entity types EF would otherwise have discovered. And adding a
`DbSet<CardMethod>` to your context turns what was a TPH subtype into
something you can query directly — without changing the storage at all.

The finished `IModel` is immutable and cached against the context type plus
the model-configuration inputs. In a service that is once per process.

```csharp
var entity = db.Model.FindEntityType(typeof(Invoice))!;
Console.WriteLine(entity.GetTableName());
Console.WriteLine(entity.FindProperty(nameof(Invoice.Reference))!.GetMaxLength());
Console.WriteLine(entity.GetIndexes().Single().IsUnique);
```

Startup assertions over that metadata are cheap insurance for the properties
you truly cannot afford to get wrong — a tenant discriminator, a money
precision, a unique constraint.

## Owned types, in three configurations

```csharp
// 1. Table splitting (default): columns live in the owner's table.
builder.OwnsOne(c => c.Billing, a =>
{
    a.Property(x => x.Line1).HasColumnName("billing_line1").IsRequired();
    a.Property(x => x.City).HasColumnName("billing_city").IsRequired();
});

// 2. Its own table, still owned, still loaded with the owner.
builder.OwnsOne(c => c.Billing, a => a.ToTable("customer_addresses"));

// 3. A collection, which is always a separate table.
builder.OwnsMany(o => o.Lines, l =>
{
    l.ToTable("order_lines");
    l.WithOwner().HasForeignKey("OrderId");
    l.HasKey("OrderId", nameof(Line.LineNo));
});
```

All three share the defining property: the owned value has no independent
existence. You cannot `db.Set<Address>()`, you cannot load one without its
owner, and deleting the owner deletes it.

## The comparer, in full

```csharp
var converter = new ValueConverter<List<string>, string>(
    v => V3Db02Json.Serialise(v),
    v => V3Db02Json.Deserialise(v));

var comparer = new ValueComparer<List<string>>(
    (a, b) => a!.SequenceEqual(b!),                                   // equality
    v => v.Aggregate(0, (h, s) => HashCode.Combine(h, s.GetHashCode())), // hash
    v => v.ToList());                                                 // snapshot

builder.Property(i => i.Tags).HasConversion(converter, comparer);
```

Three functions, three jobs. The snapshot function is the one that fixes the
bug: without a deep copy, the "original value" EF keeps is the same object you
are about to mutate, so by the time it compares, both sides have your change.
The equality function then decides whether an UPDATE is emitted; the hash is
used when the value is part of a key or a `Distinct`.

## Common mistakes

- **Mutating a converted collection and expecting a write.** The headline bug
  of this sector. Either supply a comparer with a real snapshot function, or
  make the property immutable and assign a new instance.
- **An optional owned type whose columns are all nullable.** Comes back
  `null` when all fields are empty. Make the navigation required, or make one
  column non-nullable.
- **Using `Include` on an owned reference.** Unnecessary at best, an exception
  at worst; owned values always come with the owner.
- **Letting EF invent the discriminator.** You get CLR type names in the
  database and a data migration the day someone renames a class.
- **Filtering subtypes in C#.** `list.Where(m => m is CardMethod)` after a
  `ToListAsync` loads every method. `OfType<CardMethod>()` on the queryable is
  a `WHERE`.
- **`decimal` with no precision.** Provider default, usually `decimal(18,2)`,
  and your four-decimal FX rate silently rounds. Configure precision on every
  money and rate column.
- **Enums as ints because it is the default.** Then reordering the enum
  reinterprets historical rows.
- **`DateTime` without a UTC convention.** Comes back `Unspecified`,
  formats as local, and the bug appears twice a year.
- **A 900-line `OnModelCreating`.** Split into `IEntityTypeConfiguration<T>`
  and call `ApplyConfigurationsFromAssembly(Assembly.GetExecutingAssembly())`.

## Interview answer

> *"When would you use an owned type, and what is the catch?"*

Say: an owned type models a value object — an address, a money amount, an
audit stamp — something with no identity and no lifetime apart from its owner.
By default it is table-split into the owner's table with prefixed columns, so
there is no join and no separate entity to query, which matches the domain
meaning. The catch is that EF decides an *optional* owned value is absent by
checking whether all of its columns are null, because table splitting leaves
nowhere else to record presence. So an all-empty value object round-trips as
`null` and your code gets a `NullReferenceException` in production and not in
the test. The fixes are to mark the navigation required or to keep at least
one column non-nullable. Then add: in EF 8 and later, a value object with no
optionality is better modelled as a complex type, which has no key, cannot be
null, and cannot accidentally become a separate table.

That answer names the feature, the mechanism, the failure, two fixes and the
modern alternative.

## Check yourself

1. Where in the pipeline do your fluent calls run relative to conventions, and
   why does that make configuring one side of a relationship enough?
2. How does EF decide an optional owned value is `null`, and what is the
   cheapest fix?
3. Name three things you can only say in the fluent API.
4. What are the three functions of a `ValueComparer`, and which one fixes the
   mutable-collection bug?
5. Why does a converted key need care around `ValueGeneratedOnAdd`?
6. In TPH, why must subclass-only columns be nullable, and what would you
   change if that constraint mattered?
7. What SQL does `OfType<CardMethod>()` produce, and what does the C# `is`
   filter produce after `ToList`?
8. When is TPC the right choice, and what does it make awkward?
9. How do you read a shadow property, and name a real use for one.
10. What does `PropertyAccessMode.Field` buy an aggregate root?
11. What key does EF invent for an owned collection, and why would you replace
    it?
12. Contrast a complex type and an owned type in four words each.
13. Your `decimal` column silently rounds. What did you not configure?
14. How would you assert at startup that a column is still unique?
15. A converter is defined but `Where(x => x.Id == typedId)` throws. What is
    the most likely cause?
lessons.fullReading:
# Reading - dotnet/v3db02_mapping_conversions

## The model is a compiler output

It helps to stop thinking of `OnModelCreating` as configuration and start
thinking of it as a compilation step. You supply a set of CLR types and a set
of adjustments; EF produces an immutable `IModel` containing entity types,
properties, keys, foreign keys, indexes, conversions, comparers and query
filters, along with generated materialisation and comparison logic. That
output is cached and used for the life of the process.

The consequence is that mapping errors are *compile-time* errors in the sense
that matters: they happen once, at startup, before any request. Which is a
good property, and it is why `ValidateOnStart`-style thinking applies here
too. If a mapping is load-bearing — a tenant filter, a money precision, a
unique reference — assert it at startup by reading `db.Model`. It costs
microseconds and it converts a silent data-corruption class of bug into a boot
failure.

The other consequence is that anything you want to vary per request cannot
live in the model. A common attempt is a query filter that reads the current
user; it works, but only because the filter closes over a service resolved
from the same scope as the context, and the *shape* of the filter is fixed
forever at model build. Change the shape and you need a different model, which
means a different model cache key — `IModelCacheKeyFactory`. That is a real
extension point and it is a sign you have gone somewhere unusual.

## Where value converters sit

A converter is a pair of `Expression`s, not delegates. That distinction is the
whole reason converters work in queries: EF can splice the model-to-provider
expression into the SQL translation, so `Where(a => a.Id == id)` becomes
`WHERE id = @p0` with the converted value. Write a converter using a method
the translator cannot inline — say, one that calls into a service — and the
comparison fails to translate.

Converters also compose badly with a few things, and it is better to know
which. Ordering and comparison operators translate only if the provider
representation orders the same way as the model type; a converter from an enum
to a string makes `Where(x => x.Status > Status.Draft)` produce a *string*
comparison, which is nonsense. `LIKE` on a converted column is generally not
what you want. And a converted column cannot participate in some
provider-specific operations — a computed column that references it, for
instance — because the database has no idea a conversion exists.

The performance story is mild: one delegate invocation per value per direction
plus, for a JSON converter, a serialisation. That is invisible next to the
network round trip until you materialise a hundred thousand rows, at which
point serialising a JSON column per row is very visible indeed. EF 8's native
`ToJson()` mapping is faster because the provider does the work, and it also
gives you the ability to query inside the document, which a converter cannot.

## Snapshotting, and why the comparer is not optional

Change detection is a diff between a snapshot taken at materialisation and the
current values at `SaveChanges`. For scalar types the snapshot is a copy
because the values are copies — a `string` is immutable, an `int` is a value
type. The moment a property's CLR type is a mutable reference type, "take a
snapshot" becomes an ambiguous instruction, and EF's default answer is to
store the reference.

That default is not laziness. EF cannot know how to copy an arbitrary type,
and copying could be expensive or wrong. So it demands that you say so, and
the way you say so is the third argument of `ValueComparer`. The mistake
almost everyone makes once is to supply a comparer with an equality function
and a hash but leave the snapshot as the identity function, which fixes
nothing — the equality comparison is still between an object and itself.

The deeper lesson generalises past EF: **any diff-based system needs a copy,
and any system that stores a reference instead of a copy will report no
changes.** The same bug exists in React state, in Redux reducers, in any
immutable-comparison cache. Recognising the shape is worth more than
memorising the API.

## Inheritance: the honest comparison

TPH stores every subtype in one table. Queries over the base type are a single
select with no join; queries over a subtype add one predicate. Inserts touch
one table. The cost is nullable columns — a card expiry column that must be
null for every transfer row — and therefore no database-level guarantee that a
card has an expiry. Storage is cheap because null columns are cheap in most
engines; correctness is the thing you gave up.

TPT stores base columns in one table and each subtype's columns in its own,
joined by the shared key. Every column can be `NOT NULL` where the domain says
so. The cost is a join per level on every read and an insert into two tables
per write, and — the part that surprises people — a query over the base type
that needs subtype columns becomes a `LEFT JOIN` to every subtype table at
once. EF Core's TPT support is complete and its query performance is
frequently the reason teams migrate back to TPH.

TPC gives each concrete type its own complete table. No joins, no nulls, fast
subtype queries. Base-type queries become a `UNION ALL` across tables, and key
generation has to be unique across all of them, which rules out per-table
identity columns and pushes you towards sequences or GUIDs. It is the right
answer when subtype queries dominate and base-type queries are rare.

The default is TPH and the default is usually right. Change it when a
constraint you actually need is impossible, not because the nullable columns
are aesthetically displeasing.

## When not to model it in EF at all

Two boundaries are worth naming.

The first is when the persisted shape and the domain shape genuinely differ —
event sourcing, a document store shape, a heavily denormalised read model. You
can express a great deal with converters and owned types, and past a point you
are fighting. A separate persistence model with an explicit mapping layer is
more code and less surprise.

The second is the "flexible schema" pull: a `Dictionary<string, object>` of
custom fields, converted to JSON. It maps easily and it queries terribly,
because the database sees an opaque blob. EF 8's JSON columns help — you can
query into them and index them on some providers — but if those fields are
searched, filtered or aggregated regularly, they are columns, and the right
move is a migration rather than a converter.

Finally, resist configuring things you do not need. Every `HasColumnName` that
just restates the convention is a line someone has to read and a thing that
can drift. Configure what the domain requires — precision, required-ness,
uniqueness, conversions, inheritance — and let convention handle the rest.

exercises.title: Ex1
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 — say it in the fluent API

Edit `src/Api/V3DB02_MappingConversions/Ex1.cs`. Implement
`Ex1Model.Configure(ModelBuilder)` so the `Invoice` entity is mapped like
this:

- table `invoices`;
- `Reference` — required, `HasMaxLength(20)`, and a **unique** index named
  `IX_Invoice_Reference`;
- `Notes` — optional, no length limit;
- `Total` — column type `decimal(12,4)`.

`GET /v3db02/model/invoice` is already written. It reads `db.Model` and
answers **200** with:

```json
{
  "table": "invoices",
  "referenceMaxLength": 20,
  "referenceNullable": false,
  "notesNullable": true,
  "indexName": "IX_Invoice_Reference",
  "indexUnique": true,
  "totalColumnType": "decimal(12,4)"
}
```

Do not touch the handler. The gate also creates the schema and asserts that an
insert of a duplicate reference fails.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db02_mapping_conversions ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Every one of the seven facts in that JSON is one fluent call. Work down the
list and translate each into `builder.Entity<Invoice>()...` — the naming is
close enough to the English that guessing is usually right.

## Hint 2

Indexes are declared on the entity, not the property, and the two things the
gate wants are separate calls:

```csharp
builder.Entity<Member>()
    .HasIndex(m => m.Email)
    .IsUnique()
    .HasDatabaseName("IX_Member_Email");
```

## Hint 3

`ToTable`, `Property(...).IsRequired()`, `.HasMaxLength(20)`,
`.HasColumnType("decimal(12,4)")`, and the index chain above. `Notes` is
already optional by convention if it is a `string?` — write the call anyway
and think about why an explicit no-op is still worth the line.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Run the gate before writing anything and read what the current model believes.
Every wrong value in that JSON is a convention doing something reasonable in
the absence of instruction. Naming which convention produced each one is a
better use of five minutes than writing the fix immediately.

## Hint 2

`decimal` is the one where the default is actively dangerous. With no
`HasColumnType` or `HasPrecision`, the provider picks — typically
`decimal(18,2)` — and your four-decimal amounts round on the way in, with no
error. That is why the gate checks the column type rather than a round trip:
a two-decimal round trip of a two-decimal value passes on a broken mapping.

## Hint 3

Two spellings exist for precision — `HasColumnType("decimal(12,4)")` is
provider-specific and exact, `HasPrecision(12, 4)` is provider-agnostic and
usually produces the same thing. The gate asks for the column type string, so
pick accordingly, and know why you might prefer the other one in real code.

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — owned types share the table

Edit `src/Api/V3DB02_MappingConversions/Ex2.cs`. `Customer` has
`Address Billing { get; set; }` with `Line1`, `City` and `Postcode`.

Configure it as an owned type stored **in the customers table**, with columns
`billing_line1`, `billing_city` and `billing_postcode`, all required, and the
table named `customers`.

Implement three endpoints:

- `POST /v3db02/customers` — takes a `CustomerRequest`, stores it, answers
  **201** with the new id in the body and a `Location` header.
- `GET /v3db02/customers/{id:int}` — **200** with `{"id":…,"name":…,
  "billing":{"line1":…,"city":…,"postcode":…}}`, or **404**.
- `GET /v3db02/model/customer` — **200** with the customers table's column
  names, ascending:

```json
["billing_city","billing_line1","billing_postcode","id","name"]
```

The gate checks the column list first, because a passing round trip proves
nothing about where the data landed.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db02_mapping_conversions ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

An owned type is declared from the owner, and the lambda you pass configures
the owned value's properties. Nothing about it is a relationship you have to
wire up — no foreign key, no navigation on the other side, and no `Include`
when you load.

## Hint 2

The shape:

```csharp
builder.Entity<Order>().OwnsOne(o => o.Ship, a =>
{
    a.Property(x => x.Country).HasColumnName("ship_country").IsRequired();
});
```

If you find yourself writing `HasOne`/`WithOne` you have configured a second
entity type by mistake, and the gate's column list will show it.

## Hint 3

For the metadata endpoint, the columns you want are on the owner's entity type
plus the owned one — or, more simply, on the *table*:
`entity.GetTableMappings()` and `entity.GetDeclaredProperties()` are both
routes. One of them naturally includes the owned columns; find out which and
remember it.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask what "owned" means before writing any call. It means the value has no
identity: there is no `AddressId`, you can never load an address on its own,
and deleting the customer deletes it. Every API decision follows from that,
including why there is no `DbSet<Address>` and never will be.

## Hint 2

Prove the mapping before you trust the round trip. Add the metadata endpoint
first, run the gate, and look at the column names EF chose with no
configuration — they will be `Billing_Line1` and friends, in the customers
table, because table splitting with a prefix is the *default*. All you are
doing is renaming.

## Hint 3

For the write path, `Customer` needs a `Billing` assigned before `Add`;
required owned columns mean a null billing address is an insert failure rather
than three nulls. `TypedResults.Created($"/v3db02/customers/{id}", body)` gives
you the header and the body in one call.

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — the optional owned type that vanishes

Edit `src/Api/V3DB02_MappingConversions/Ex3.cs`. `Supplier` has
`Address Registered { get; set; }`, mapped as an owned type into the
suppliers table with columns `reg_line1`, `reg_city`, `reg_postcode`.

The gate stores a supplier whose address is `new Address("", "", "")` — three
empty strings — and then reads it back:

- `GET /v3db02/suppliers/{id:int}` must answer **200** with the address
  exactly as stored, or **404** for an unknown id;
- `GET /v3db02/suppliers/{id:int}/registered-null` must answer **200** with
  `{"isNull":false}`.

As shipped, the read throws a `NullReferenceException`, because EF decided
there was no address at all. Fix the **mapping**. Adding a null check to the
handler fails the gate.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db02_mapping_conversions ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Table splitting means the address has no row of its own, so there is nowhere
to record "an address is present". EF has to infer presence from the columns
themselves, and it has exactly one rule available.

## Hint 2

The rule is: if **every** mapped column of the owned value is null, the owned
value is null. Which means the question to ask is not "why is it null" but
"which of my three columns is allowed to be null, and why".

## Hint 3

Two mappings fix this and both are defensible. Declaring the navigation
required —

```csharp
builder.Entity<Supplier>().Navigation(s => s.Registered).IsRequired();
```

— or making at least one column non-nullable so the all-null case can never
occur. Pick one, and be able to say what it means for a supplier that
genuinely has no registered address.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The bug is not that empty strings become nulls. Check that first: store the
supplier, then query the raw table and look at what is actually in the three
columns. Knowing whether the data is wrong or the *interpretation* is wrong
changes which half of the stack you fix.

## Hint 2

This failure has a characteristic shape in the wild. It appears months after
launch, on one record, in production, because that customer left the address
fields blank — and it is unreproducible locally because your seed data always
has an address. Any value object with all-optional fields has it.

## Hint 3

Once the navigation is required, think about what EF now does on insert when
`Registered` is genuinely `null`: it throws, at `SaveChanges`, naming the
navigation. That is the behaviour you want, and it is the trade you are
making — "always present" is a modelling claim, and the alternative is to keep
it optional and handle `null` honestly everywhere. The gate wants the first.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — strongly typed ids

Edit `src/Api/V3DB02_MappingConversions/Ex4.cs`. `Account.Id` is an
`AccountId` — `public readonly record struct AccountId(int Value)`.

Configure it so that:

- the key persists as a plain `int` column named `id`;
- the value is generated by the database on insert;
- `db.Accounts.Where(a => a.Id == new AccountId(42))` translates to SQL.

Endpoints:

- `POST /v3db02/accounts` — takes `{"name":"…"}`, answers **201** with
  `{"id":7}` (the integer, not the wrapper's JSON shape);
- `GET /v3db02/accounts/{id:int}` — **200** with `{"id":7,"name":"…"}`, or
  **404**.

The gate asserts the provider clr type of the key is `System.Int32`, that the
insert assigns a non-zero id, and that the lookup issues exactly **one**
command.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db02_mapping_conversions ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A converter is a pair of expressions: model to provider, provider to model.
For a one-field wrapper both directions are one-liners, and because they are
*expressions* rather than delegates, EF can splice them into the SQL for a
comparison.

## Hint 2

```csharp
builder.Entity<Ticket>()
    .Property(t => t.Id)
    .HasConversion(id => id.Value, value => new TicketId(value));
```

That is the conversion. Database generation is a separate call on the same
property, and it is the one people forget.

## Hint 3

`HasColumnName("id")`, `HasConversion(...)`, `ValueGeneratedOnAdd()`. For the
lookup, wrap the route's `int` back into an `AccountId` before comparing, so
the expression tree has something the converter can transform. Then decide
whether to use `FindAsync` — and note what it wants as an argument.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The point of the type is the bug it prevents. Write down a signature that
takes two `int` ids and imagine transposing them; now write the same signature
with two wrapper structs. The conversion machinery exists purely so that
safety costs nothing at the storage layer.

## Hint 2

Watch the value you read *before* `SaveChangesAsync`. With database
generation, EF puts a temporary value in the property until the insert
returns, so logging `account.Id` too early gives you something meaningless.
Read it after the save.

## Hint 3

Two lookups both work and one is worth knowing about: `FirstOrDefaultAsync(a
=> a.Id == new AccountId(id))` and `FindAsync(new AccountId(id))`. The second
checks the change tracker first, and it needs the *model-side* value — passing
the raw `int` throws an argument exception that reads confusingly if you have
not seen it before.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — the comparer, and the write that never happened

Edit `src/Api/V3DB02_MappingConversions/Ex5.cs`. `Invoice.Tags` is a
`List<string>`, and it must persist as one JSON text column named `tags`.
`V3Db02Json.Serialise(List<string>)` and `V3Db02Json.Deserialise(string)` are
given.

`POST /v3db02/invoices/{id:int}/tags` takes `{"tag":"urgent"}` and:

- **404** when there is no such invoice;
- **409** when the invoice already carries that tag (case-insensitive);
- **200** otherwise, with the full tag list ascending, having appended the tag
  to the loaded invoice's `Tags` list and saved.

The obvious implementation — converter, `invoice.Tags.Add(tag)`,
`SaveChangesAsync()` — returns the right JSON and writes nothing. Re-read the
invoice in a new context and the tag is gone. Fix the model so the mutation is
detected; do not work around it by reassigning the property in the handler.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db02_mapping_conversions ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Change detection is a diff against a snapshot taken when the entity was
loaded. Ask what EF stored as the snapshot for a `List<string>`, and then ask
what comparing that snapshot with the current value can possibly tell it after
you mutate the list in place.

## Hint 2

`HasConversion` has an overload that takes a second argument:

```csharp
builder.Property(x => x.Items).HasConversion(converter, comparer);
```

A `ValueComparer<T>` is constructed from three expressions — equality, hash
code, and snapshot. Only one of the three is the fix.

## Hint 3

```csharp
new ValueComparer<List<string>>(
    (a, b) => /* … */,
    v => /* … */,
    v => v.ToList());
```

The third expression is what makes the original value a genuine copy. Fill in
the first two so that equality means "same items in the same order" and the
hash agrees with it — an inconsistent pair produces bugs that are much harder
to find than the one you are fixing.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Prove the bug before you fix it. Post a tag, then read the invoice back
through a *fresh* context — the one in the request scope will happily show you
the in-memory list you just mutated. `SaveChangesAsync` returning `0` is the
tell.

## Hint 2

There is a second, entirely valid fix that needs no comparer at all: make the
property immutable and assign a new list rather than mutating.

```csharp
invoice.Tags = invoice.Tags.Append(tag).ToList();
```

Reference equality now tells the truth, because the reference really did
change. The gate forbids this route here so that you meet the comparer — but
in real code it is often the better answer, and knowing why is the point.

## Hint 3

Write the comparer's three expressions in this order: snapshot
(`v => v.ToList()`), equality (`SequenceEqual`), hash (fold the elements'
hashes with `HashCode.Combine`). Then check the 409 rule — case-insensitive
membership is a `StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase` question, and it is not the
same comparer as the one EF needs.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — enums as text, and instants that stay UTC

Edit `src/Api/V3DB02_MappingConversions/Ex6.cs`. Configure `Payment` so that:

- `Status` (enum `PaymentStatus { Pending, Settled, Failed }`) persists as its
  **name**, in a column named `status`;
- `SettledAt` (a `DateTime`) is stored as UTC whatever `Kind` it arrives with,
  and always comes back with `Kind == DateTimeKind.Utc`.

Endpoints:

- `POST /v3db02/payments` — stores a payment, answers **201** with its id;
- `GET /v3db02/payments/{id:int}` — **200** with
  `{"id":…,"status":"Settled","settledAtUtc":"…Z","settledAtKind":"Utc"}`, or
  **404**;
- `GET /v3db02/model/payment-status` — **200** with the status column's
  provider CLR type name, which must be `"System.String"`.

The gate posts one payment whose `SettledAt.Kind` is `Local` and one whose
`Kind` is `Unspecified`, and requires both to name the same instant afterwards
that they named before.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db02_mapping_conversions ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two conversions, two different reasons. The enum one is about making the
database readable and immune to someone reordering the members. The
`DateTime` one is about a type that carries a flag the database cannot store.

## Hint 2

The enum has a one-liner:

```csharp
builder.Property(p => p.Status).HasConversion<string>();
```

The instant does not, because the two directions are not symmetric — going out
you convert, coming back you only *label*.

## Hint 3

```csharp
new ValueConverter<DateTime, DateTime>(
    v => /* normalise to UTC */,
    v => DateTime.SpecifyKind(v, DateTimeKind.Utc));
```

Think carefully about the outbound half for `Kind == Unspecified`:
`ToUniversalTime()` treats it as local, which may or may not be what your
system means by an unspecified timestamp. State an assumption and encode it.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask what the database column actually stores. On most providers a
`datetime2`/`TEXT` timestamp is an instant with no zone and no kind flag. The
`Kind` on your `DateTime` is a .NET-only annotation that is thrown away on
write and invented on read — invented as `Unspecified`, which formats as local
time in every serialiser that cares.

## Hint 2

There is a way to apply the same convention to every `DateTime` in the model
at once rather than property by property:

```csharp
builder.Entity<Payment>().Properties<DateTime>() // per entity
// or, on the context:
configurationBuilder.Properties<DateTime>().HaveConversion<UtcConverter>();
```

The second is `ConfigureConventions`, and it is how real codebases stop this
bug from recurring.

## Hint 3

Consider whether `DateTimeOffset` would make the whole exercise unnecessary —
it stores the offset, so nothing is inferred. It usually would. The reason to
know the converter anyway is that you will inherit a `DateTime` model you
cannot change, and this is the fix that works on it.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 — one table, three kinds of payment method

Edit `src/Api/V3DB02_MappingConversions/Ex7.cs`. Map the `PaymentMethod`
hierarchy — `CardMethod` (`Last4`, `ExpiryMonth`), `TransferMethod` (`Iban`),
`WalletMethod` (`Provider`) — as **table-per-hierarchy** into a table named
`payment_methods`, with a discriminator column `kind` holding `"card"`,
`"transfer"` and `"wallet"`.

Endpoints:

- `POST /v3db02/methods` — takes a `MethodRequest` (`kind`, `label`, and the
  subtype's field), creates the right subclass, answers **201** with its id;
  **400** for an unrecognised kind.
- `GET /v3db02/methods/cards` — **200** with every card method as
  `{"id":…,"label":…,"last4":"…"}`, ordered by id, fetched with a subtype
  query so the SQL carries a predicate on `kind`.
- `GET /v3db02/model/methods` — **200** with
  `{"column":"kind","values":["card","transfer","wallet"]}`.

The gate reads the generated SQL for the cards endpoint and fails it if there
is no discriminator predicate — loading everything and filtering with `is` in
C# does not pass.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db02_mapping_conversions ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Left alone, EF already maps this hierarchy as TPH — one table, a
`Discriminator` column, CLR type names as values. Everything you are doing is
replacing those defaults with names you chose, so that renaming a class is not
a data migration.

## Hint 2

```csharp
builder.Entity<Shape>()
    .HasDiscriminator<string>("shape_kind")
    .HasValue<Circle>("circle")
    .HasValue<Square>("square");
```

The base type declares the column; each `HasValue` names one subtype's value.

## Hint 3

For the query, `db.Set<PaymentMethod>().OfType<CardMethod>()` becomes
`WHERE kind = 'card'`. So does `.Where(m => m is CardMethod)`. Both are fine;
`OfType` also narrows the static type, which saves you a cast. For the
metadata, the discriminator is a property on the base entity type and each
subtype has a `GetDiscriminatorValue()`.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Before writing configuration, work out what the table must look like. Three
subtypes, one table, so every subtype-only column has to be nullable — a
transfer row has no expiry month. Write the CREATE TABLE on paper. That tells
you both the mapping and the cost you are accepting.

## Hint 2

The cost is worth naming precisely: you cannot enforce "a card always has an
expiry" at the database level under TPH, because the column must accept nulls
for the other subtypes. If that constraint is genuinely load-bearing, the
alternatives are TPT (a join per read) and TPC (no base-type table, `UNION
ALL` for base queries, awkward key generation).

## Hint 3

The `POST` is a switch over the kind string producing one of three
constructions; a `default` arm gives you the 400. Consider whether you add
`DbSet<CardMethod>` to the context — you do not need it, `db.Set<T>()` works
without one, and knowing that is worth more than the property.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — shadow properties and a collection nobody can corrupt

Edit `src/Api/V3DB02_MappingConversions/Ex8.cs`. `Basket` (given, do not
change it) exposes:

```csharp
private readonly List<Line> _lines = new();
public IReadOnlyCollection<Line> Lines => _lines;
public void AddLine(string sku, int qty) { /* enforces invariants */ }
```

Configure the model so that:

- EF populates and persists the collection through the `_lines` **backing
  field**, not through the read-only property;
- `Basket` has a **shadow property** `LastTouchedUtc` of type `DateTime`.

`Ex8Db.SaveChangesAsync` is already overridden to stamp `LastTouchedUtc` on
every added or modified basket; it will throw if the property is not in the
model.

Endpoints:

- `POST /v3db02/baskets/{id:int}/lines` — takes `{"sku":"…","qty":2}`, calls
  `AddLine`, saves, answers **200** with `{"lineCount":3}`; **404** for an
  unknown basket; **400** when `qty` is not positive.
- `GET /v3db02/baskets/{id:int}/touched` — **200** with
  `{"lastTouchedUtc":"…"}` read through `EF.Property`, or **404**.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db02_mapping_conversions ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two independent problems. One is "EF cannot write to a read-only property, so
tell it about the field". The other is "this column has no CLR property at
all, so declare it in the model and address it by name".

## Hint 2

For the field:

```csharp
builder.Entity<Order>()
    .Metadata
    .FindNavigation(nameof(Order.Lines))!
    .SetPropertyAccessMode(PropertyAccessMode.Field);
```

For the shadow property, `builder.Entity<Order>().Property<DateTime>("Name")`
— note the generic argument and the string, which together are the giveaway
that no property exists.

## Hint 3

Reading a shadow value needs the entry or the helper:
`EF.Property<DateTime>(basket, "LastTouchedUtc")` on a tracked entity, or
`db.Entry(basket).Property<DateTime>("LastTouchedUtc").CurrentValue`. Both
require the basket to be *tracked* — think about what that rules out for the
GET handler.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start with the encapsulation question, not the API. `Basket` deliberately has
no way for an outsider to add a `Line` except a method that enforces
invariants. If EF needed a public setter, persistence would have forced you to
break your own domain rules — so the field mapping is not a trick, it is the
feature that makes rich domain models possible at all.

## Hint 2

EF's conventions already look for a backing field named `_lines`, `_Lines`,
`m_lines` or `Lines` for a property called `Lines`, and will often find it
without help. Configure it explicitly anyway: the convention is a naming
coincidence and the configuration is a statement.

## Hint 3

For the GET, remember `AsNoTracking` and shadow properties do not mix — an
untracked entity has no entry, so `EF.Property` has nothing to read. If you
would rather not track, the alternative is to project the shadow value
directly in the query: `Select(b => EF.Property<DateTime>(b, "LastTouchedUtc"))`
translates.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — an aggregate that maps itself correctly

Edit `src/Api/V3DB02_MappingConversions/Challenge.cs`. Configure `Order` as a
single aggregate:

- `Order.Id` is an `OrderId` record struct wrapping a `Guid`; convert it to
  `Guid` and generate it client-side on add.
- `Order.Total` is a `Money(decimal Amount, string Currency)`, owned, mapped
  into `total_amount` (`decimal(18,4)`) and `total_currency` (`char(3)`), both
  required.
- `Order.Lines` is an owned collection in its own table `order_lines`, keyed
  by `(OrderId, LineNo)`, each line carrying its own owned `Money` in columns
  `line_amount` and `line_currency`.
- `Order.Status` (an enum) persists as text.
- The order table is `orders`.

Endpoints:

- `POST /v3db02/orders` — takes an `OrderRequest` with a list of lines,
  answers **201** with `{"id":"<guid>"}`; **400** when there are no lines or
  any quantity is not positive.
- `GET /v3db02/orders/{id:guid}` — **200** with the whole aggregate (lines
  ordered by `lineNo`) in **one** SQL command, or **404**.
- `GET /v3db02/model/orders` — **200** with
  `{"orderTable":"orders","lineTable":"order_lines","lineKey":["OrderId","LineNo"]}`.

The part that catches people: an owned collection needs a key, and the one EF
invents for you is a shadow property you cannot address.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db02_mapping_conversions challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Build this in three passes and run the gate between each: the id conversion
and the table names first; then the owned `Money` on the order; then the owned
collection with `Money` inside it. Nested owned types are easier to debug one
level at a time.

## Hint 2

An owned collection is configured from the owner and gets its own builder:

```csharp
builder.Entity<Order>().OwnsMany(o => o.Lines, l =>
{
    l.ToTable("order_lines");
    l.WithOwner().HasForeignKey("OrderId");
    l.HasKey("OrderId", nameof(Line.LineNo));
});
```

Note that the foreign key is named as a string — it is a shadow property on
the line.

## Hint 3

Inside that same `l` builder you can call `OwnsOne` again for the line's
`Money`. For the "one command" requirement, remember that an owned collection
always loads with its owner — you do not need `Include`, and adding one is
either redundant or an error. The 404 and the payload come from the same
`FirstOrDefaultAsync`.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask what makes this one aggregate rather than two entities. Lines have no
independent existence, no meaning outside the order, and no other table
references them. That is the definition of owned, and it is why the key is
`(OrderId, LineNo)` rather than a surrogate: the line's identity *is* its
position within its order.

## Hint 2

Leave the key out and look at what EF invents. You will get a shadow `Id`,
usually an integer, generated by the database — which works, until you need to
address a line from an API, or a re-insert renumbers them, or you want the
same line number to mean the same thing in two systems. The default is not
wrong; it is a decision made for you.

## Hint 3

`OrderId` wrapping a `Guid` with client-side generation means you assign it
yourself before `Add` — `new OrderId(Guid.NewGuid())` — rather than reading it
back after the save. That is a genuine advantage of GUID keys and worth
noticing: the whole aggregate, including the lines' foreign keys, is complete
before it ever reaches the database.

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.prompt:
## Review 1 — complex types, and what they refuse to do

Edit `src/Api/V3DB02_MappingConversions/Review1.cs`. `Quote` has a
`Money Price` property. Map it as a **complex type** — `ComplexProperty`, not
`OwnsOne` — into columns `price_amount` (`decimal(18,4)`) and
`price_currency`, both required, in a table named `quotes`.

Endpoints:

- `POST /v3db02/quotes` — stores a quote, answers **201** with its id;
  **400** when the currency is not exactly three characters.
- `GET /v3db02/quotes/{id:int}` — **200** with
  `{"id":…,"price":{"amount":…,"currency":"GBP"}}`, or **404**.
- `GET /v3db02/model/quote` — **200** with:

```json
{
  "isComplexType": true,
  "hasOwnEntityType": false,
  "canBeNull": false,
  "columns": ["price_amount","price_currency"]
}
```

Read those three facts out of the model rather than hard-coding them —
`FindComplexProperty` is the entry point. Be able to say, afterwards, why a
`Money` is better modelled this way than as an owned type, and what you would
lose.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db02_mapping_conversions review1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Everything you learned about `OwnsOne` transfers except the shape of the call
and one guarantee. The guarantee is the interesting part: a complex type has
no key and therefore no identity, which is why it cannot be `null` and why the
`ex3` trap cannot happen to it.

## Hint 2

```csharp
builder.Entity<Quote>().ComplexProperty(q => q.Price, p =>
{
    p.Property(x => x.Amount).HasColumnName("price_amount");
});
```

Same nested-builder feel, different metadata behind it. `IsRequired()` on the
complex property itself is redundant — think about why.

## Hint 3

For the metadata endpoint: `entity.FindComplexProperty(nameof(Quote.Price))`
gives you a complex property whose `ComplexType` has `GetProperties()`; and
`entity.GetNavigations()` will be empty, which is exactly the
`hasOwnEntityType: false` fact. Decide how you compute `canBeNull` — the
complex property exposes it directly.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Do this one by first writing the owned-type version, running it, and then
converting. The diff is small and the *behavioural* difference — no
navigation, no key, no nullability — is what you are meant to notice.

## Hint 2

Complex types arrived in EF 8 to fix a category error. Owned types were sold
as the way to map value objects, but they are entity types underneath, with a
hidden key and an optional existence, which is why an all-null address
disappears and why an owned type can be given its own table. `Money` is not a
row; it is a value, and a complex type says so in the model.

## Hint 3

Name the trade-offs before you finish. A complex type cannot be null, cannot
live in another table, cannot be the target of a navigation, and — in EF 8 —
cannot be a collection. Those restrictions are the point for a `Money`, and
they are exactly why an order's `Lines` still has to be owned rather than
complex.

lessons.title: V3·DB3 — Migrations, seeding and schema changes that do not take the site down
lessons.summary: Eight problems about changing a schema under live traffic: what a migration file really is, why Database.Migrate at startup races itself across replicas, idempotent scripts, expand-and-contract for a NOT NULL column, resumable backfills, seeding that survives being run twice, drift detection and the history table.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·DB3 — Migrations, seeding and schema changes that do not take the site down

Everything so far assumed the schema already existed and matched your model.
This sector is about the half-hour where that stops being true.

A migration is not a hard concept. `dotnet ef migrations add AddReturnedAt`
diffs your current model against a snapshot of the last one, writes the
difference as `Up` and `Down` methods, and updates the snapshot. What makes
this a genuine engineering topic is everything around it: several replicas
starting at once and all deciding to migrate; a `NOT NULL` column added to a
table that already has forty million rows; a backfill that times out at 70%
and has to be resumable; seed data that gets inserted twice; and a database
that has drifted from the model because somebody fixed something by hand at 2
a.m. and never told the repository.

The rule that organises all of it: **a deploy is not atomic, so your schema
change must be correct while the old code and the new code are both running.**
Every technique here — expand and contract, nullable-first, idempotent
scripts, backfill in batches — exists to satisfy that one constraint.

Everything is under `/v3db03/...`. The entities, the `V3Db03Db` context, the
committed migrations and the helpers live in
`src/Api/V3DB03_MigrationsSchema/Model.cs` — given code, read it first. The
domain is shipments: a `Shipment` with a `Reference`, a `Status`, a
`DispatchedAt`, and a `Carrier` reference table. `V3Db03Lock.AcquireAsync`
gives you a database-backed advisory lock; `V3Db03Clock` gives you a
controllable clock. The gate runs each exercise against a fresh SQLite file,
so migrations really are applied.

## Exercise 1 — what does this database actually have

Edit `src/Api/V3DB03_MigrationsSchema/Ex1.cs`. `GET /v3db03/schema/status`
answers **200** with a `SchemaStatus`:

```json
{"canConnect":true,"applied":["20260101_Initial"],"pending":["20260210_AddCarrier"],"upToDate":false}
```

`applied` comes from the history table, `pending` from the difference between
the assembly's migrations and that table, both in migration order. When the
database cannot be reached, answer **503** with
`{"canConnect":false}` and nothing else — do not throw.

This endpoint is the one you will wish you had during an incident, and it is
four framework calls.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db03_migrations_schema ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — five replicas, one migration

Edit `src/Api/V3DB03_MigrationsSchema/Ex2.cs`.
`POST /v3db03/schema/migrate` applies pending migrations and answers **200**
with `{"applied":[…],"skipped":false}`, or `{"applied":[],"skipped":true}`
when another caller is already migrating.

The gate fires **five concurrent requests** at a database with two pending
migrations. Exactly one may report `skipped: false`; the other four must
report `skipped: true`; and afterwards `pending` must be empty. No request may
fail with a duplicate-table error.

`await using var lease = await V3Db03Lock.AcquireAsync(db, "migrate", timeout)`
returns `null` when the lock is held elsewhere. Calling `Migrate()` from
`Program.cs` is what most services do and is exactly the bug this exercise is
about.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db03_migrations_schema ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — the script you hand to a DBA

Edit `src/Api/V3DB03_MigrationsSchema/Ex3.cs`.
`GET /v3db03/schema/script?from={a}&to={b}` answers **200** with
`{"sql":"…","idempotent":true}` — the SQL that moves the schema from
migration `a` to migration `b`, generated so that running it against a
database already at `b` is harmless.

**400** when either name is not a known migration. `from` may be omitted,
meaning "from empty"; `to` may be omitted, meaning "to latest".

`db.Database.GetService<IMigrator>()` is the entry point, and the option you
need is the difference between a script that a human must be careful with and
one that a pipeline can run.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db03_migrations_schema ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — expand: add the column, then fill it

Edit `src/Api/V3DB03_MigrationsSchema/Ex4.cs`. The `AddDispatchedAt` migration
added `dispatched_at` as a **nullable** column. Forty thousand existing
shipments have `null` in it, and the value should be derived from
`created_at` plus the carrier's lead time.

`POST /v3db03/backfill?batch={n}` answers **200** with a `BackfillReport`:

```json
{"updated":500,"remaining":39500,"complete":false}
```

Rules: `batch` defaults to 500 and must be 1–5000 (**400** otherwise); one
call updates at most `batch` rows; calling it repeatedly must eventually
report `complete: true` with `remaining: 0`; and two concurrent calls must not
double-count. No entity may be loaded — the gate fails the exercise if the
change tracker is non-empty.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db03_migrations_schema ex4
```

## Exercise 5 — contract: make it required, but only when it is safe

Edit `src/Api/V3DB03_MigrationsSchema/Ex5.cs`.
`POST /v3db03/schema/contract` finishes the change started in ex4:

- **409** with `{"remainingNulls":n}` when any `dispatched_at` is still null —
  the constraint must not be attempted;
- **200** with `{"altered":true}` when it applies the `NOT NULL` constraint;
- **200** with `{"altered":false}` when the column is already `NOT NULL`,
  because the endpoint has to be safe to call twice.

Read the current nullability from the **database**, not from `db.Model` —
the model already says required, which is the whole point of the exercise and
the reason a naive implementation reports `altered: false` before doing
anything.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db03_migrations_schema ex5
```

## Exercise 6 — seeding that survives being run twice

Edit `src/Api/V3DB03_MigrationsSchema/Ex6.cs`. `POST /v3db03/seed` inserts the
reference carriers from `V3Db03Seed.Carriers` (code, name, lead-time days) and
answers **200** with `{"inserted":3,"updated":0,"unchanged":0}`.

Rules: match on `Code`, which is the natural key, not on `Id`; insert what is
missing; update a carrier whose name or lead time differs; leave identical
rows alone; and do the whole thing in **one** transaction with at most three
commands. Running it twice in a row must give `{"inserted":0,"updated":0,
"unchanged":3}`.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db03_migrations_schema ex6
```

## Exercise 7 — HasData, and what it commits you to

Edit `src/Api/V3DB03_MigrationsSchema/Ex7.cs`. Configure `ShipmentStatus` (a
small lookup table) with `HasData` for its four rows, keys **fixed in the
configuration**.

`GET /v3db03/model/seeded` answers **200** with
`{"count":4,"keys":[1,2,3,4],"names":["Booked","Collected","Delivered","Lost"]}`
read out of the model with `GetSeedData()`, and
`GET /v3db03/statuses` answers **200** with the rows actually in the table.

Then answer, in the comment the gate reads at the top of your file, why
`HasData` cannot be used for the carriers in ex6. The gate checks that the
model seed and the table agree, which is the property `HasData` gives you and
a runtime seeder does not.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db03_migrations_schema ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — has anybody been editing the database by hand

Edit `src/Api/V3DB03_MigrationsSchema/Ex8.cs`. `GET /v3db03/schema/drift`
answers **200** with a `DriftReport`:

```json
{"hasPendingModelChanges":true,"operations":2,"summary":["AddColumnOperation:shipments.notes","CreateIndexOperation:shipments"]}
```

Compute it by diffing the current model against the last migration's snapshot
with `IMigrationsModelDiffer`, not by guessing. `summary` lists each operation
as `"{OperationTypeName}:{target}"`, ordered as the differ produced them; an
in-sync model gives `hasPendingModelChanges: false` and an empty list.

This is the check that belongs in CI: a model change with no migration is a
deployment that will not work, and it is silent until it is not.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db03_migrations_schema ex8
```

## Challenge — a deploy endpoint you would actually trust

Edit `src/Api/V3DB03_MigrationsSchema/Challenge.cs`.
`POST /v3db03/deploy` performs a guarded schema deployment and answers **200**
with a `DeployReport`:

```json
{"outcome":"applied","applied":["20260210_AddCarrier"],"durationMs":41,"auditId":7}
```

Behaviour:

- take the advisory lock; if it is held, answer **409** with
  `{"outcome":"busy"}` and change nothing;
- if there are no pending migrations, answer **200** with
  `{"outcome":"up-to-date","applied":[]}` and still write no audit row;
- otherwise apply them, write one `DeployAudit` row recording the migrations
  applied and the duration, and return its id;
- if applying throws, write an audit row with the failure, release the lock,
  and answer **500** with `{"outcome":"failed","error":"…"}`;
- the whole thing must be safe under five concurrent calls, and safe to
  retry after a failure.

The part that catches people is the audit row: it must be written on the
failure path too, and a migration failure has already rolled back the
transaction you were probably going to use.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db03_migrations_schema challenge
```

## Review

`review1` is not part of finishing this sector; the scheduler brings it back
later. Edit `src/Api/V3DB03_MigrationsSchema/Review1.cs`:
`GET /v3db03/schema/history` reads `__EFMigrationsHistory` directly and
compares it with the migrations compiled into the assembly, answering **200**
with `applied`, `knownButUnapplied` and — the interesting one —
`appliedButUnknown`: rows in the history table naming migrations this build
has never heard of. Be able to say what that list means at 3 a.m.
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - dotnet/v3db03_migrations_schema

## Notes

**A migration is three artefacts, and the snapshot is the important one.**
`20260210_AddCarrier.cs` holds `Up` and `Down`. `20260210_AddCarrier.Designer
.cs` holds the model as it was *after* this migration.
`V3Db03DbModelSnapshot.cs` holds the model as of the latest migration. `add`
diffs your current model against the snapshot; that is why deleting a
migration file without `dotnet ef migrations remove` leaves the snapshot
ahead and produces an empty next migration.

**`Database.Migrate()` in `Program.cs` is the default and the trap.** It works
perfectly with one replica. With three, all three call it at boot, all three
see the same pending list, and two of them race the first into a
duplicate-object error — or worse, into a half-applied schema, because a
failed migration on a provider without transactional DDL leaves the database
between states. The fix is that migrating is a *deployment step*, not an
application step: a job, an init container, a pipeline stage running
`dotnet ef database update` or a generated script, or — if it must be in the
app — a leader elected through a lock, which is `ex2`.

**`EnsureCreated` and `Migrate` do not mix.** `EnsureCreated` builds the
schema from the model and writes no history rows, so a later `Migrate` tries
to create tables that exist. `EnsureCreated` is for tests and throwaway
databases; anything you will ever have to change uses migrations from day one.

**Idempotent scripts are how a pipeline stays safe.** `GenerateScript` with
`MigrationsSqlGenerationOptions.Idempotent` wraps each migration in a guard
that checks the history table first, so running the same script twice is a
no-op and running a script that partially applied is a resume.

**Expand and contract is the only way to change a column under traffic.** Old
code and new code overlap during a rollout, so a schema must be compatible
with both. Add nullable, deploy code that writes both, backfill, deploy code
that reads the new column, then add the constraint and drop the old column.
Five steps, at least three deployments, and every one of them individually
safe. Skipping to `ALTER COLUMN ... NOT NULL` takes a lock on a large table,
blocks writers for the duration, and fails if any row is null — which,
because old code is still running, it will be.

## ex1 - the three sources of truth

`GetAppliedMigrationsAsync()` reads `__EFMigrationsHistory`.
`GetPendingMigrationsAsync()` subtracts that from the assembly's migrations.
`db.Database.GetMigrations()` is the assembly's list alone. All three are
useful; the pending list is what an operator wants.

`CanConnectAsync()` deserves the try/catch it looks like it does not need: it
returns `false` for a refused connection but still throws for some
authentication and DNS failures, and a status endpoint that throws is worse
than useless. The 503 with a small body is the honest answer.

## ex2 - one migrator at a time

The lock turns "everyone migrates" into "one migrates, everyone else waits or
skips". The details that matter: the lock must live in the same database as
the schema (a Redis lock is a second failure domain in the worst possible
place), the lease must be released even when the migration throws — hence
`await using` — and the skipped callers must return success, not an error,
because from the deployment's point of view "someone else is doing it" is a
fine outcome.

`GetPendingMigrationsAsync` *before* taking the lock is an optimisation; the
authoritative check happens after, because the answer can change while you
wait.

## ex3 - scripts, and why idempotent

`GenerateScript(fromMigration, toMigration, options)` produces the SQL without
touching the database, which is the point: a human or a change-control process
can read it before anything happens. The idempotent option emits, per
migration, a guard like `IF NOT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM __EFMigrationsHistory
WHERE MigrationId = '…')` around the body plus the history insert.

The two failure modes it removes are the ones you get in real pipelines: a
re-run after a partial failure, and a script applied to an environment that
was already ahead.

Validating `from` and `to` against `db.Database.GetMigrations()` before
calling is what turns a confusing framework exception into a 400.

## ex4 - a backfill is a loop you do not write in a migration

Putting `UPDATE shipments SET dispatched_at = …` in a migration works on a
small table and locks a large one for minutes. Batching is the standard shape:
select a bounded set of rows still needing work, update them, report progress,
and let the caller drive the loop.

`ExecuteUpdateAsync` over a `Take(batch)` subquery does it in one command with
no entities. The "two concurrent calls must not double-count" requirement is
satisfied for free by the `WHERE dispatched_at IS NULL` predicate — a row
already fixed is no longer selected — which is what *idempotent* means here.
Reporting `remaining` lets the caller decide when to stop, and makes progress
visible during the hour it takes.

## ex5 - contract, and reading the database rather than the model

The trap is that `db.Model` already says the column is required. It has said
so since you edited the entity. Asking the model whether the constraint is
applied gets you a confident `true` and an endpoint that does nothing.

The database knows: `PRAGMA table_info` on SQLite,
`INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS` on most others. Read the nullability from there,
count the remaining nulls, and only then attempt the `ALTER`. The 409 is not
defensive politeness — an `ALTER COLUMN ... NOT NULL` against a table with
nulls fails, and failing at your own gate with a useful number beats failing
in the database with a constraint violation.

## ex6 - idempotent seeding

The shape is: load the existing rows keyed by the *natural* key, compare
against the desired set, and produce inserts and updates. Matching on `Id`
is the mistake, because the id is assigned by whichever database ran the
seeder first and is not stable across environments.

One transaction and three commands: one select, one `SaveChanges` (which
batches the inserts and updates), and the transaction itself. The
"unchanged" count is worth returning — a seeder that reports what it did is a
seeder you can run in production without holding your breath.

## ex7 - HasData and its price

`HasData` puts seed rows *into the model*, which means `migrations add`
generates `InsertData` operations for them and changing them generates
`UpdateData` or `DeleteData`. That is a real benefit: your reference data is
version-controlled, diffable, and applied exactly once by the same mechanism
as the schema.

The price is what makes it wrong for the carriers. Keys must be specified
explicitly and constant, so no database-generated ids. Values must be
constant, so no `DateTime.UtcNow` and no computed anything. Related data needs
foreign keys stated by hand. And the rows are managed by migrations forever —
deleting a `HasData` entry generates a `DELETE`, which is either exactly what
you wanted or a production incident.

Rule: `HasData` for small, static, code-adjacent lookup tables. A runtime
seeder for anything with generated keys, environment-specific values, or a
lifecycle.

## ex8 - drift

`IMigrationsModelDiffer.HasDifferences(source, target)` compares two relational
models; `GetDifferences` returns the operations. Comparing the current model
against the last migration's snapshot answers "does someone need to run
`migrations add`", which is exactly the check that should fail a pull request.

EF 9 exposes this as `Database.HasPendingModelChangesAsync()`, which is the
same computation with a friendlier name. Doing it by hand once is worth it,
because the same differ is what generates your migrations in the first place.

## challenge - the audit row on the failure path

Two things collide. First, the lock must be released whatever happens, which
`await using` handles. Second, the audit row must survive a failure — and a
migration that throws has already rolled back its own transaction, so an audit
row written inside it is gone. Write the audit through a **separate**
connection or after the failure is caught, and do not wrap the migration and
the audit in one transaction hoping for the best.

The `up-to-date` case writing no audit row is deliberate: a deploy endpoint
called by a health-checking pipeline every minute should not fill a table with
"nothing happened".

## review1 - the history table as evidence

`appliedButUnknown` is the interesting list. It means the database has been
migrated by a build newer than the one running — a rollback that did not roll
back the schema, a deploy that reached one environment and not another, or two
services sharing a database. Every one of those is a real incident with a
different remedy, and the list is the first thing that tells you which.

## Further reading

- [Migrations overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/managing-schemas/migrations/) — the files, the snapshot and the commands.
- [Applying migrations](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/managing-schemas/migrations/applying) — scripts, idempotent scripts, bundles, and why not `Migrate()` at startup.
- [Custom migrations operations and raw SQL](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/managing-schemas/migrations/operations) — `migrationBuilder.Sql` and data motion.
- [Data seeding](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/modeling/data-seeding) — `HasData`, its constraints, and the alternatives.
- [Managing schemas](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/managing-schemas/) — `EnsureCreated` versus migrations.
- [Migrations in team environments](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/managing-schemas/migrations/teams) — snapshot conflicts and how to resolve them.

# V3·DB3 — Migrations, seeding and schema changes that do not take the site down

The archive version. The briefing tells you what to build; this is what to
know before you run a schema change against something that matters.

## Anatomy of a migration

Three files change when you run `dotnet ef migrations add AddCarrier`:

```
Migrations/20260210120000_AddCarrier.cs           // Up and Down
Migrations/20260210120000_AddCarrier.Designer.cs  // model after this migration
Migrations/V3Db03DbModelSnapshot.cs               // model after the latest migration
```

`Up` contains `MigrationBuilder` operations — `CreateTable`, `AddColumn`,
`CreateIndex`, `Sql`. `Down` contains the inverse. The snapshot is a
compiled representation of the model, and it is the *only* thing `add`
compares against. Consequences worth internalising:

- Deleting a migration file by hand leaves the snapshot ahead of the
  migrations. The next `add` produces an empty migration and you are now
  confused. `dotnet ef migrations remove` exists for this.
- Two developers adding migrations on branches both edit the snapshot, so it
  is a guaranteed merge conflict. The resolution is to take one side, re-add
  the other migration on top, and never hand-merge the snapshot.
- The snapshot is code, so a model that will not compile makes every EF
  command fail with an unrelated-looking error.

## Applying migrations: four options ranked

```csharp
// 1. Worst: every replica races at startup.
app.Services.CreateScope().ServiceProvider
   .GetRequiredService<AppDb>().Database.Migrate();

// 2. Acceptable: one replica wins the lock, the rest continue.
await using var lease = await Lock.AcquireAsync(db, "migrate", TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5));
if (lease is not null) await db.Database.MigrateAsync();

// 3. Good: a separate job or init container.
//    dotnet ef database update --connection "$CONN"

// 4. Best for regulated environments: a reviewed idempotent script.
//    dotnet ef migrations script --idempotent --output deploy.sql
```

Option 3 is the default answer for containerised services: the deployment
runs a migration job to completion, then rolls out the new pods. It separates
"the schema changed" from "the code changed", which is exactly the separation
expand-and-contract needs.

## Expand and contract, step by step

Adding a required `dispatched_at` to a live table:

1. **Expand.** Migration adds `dispatched_at` as nullable. Deploy. Old code
   ignores it; new code writes it. Both work.
2. **Backfill.** A batched, resumable job fills historical rows. It can run
   for hours and be interrupted.
3. **Verify.** Count remaining nulls. This is a real gate, not a formality.
4. **Contract.** Migration adds `NOT NULL`. Deploy. Now the constraint holds
   and the model can declare it required.
5. **Clean up.** If this replaced an old column, drop it in a *later* deploy,
   once nothing reads it.

A rename is the same dance: add the new column, dual-write, backfill, switch
reads, stop writing the old one, drop it. EF's `RenameColumn` operation is
correct and atomic and is still wrong under a rolling deploy, because for the
duration of the rollout half your replicas are looking for a column that no
longer exists.

## Backfills that finish

```csharp
int updated = await db.Shipments
    .Where(s => s.DispatchedAt == null)
    .Take(batch)
    .ExecuteUpdateAsync(s => s.SetProperty(
        x => x.DispatchedAt,
        x => x.CreatedAt.AddDays(x.Carrier.LeadTimeDays)));
```

Properties that make this survive production: bounded by `Take`, so no lock
is held long; predicated on the thing it fixes, so it is idempotent and safe
to run twice or concurrently; no entities, so memory is flat; and it reports
progress so an operator can watch it.

What to avoid: a single unbounded `UPDATE` (lock escalation, replication lag,
a transaction log that fills the disk), and a loop in C# that loads entities
(400,000 tracked objects and a `SaveChanges` that takes a minute).

## Seeding: three mechanisms

| mechanism | applied by | keys | good for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `HasData` | migrations | must be constant | small static lookups |
| a hosted service at startup | the app | any | dev/test data, idempotent reference data |
| an explicit endpoint or CLI | an operator | any | anything you want to observe |

`HasData` is the only one that is version-controlled and applied exactly once
by the same mechanism as the schema, and the only one that cannot use a
generated key. A runtime seeder must be idempotent, must match on a natural
key, and should report what it did.

## Common mistakes

- **`Migrate()` at startup with more than one replica.** The headline bug.
- **Mixing `EnsureCreated` and migrations.** No history rows, then every
  migration fails.
- **`ALTER COLUMN ... NOT NULL` in one step.** Fails on existing nulls, locks
  the table when it does not.
- **Data motion using your `DbContext` inside a migration.** The migration
  runs against the *old* model; using the current entity classes will compile
  and then break the day the model moves on. Use `migrationBuilder.Sql`.
- **Seeding on natural-key-less rows.** Re-running duplicates everything.
- **Hand-merging a model snapshot.** Regenerate instead.
- **Down migrations nobody has ever run.** Either test them or accept that
  rollback means restore-from-backup and stop pretending.
- **Assuming DDL is transactional.** It is on PostgreSQL and SQL Server; it is
  not on MySQL, where a failed migration leaves you halfway.
- **Not checking for pending model changes in CI.** The commit that changes
  an entity and forgets the migration deploys fine and then cannot start.

## Interview answer

> *"How do you add a non-nullable column to a big table with no downtime?"*

Answer with the sequence: you cannot do it in one step, because old code is
still running during the rollout and a `NOT NULL` constraint fails on the rows
it has not written yet. So: migration one adds the column nullable and deploys
alongside code that populates it on write. Then a batched, resumable backfill
job fills the history — bounded batches, predicated on `IS NULL` so it is
idempotent, reporting progress. Then you verify the null count is zero. Then a
second migration adds the constraint, which is now instant on some engines and
still a lock on others, so you schedule it. Finally the model declares the
property required. Mention that the migration itself should be applied by a
deployment job rather than by the application at startup, so that "schema
changed" and "code changed" are separate, observable events — which is the
thing that makes the whole sequence possible.

## Check yourself

1. What are the three files a migration touches, and which one does `add`
   compare against?
2. Why does deleting a migration `.cs` file by hand break the next `add`?
3. Give the failure mode of `Database.Migrate()` with three replicas.
4. What does the idempotent script option actually emit?
5. Why must a backfill be predicated on the condition it repairs?
6. Name two things `HasData` cannot express.
7. Why is `EnsureCreated` incompatible with migrations?
8. Why should data motion inside a migration use raw SQL rather than your
   `DbContext`?
9. What does a non-empty `appliedButUnknown` list tell you?
10. How would you detect, in CI, that a model change has no migration?
11. On which engines is DDL transactional, and why does it matter?
12. Describe the five deploys of a column rename under rolling deployment.
13. Where should the migration lock live, and why not Redis?
14. What is the argument against ever writing a `Down` migration?

# Reading - dotnet/v3db03_migrations_schema

## The problem migrations actually solve

Before migrations, changing a schema meant a folder of numbered SQL files and
a convention that everybody applied them in order. That works. What it does
not give you is a machine-checkable relationship between the code's idea of
the schema and the database's. EF migrations add exactly that: the snapshot.
Because the snapshot is a compiled model, the tooling can tell you the
difference between what your classes say and what the last migration built —
which is the check in `ex8`, and the reason "did we forget a migration" stops
being a question a human has to remember to ask.

The trade is that migrations are generated, and generated code is code you did
not read. The healthiest habit in this whole area is to open the generated
migration before committing it. Perhaps a third of the time it is not what you
expected: an index dropped and recreated because a property's nullability
changed, a column recreated rather than altered because the provider cannot
alter it in place, a table rebuild on SQLite because SQLite cannot drop a
column at all. None of those are bugs. All of them are things you want to know
about before they run against forty million rows.

## What the differ does

`IMigrationsModelDiffer` compares two `IRelationalModel`s and produces an
ordered list of `MigrationOperation`s. The ordering is not incidental: the
differ topologically sorts operations so that tables are created before the
foreign keys that reference them, columns are added before indexes over them,
and drops happen in the reverse order. This is why hand-editing a migration to
reorder operations occasionally produces something that will not apply.

The differ works on the *relational* model — tables, columns, constraints —
not on your entity classes. So two very different models that map to the same
tables produce no operations. Renaming a C# property and adding
`HasColumnName` with the old name generates nothing, which is exactly right
and occasionally startling.

The other thing worth knowing: the differ cannot see intent. Rename a property
and it emits a drop and an add, because a column called `Notes` disappearing
and a column called `Remarks` appearing is indistinguishable from a rename. It
also destroys the data. EF's `RenameColumn` exists but you have to ask for it
by editing the generated migration — and, as the briefing notes, a rename is
usually the wrong shape under a rolling deploy anyway.

## Why startup migration is so persistent

`app.Services.CreateScope()...Database.Migrate()` is in every tutorial because
it is a two-line way to make the sample run. It survives into production
because it works for a long time — one replica, or several replicas started
sequentially, or a migration that happens to be idempotent — and then fails on
the deploy where two pods start within the same second.

The failure is not always loud. On a provider with transactional DDL the loser
gets a clean error and crashes, the orchestrator restarts it, and by then the
winner has finished; you get a red pod for thirty seconds and never
investigate. On a provider without transactional DDL, a partially applied
migration leaves the schema in a state no migration file describes, and the
history table does not record it, so the next deploy tries again and fails
differently.

Which is why the recommendation is structural rather than defensive: run
migrations as a distinct step with a distinct exit code, before the new code
starts. Kubernetes calls that an init container or a Job; a platform
deployment calls it a release phase; a pipeline calls it a stage. The lock
approach in `ex2` is the fallback for when you genuinely cannot add a step,
and it is strictly worse, because it couples "the app started" to "the schema
changed" and gives you no way to stop a bad migration before the code that
depends on it is live.

## Transactions, DDL and what rollback means

PostgreSQL and SQL Server support transactional DDL: a migration's operations
are wrapped in a transaction and a failure rolls the whole thing back. MySQL
and MariaDB do not — each DDL statement commits implicitly. On those engines a
migration with four operations that fails on the third leaves two applied, no
history row, and a database that matches nothing.

The practical response is to make migrations small. One logical change per
migration, so a partial failure has a small blast radius and a human can
reason about the state. It also makes the idempotent script genuinely useful,
because re-running it resumes rather than starting over.

`Down` migrations deserve a blunt paragraph. Almost nobody runs them. In a
forward-only deployment model the rollback story for a schema is "the previous
code still works against the new schema", which is what expand-and-contract
buys you, and the rollback story for data is a backup. Writing a `Down` that
has never been executed gives you a false sense of reversibility; either test
them in CI by migrating up and down on a scratch database, or delete them and
be honest.

## Backfills and the operational reality

A backfill on a large table is not a code problem, it is a load problem. Every
row you update is a write to the table, an update to every index covering the
changed column, a write to the transaction log, and — if you have replicas —
replication traffic. Do it in one statement and you will find out which of
those is your bottleneck the hard way, usually replication lag, usually
during business hours.

Batching fixes the lock duration and the log growth. The remaining knobs are
batch size and delay between batches, and the honest way to pick them is to
run the job, watch replication lag and disk I/O, and adjust. That is why the
endpoint in `ex4` returns `remaining` — a job that reports progress is one an
operator can throttle, pause and resume, and one whose completion is
observable rather than assumed.

The subtlety that catches people is the predicate. `WHERE dispatched_at IS
NULL` makes the job self-limiting and safe to run twice. `WHERE id BETWEEN
@a AND @b` does not: rerun it and you redo work, and if the derivation is not
idempotent — appending to a string, incrementing a counter — you corrupt data.
Always predicate on the condition you are repairing.

## When not to use migrations

Two cases.

If the database is owned by another team, migrations are not yours to run.
Point EF at the existing schema, scaffold or hand-write the model, and add a
startup assertion that the schema matches what you expect. `Database
.HasPendingModelChangesAsync()` or a differ check is a good smoke test even
when you never apply anything.

If your schema changes are large data-movement projects — partitioning,
sharding, a table rewrite — the migration file is the wrong container. Those
are operations with their own runbooks, monitoring and rollback plans, and
squeezing them into `Up()` means they run inside a deployment step with a
timeout. Use the migration to record the *end state* (a small DDL change) and
run the data movement as a job you can watch.

And finally: resist the urge to make the application self-healing about
schema. Code that inspects the database and creates missing tables at startup
is a system with no version, no history and no reviewable diff of what
happened when. The whole value of migrations is that the schema has a linear,
auditable history. Keep it.
