# Reading - dotnet/v3db05_background_work

## Why this is harder than it looks

A request handler has a natural shape imposed on it: something calls it, it
returns, and if it throws the framework turns that into a 500 and logs it. A
background service has none of that. It starts when the process starts, ends
when the process ends, has no caller to report to, and runs concurrently with
everything else in the application.

That is why so much of this sector is about *structure* rather than API
surface. The API is four types — `IHostedService`, `BackgroundService`,
`IHostApplicationLifetime`, `PeriodicTimer` — and you could learn all of them
in twenty minutes. The hard part is that a background service quietly changes
the assumptions of every other piece of code it touches: lifetimes, error
handling, cancellation, and the number of things running at once.

## The startup ordering, precisely

`Host.RunAsync` does, in order: build the service provider; resolve every
`IHostedService`; call `StartAsync` on each in sequence, awaiting each one;
raise `ApplicationStarted`; then block until shutdown is requested.

In an ASP.NET Core app, Kestrel itself is a hosted service
(`GenericWebHostService`). It is registered early, so it usually starts before
your workers — but "usually" is doing work in that sentence, and the ordering
is determined by registration. If you have a warm-up that must complete before
any request is served, registering it before the web host is fragile; the
robust way is to do the work before `app.Run()`, where the ordering is
explicit and visible.

Shutdown is the mirror: `ApplicationStopping` fires, `StopAsync` is called in
reverse registration order, `ApplicationStopped` fires. Kestrel's `StopAsync`
stops accepting connections and waits for in-flight requests. Because your
worker's `StopAsync` runs at a defined point in that sequence, you can rely on
"requests are draining while I drain", which is usually what you want.

The five-second default `ShutdownTimeout` is the single most commonly wrong
setting in this area. It is not related to your orchestrator's grace period —
Kubernetes defaults to 30 seconds — and if your `ShutdownTimeout` is longer
than the grace period, SIGKILL arrives mid-drain and the graceful shutdown you
wrote never completes. The two numbers must be set together, with the host's
timeout comfortably shorter.

## Cancellation, and the three tokens

There are three cancellation tokens in play and confusing them causes real
bugs.

`stoppingToken` in `ExecuteAsync` is cancelled when shutdown *begins*. It is
your signal to stop taking new work. It is not a deadline.

The token passed to `StopAsync` is cancelled when the shutdown timeout
expires. It is a deadline, and by the time it fires you are already late.

`HttpContext.RequestAborted` is cancelled when the client disconnects. It has
nothing to do with shutdown, and honouring it is one of the highest-value,
lowest-effort optimisations available: work for a client who has gone away is
pure waste, and under load it is a meaningful fraction of everything.

The general rule for passing a token: pass it into work that is safe to
abandon, and withhold it from work that must complete. That is a design
decision per call site, and "pass `stoppingToken` everywhere" is a
plausible-looking way to guarantee data loss on every deploy.

## Timers, and why `PeriodicTimer` won

The old pattern was `System.Threading.Timer` with a callback. It has two
problems. The callback is `void`, so an async callback is `async void` and its
exceptions are unobserved and crash the process. And the timer is reentrant:
if the callback takes longer than the period, the next one starts anyway, and
you can end up with dozens of overlapping executions of a job that has slowed
down — which is the classic "the database got slow so we hammered it harder"
outage.

`PeriodicTimer.WaitForNextTickAsync` fixes both. It is awaited, so exceptions
propagate normally, and it is inherently non-reentrant because your loop
controls when you wait again. When the body overruns, the timer returns
immediately on the next wait — one catch-up tick, not a queue of them.

For anything more sophisticated — cron expressions, calendar scheduling,
missed-run policies, persistence across restarts — use a scheduler
(Quartz.NET, Hangfire) rather than growing your own. The line to draw is: a
loop with a period is a `BackgroundService`; anything a business person would
describe with the word "schedule" wants a scheduler.

## The multiplication problem

Everything in this sector changes when the deployment scales from one replica
to three, and the change is silent. "Send the daily summary at 6 a.m." becomes
three summaries. "Reconcile the ledger every minute" becomes three
reconciliations racing each other. Nothing errors; the effects are simply
wrong, and often wrong in a way that only accounting notices.

Three answers, in order of preference:

**Make the work idempotent and claimable.** Rows in a table, claimed
atomically. Three workers then means three times the throughput, which is a
feature. This is the right shape for anything queue-like.

**Elect a leader.** A database advisory lock held for the duration; the holder
runs, the others skip. Simple, and the failure mode is benign: if the leader
dies, the next poll elects another.

**Move it out.** A separate deployment with one replica, or the platform's
scheduler triggering an endpoint. This is the honest answer for a genuinely
singleton job, and it makes the constraint visible in the deployment
configuration rather than hidden in code.

## The outbox, in more detail

Two systems, one atomic operation, no distributed transaction: this is the
oldest problem in integration and the outbox is the standard answer.

Write the message into a table in the same transaction as the business data.
Now the commit is the point of no return for both. A separate publisher reads
unpublished rows and sends them.

The publisher cannot be atomic with the broker. If it marks the row published
before sending and the send fails, the message is lost. If it sends first and
the mark fails, the message is sent twice. Choose the duplicate: at-least-once
delivery with an idempotent consumer is a system whose failure modes are
recoverable, and every serious broker's delivery guarantee is at-least-once
anyway, so the consumer needs deduplication regardless.

The costs are real and worth stating. There is a delay between commit and
publish — usually milliseconds, occasionally more. The outbox table needs
pruning or it grows forever. Ordering is only guaranteed if you publish
single-threaded per partition key. And the publisher is one more thing that
can fall behind, which means it is one more thing to monitor: the age of the
oldest unpublished row is the metric that matters, not the count.

## When not to use a background service

If the work must survive a process restart, an in-memory queue is the wrong
tool and no amount of care fixes it. Use a durable store.

If the work is long-running, resource-hungry or independently scalable — image
processing, report generation, ML inference — it does not belong inside the
web application at all. It competes for the same thread pool, the same memory
limit and the same deployment cadence as your request handling, and a bad day
for the worker becomes a bad day for the API.

And if the work is genuinely "run this at a time", consider whether the
platform should own it: a scheduled trigger hitting an endpoint is observable,
configurable and restartable by an operator without a deployment. In-process
scheduling is convenient and invisible, and invisible is the property you will
regret at 3 a.m.

exercises.title: Ex1
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 — the worker that stops the app from starting

Edit `src/Api/V3DB05_BackgroundWork/Ex1.cs`. The class implements both
`IServiceRegistrar` and `IEndpointMapper`.

Register a `BackgroundService` that, every **50 ms**, appends a `WorkLog` row
with `Text = "tick"`. Expose `GET /v3db05/heartbeat` answering **200** with:

```json
{"ticks":7,"alive":true}
```

`ticks` is the number of `"tick"` rows. The gate waits 400 ms after startup
and requires at least 5 ticks.

As shipped, the gate times out waiting for the *first* response: the app never
starts listening. `ExecuteAsync` is called synchronously by
`BackgroundService.StartAsync`, and the host awaits `StartAsync` for every
hosted service **before** the web server begins accepting connections.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db05_background_work ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`StartAsync` returns when `ExecuteAsync` hits its first *incomplete* await. A
loop whose body is entirely synchronous never hits one, so `StartAsync` never
returns, so the host never gets to the line that starts the listener. There is
no exception because nothing failed.

## Hint 2

Two things fix it, and real code uses both:

```csharp
protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)
{
    await Task.Yield();                 // hand control back to the host now
    while (!stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
    {
        // …
        await Task.Delay(50, stoppingToken);
    }
}
```

## Hint 3

The worker is a singleton and needs to write rows, so it cannot hold a
`DbContext` — that is the next exercise, and here you can sidestep it by
writing through the given `V3Db05Log.Append(text)`, which is a thread-safe
in-memory sink the endpoint reads. Note that `Task.Delay` with a token throws
on shutdown; decide where you catch it.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Reproduce the symptom deliberately before fixing it, because you will see it
again in code you did not write. Start the app, curl anything, and watch it
hang with no log line, no exception, and a process that is using 100% of one
core. That triad — hang, no error, one core busy — is this bug's signature.

## Hint 2

Ask *why* the host is designed this way. `StartAsync` blocking is a feature:
it is how a warm-up guarantees it finished before traffic arrives. The
framework cannot tell the difference between "I am deliberately blocking
startup" and "I forgot to await", so the discipline has to be yours.

## Hint 3

`await Task.Yield()` is worth understanding rather than copying. It returns an
awaitable that is never already complete, so the compiler-generated state
machine always schedules a continuation and returns to the caller — which is
exactly the guarantee you want at the top of `ExecuteAsync`, regardless of
what the rest of the method does.

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — a singleton that needs a DbContext

Edit `src/Api/V3DB05_BackgroundWork/Ex2.cs`. Write a `BackgroundService` that
every **100 ms** finds the oldest `Order` with `Status == "new"`, sets its
status to `"picked"`, saves, and appends a `WorkLog` row whose `Text` is the
order's `Reference`.

`GET /v3db05/picked` answers **200** with:

```json
{"picked":["A-1","A-2","A-3"]}
```

in pick order. The gate seeds 5 orders, waits, and requires all 5 picked
exactly once.

The shipped version takes `V3Db05Db` in the worker's constructor. Run the gate
first: the app fails to start with a message naming the two lifetimes. Making
the context a singleton would "fix" it and is the worst available answer.

The gate also asserts each iteration used a **different** `DbContext`
instance.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db05_background_work ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A hosted service is resolved once, from the root provider, and lives as long
as the process. Anything scoped it holds is captured for that lifetime — hence
"captive dependency", and hence the startup error, which is scope validation
doing you a favour.

## Hint 2

The factory is a singleton, so it is safe to hold:

```csharp
public Ex2Worker(IServiceScopeFactory scopes) => _scopes = scopes;

// inside the loop
using var scope = _scopes.CreateScope();
var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<V3Db05Db>();
```

## Hint 3

Put `CreateScope()` inside the loop, not in the constructor and not outside
the `while`. One scope for the whole worker is the same bug written by hand,
and it gives you a change tracker that accumulates every entity the process
has ever touched. The gate checks for exactly this by comparing context
instances.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

There are two independent reasons for a scope per iteration and both matter.
The lifetime reason is the one the error message tells you about. The other is
that after a failed `SaveChanges` the change tracker is in an unclear state,
and the cheapest, most reliable recovery is to throw the whole context away —
which a per-iteration scope does for free.

## Hint 2

Consider what "the oldest new order" means when three replicas run this. Each
one finds the same order, each one picks it, and two of them fail on the
concurrency check — or worse, all three succeed and you have picked it three
times. This exercise runs one worker; ex8 is where that assumption is removed.

## Hint 3

Think about memory. A singleton context tracking one entity per 100 ms
accumulates 864,000 tracked entities per day, each with a snapshot, and every
`SaveChanges` walks all of them. The service does not crash; it gets
quadratically slower and then it crashes. That shape — fine for a week, then
sudden — is the signature of a lifetime bug.

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — stopping without losing work

Edit `src/Api/V3DB05_BackgroundWork/Ex3.cs`. The worker takes items from
`V3Db05Work.Pending` (a thread-safe queue, `TryDequeue`) and processes each
with:

```csharp
await V3Db05Work.ProcessAsync(item, ct);   // ~40 ms; writes a WorkLog row on completion
```

Requirements:

- while running, process items continuously; when the queue is empty, wait
  briefly and look again;
- when shutdown begins, **finish the item currently in flight** and then stop
  without starting another;
- do not exceed the host's `ShutdownTimeout`, which the gate sets to 1 second.

`GET /v3db05/drain` answers **200** with:

```json
{"completed":12,"abandoned":0,"stopped":true}
```

The gate enqueues work, triggers `IHostApplicationLifetime.StopApplication()`
mid-item, and requires `abandoned: 0` — every item that was started finished.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db05_background_work ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The token means "stop taking new work", not "abandon what you are doing".
Those are two different places in the loop: one is the `while` condition, the
other is what you pass into `ProcessAsync`.

## Hint 2

```csharp
while (!stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
{
    if (!Queue.TryDequeue(out var item)) { await Task.Delay(20, stoppingToken); continue; }
    await ProcessAsync(item, CancellationToken.None);   // finish it
}
```

Passing `stoppingToken` into `ProcessAsync` is the ungraceful version, and it
is what the shipped code does.

## Hint 3

`CancellationToken.None` is honest but unbounded — an item that hangs blocks
shutdown until the host gives up on you. A budget token derived from the
remaining shutdown time is the production answer:
`new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(600)).Token`. Decide
which you use and be able to defend it.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Write down what "graceful" is protecting. An abandoned item is not just slow —
it is a half-done unit of work whose side effects may already have happened.
Every deploy abandons something, and deploys are frequent, so "occasionally
loses an item" compounds into a steady trickle of corruption nobody traces
back to the rollout.

## Hint 2

Two timeouts must be reasoned about together and this exercise only shows you
one. `HostOptions.ShutdownTimeout` is how long the host waits for you. The
orchestrator's termination grace period is how long it waits before SIGKILL.
If the first is longer than the second, your careful drain is killed halfway
and you have written nothing but false confidence.

## Hint 3

`Task.Delay(20, stoppingToken)` throws `OperationCanceledException` at
shutdown, which exits your loop through the catch rather than the `while`
condition. That is fine and normal, but it means the "finish the current item"
guarantee has to come from the structure of the loop, not from the condition —
check where your `await` on the item actually sits.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — the exception that took the process with it

Edit `src/Api/V3DB05_BackgroundWork/Ex4.cs`. The worker calls
`V3Db05Work.NextFlaky()` every 30 ms. It returns a string most of the time and
throws `InvalidOperationException` roughly one time in three.

`GET /v3db05/flaky` answers **200** with:

```json
{"processed":18,"failures":7,"alive":true}
```

The gate runs for one second and requires **at least five** failures and a
still-responsive endpoint afterwards.

As shipped, the first throw ends `ExecuteAsync`, and because .NET 6 made
`BackgroundServiceExceptionBehavior.StopHost` the default, the whole
application exits. The gate sees the process die.

Contain the failure where it happens. Do **not** set the behaviour to
`Ignore` — the gate checks that you did not, and you should be able to say why
it exists and why it is the wrong tool here.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db05_background_work ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A loop body that can fail needs the try/catch *inside* the loop, around one
iteration. Around the loop is the shipped bug with extra steps: it catches the
exception and then exits anyway, because there is nowhere to continue to.

## Hint 2

Distinguish the two kinds of cancellation-shaped exception you will see:

```csharp
catch (OperationCanceledException) when (stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
{
    break;                       // shutting down, not a failure
}
catch (Exception ex)
{
    failures++;                  // a real failure, keep going
}
```

## Hint 3

Add a backoff. A loop that fails instantly and retries instantly is a tight
loop against a dependency that is already unhappy, and it turns one flaky
service into two outages. Even a small delay after consecutive failures
changes the character of the failure completely.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Answer the `Ignore` question before you write the fix, because it is the
interesting part. `StopHost` is the right default: a worker that has silently
died looks identical to a worker with nothing to do, and you find out weeks
later from a customer. A crashed process is loud, restarts, and shows up in
your dashboard. `Ignore` converts every fatal bug into that silent failure —
globally, for every hosted service in the app.

## Hint 2

The distinction that makes this coherent: handle failures you *expect* (a
flaky dependency, a bad row, a transient network error) at the point they
happen, and let failures you did not anticipate end the service loudly. Broad
catch blocks at the top of a loop erase that distinction, which is why the
catch should be as tight as you can make it and should log the exception
rather than swallow it.

## Hint 3

Think about the log line, not just the counter. "Iteration failed" with a
stack trace and no identifier is nearly useless when it appears 4,000 times.
The item's id, the attempt number and the consecutive-failure count are what
turn a wall of exceptions into a diagnosis.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — a timer that does not drift

Edit `src/Api/V3DB05_BackgroundWork/Ex5.cs`. The worker must run its body once
every **100 ms**. The body is `await V3Db05Work.VariableAsync()`, which takes
a random 10–60 ms and records `DateTime.UtcNow` in the tick log.

`GET /v3db05/drift` answers **200** with:

```json
{"ticks":19,"maxGapMs":118,"cumulativeDriftMs":22}
```

- `ticks` — how many times the body ran;
- `maxGapMs` — the largest interval between consecutive recorded times;
- `cumulativeDriftMs` — `(last - first) - (ticks - 1) * 100`, i.e. how far
  behind schedule the whole run ended up.

`V3Db05Work.Ticks` gives you the recorded times. The gate runs for two seconds
and requires `maxGapMs < 160` and `cumulativeDriftMs < 60`.
`await Task.Delay(100)` after the body fails both, and the reason is
arithmetic rather than bad luck.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db05_background_work ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Do the arithmetic on the shipped version before changing it. Body 10–60 ms,
average 35; delay 100; period 135. Over two seconds that is 14 ticks where you
wanted 20, and the cumulative drift is 500 ms. Nothing went wrong — the delay
is measured from the wrong moment.

## Hint 2

```csharp
using var timer = new PeriodicTimer(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(100));
while (await timer.WaitForNextTickAsync(stoppingToken))
{
    await BodyAsync();
}
```

The timer ticks on a schedule; the body's duration comes out of the gap rather
than adding to it.

## Hint 3

Consider what happens when the body overruns a tick — say it takes 130 ms.
`PeriodicTimer` does not queue missed ticks: the next `WaitForNextTickAsync`
returns immediately once and then resumes the schedule. Compare that with a
`System.Threading.Timer`, which would have started a second overlapping
callback, and you have the reason `PeriodicTimer` exists.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about which of these two you actually want, because they are different
requirements and people conflate them: "start every 100 ms" and "wait 100 ms
between runs". A drift-free schedule is the first. A rate limit on a
dependency is the second. `PeriodicTimer` gives you the first; `Task.Delay`
after the body gives you the second, and it is not always the wrong choice.

## Hint 2

Notice that `WaitForNextTickAsync` returns `bool`, not `void`. It returns
`false` when the token is cancelled or the timer is disposed, which is why the
`while` condition can be the await itself and why this loop needs no
try/catch for shutdown. That is a small API design worth admiring.

## Hint 3

The non-reentrancy is the property that saves you in production. Under a
timer-with-callback the sequence "database slows down, callbacks overlap, each
one takes a connection, the pool exhausts, everything times out" is a
well-trodden path to an outage. A loop that awaits its own body cannot do
that: it is structurally incapable of running twice at once.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — a queue with a limit

Edit `src/Api/V3DB05_BackgroundWork/Ex6.cs`. Register a **bounded**
`Channel<PickJob>` with capacity **8**, and a worker that consumes it, taking
about 30 ms per job (`await V3Db05Work.PickAsync(job)`) and appending a
`WorkLog` row.

Endpoints:

- `POST /v3db05/jobs` takes `{"reference":"A-9"}` and answers **202** with
  `{"queued":true,"depth":n}`, or **429** with `{"queued":false,"depth":8}`
  when the channel is full. It must **never** wait for room.
- `GET /v3db05/jobs` answers **200** with `{"processed":n,"rejected":m}`.

The gate posts 200 jobs as fast as it can and requires: some 429s, **no
request taking longer than 50 ms**, and every accepted job eventually
processed.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db05_background_work ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two writer APIs, and the whole exercise is choosing correctly between them.
One waits for room; one tells you immediately that there is none. In an HTTP
handler, waiting means your queue depth is expressed as customer latency.

## Hint 2

```csharp
var channel = Channel.CreateBounded<PickJob>(new BoundedChannelOptions(8)
{
    FullMode = BoundedChannelFullMode.Wait,
    SingleReader = true,
});

if (!channel.Writer.TryWrite(job)) { /* 429 */ }
```

The consumer side is `await foreach (var job in channel.Reader.ReadAllAsync(
stoppingToken))`.

## Hint 3

Register the channel as a singleton so the endpoint and the worker share it —
injecting `Channel<PickJob>` directly works, or register the reader and writer
separately if you prefer the endpoint not to be able to read. Then decide
where the `processed` and `rejected` counters live; they are touched from two
threads.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The capacity is the interesting decision, not the API. Eight is a claim: "I am
willing to owe the world eight units of unstarted work." Too small and you
reject requests you could have served; too large and a failure means a long
queue of stale work that nobody is waiting for any more. Pick it from the
consumer's throughput and the acceptable staleness, not from a round number.

## Hint 2

Notice that an **unbounded** channel does not remove the limit; it moves it to
the process's memory and removes your ability to react. The failure mode
changes from "some clients get a 429 and retry" to "the container is OOM-killed
and every in-flight job is lost". Backpressure is not a degradation, it is the
feature.

## Hint 3

Consider what happens to queued jobs when the process stops. They are in
memory; they are gone. For a nudge email that is acceptable; for anything a
customer paid for it is not, and the answer is the database-backed queue in
ex8. Knowing which side of that line a piece of work falls on is the actual
engineering judgement here.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 — work that must finish before the first request

Edit `src/Api/V3DB05_BackgroundWork/Ex7.cs`. Two pieces of startup work, and
they are deliberately different kinds:

- **Blocking:** `await V3Db05Work.WarmAsync()` (about 200 ms) must complete
  before the application accepts any traffic.
- **Non-blocking:** a `WorkLog` row with `Text = "started"`, written *after*
  the server is listening — its timestamp must be later than the
  `ApplicationStarted` event.

`GET /v3db05/warm` answers **200** with:

```json
{"warm":true,"announced":true,"warmedBeforeFirstRequest":true}
```

`V3Db05Work.WarmedAt`, `V3Db05Work.StartedEventAt` and
`V3Db05Work.FirstRequestAt` are recorded for you; the gate sends its first
request the instant the host reports started and asserts
`WarmedAt < FirstRequestAt` and `StartedEventAt < announcement`.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db05_background_work ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The host awaits `StartAsync` for every hosted service before the listener
starts. That property is a bug in ex1 and a feature here — it is exactly the
"must finish before traffic" guarantee, and you get it by putting the work in
`StartAsync` rather than in `ExecuteAsync`.

## Hint 2

For the non-blocking half, the lifetime object has three tokens you can
register callbacks on:

```csharp
lifetime.ApplicationStarted.Register(() => V3Db05Log.Append("started"));
```

`ApplicationStopping` and `ApplicationStopped` are its siblings and are worth
knowing for the same reason.

## Hint 3

Implement `IHostedService` directly rather than deriving from
`BackgroundService` — you want `StartAsync` to actually block, which is the
one thing `BackgroundService` is designed to avoid. `StopAsync` returns
`Task.CompletedTask`.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask what belongs in each half before writing either. Blocking startup work is
anything that would produce errors or unacceptable latency if a request
arrived first: building the EF model, opening a connection, loading a required
cache. Everything else — announcements, metrics registration, warming a
nice-to-have — belongs after started, because every millisecond of blocking
startup is a millisecond added to every deployment.

## Hint 2

There is a real operational cost to getting this wrong in the generous
direction. Blocking startup work delays the moment your readiness probe can
pass, which delays the rollout of every pod, which lengthens every deploy and
every rollback. A 200 ms warm-up across 40 pods rolled two at a time is four
seconds; a 20-second warm-up is six minutes of degraded capacity.

## Hint 3

Note that a failure in `StartAsync` stops the host from starting at all. That
is usually right for a warm-up — a service that cannot reach its database
should not report itself ready — and it means you should not swallow
exceptions there. Compare with the announcement, where a failure should
clearly not prevent the service from running.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — three replicas, one job

Edit `src/Api/V3DB05_BackgroundWork/Ex8.cs`. The gate registers **three**
instances of your worker against one database, all polling the `Jobs` table.
Each of the 100 seeded jobs must be processed exactly once.

Use the given atomic claim:

```csharp
// UPDATE jobs SET status='claimed', worker=@worker
// WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE status='ready' ORDER BY id
//              LIMIT @batch FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)
// RETURNING *;
IReadOnlyList<Job> claimed = await V3Db05Sql.ClaimBatch(db, workerId, batchSize);
```

For each claimed job: `await V3Db05Work.RunJobAsync(job)`, then set its status
to `"done"` and save. A claim of zero rows means wait briefly and try again.

`GET /v3db05/jobs/report` answers **200** with:

```json
{"total":100,"processed":100,"duplicates":0,"workers":3}
```

`duplicates` counts jobs whose `RunCount` exceeds 1. Any implementation that
selects a batch and *then* marks it produces duplicates, and the gate counts
them.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db05_background_work ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`SELECT … WHERE status = 'ready'` followed by `UPDATE … SET status =
'claimed'` has a gap, and three workers polling the same table all read the
same rows inside it. Claiming has to be one statement, and the statement has
to return what it claimed.

## Hint 2

`FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` is the clause that makes this work well rather than
merely correctly. Without `SKIP LOCKED`, worker two waits for worker one's
lock and you have serialised three workers into one. With it, worker two
ignores the locked rows and takes the next ones.

## Hint 3

Structure: claim a batch; if it is empty, delay and continue; otherwise
process each job and mark it done. Think about what happens if a worker dies
between claiming and finishing — the jobs are stuck in `"claimed"` forever
unless something reclaims them, and a `claimed_at` timestamp with a reaper is
how real queues handle it.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The multiplication problem is the thing to internalise, not the SQL. Every
background job you have ever written silently changes meaning when the
deployment scales to three replicas: "runs every five minutes" becomes "runs
three times every five minutes". Nothing errors. The effects are just wrong.

## Hint 2

There are two shapes of answer and they suit different work. Claiming rows —
this exercise — means three workers is three times the throughput, which is a
feature; it suits anything queue-like. Electing a leader with a database lock
means exactly one worker runs and the others idle; it suits work that is
inherently singular, like "send the daily summary". Picking the wrong one
gives you either duplicates or a third of the capacity you paid for.

## Hint 3

Think about the batch size. One row per claim is a round trip per job and
maximum fairness. A hundred rows per claim is efficient and means a worker
that dies holds a hundred jobs hostage until they are reclaimed. The right
answer depends on job duration and on whether you have a reaper, which is the
sort of thing worth writing in a comment above the constant.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — the transactional outbox

Edit `src/Api/V3DB05_BackgroundWork/Challenge.cs`. Two halves.

**The writer.** `POST /v3db05/orders` takes `{"reference":"A-9"}` and, in
**one** transaction, creates an `Order` and an `Outbox` row whose `Payload` is
`V3Db05Bus.Describe(order)` and whose `MessageId` is a fresh GUID. **201**
with `{"orderId":…}`; **400** for a blank reference.

**The publisher.** A worker (the gate runs **three**) that:

- claims unpublished outbox rows atomically with
  `V3Db05Sql.ClaimOutbox(db, workerId, batch)` — same `SKIP LOCKED` shape as
  ex8;
- calls `await V3Db05Bus.PublishAsync(row.MessageId, row.Payload, ct)`, which
  throws about one time in four;
- marks the row published on success, and leaves it claimable again on
  failure.

`GET /v3db05/outbox` answers **200** with:

```json
{"written":50,"published":50,"delivered":50,"duplicatesDelivered":0}
```

`delivered` and `duplicatesDelivered` come from `V3Db05Bus.Stats` — the bus
deduplicates on `MessageId`, which is what makes at-least-once delivery
survivable. The gate creates 50 orders and requires `published == written`.

The trap: publishing and marking published cannot be atomic with each other.
One of them happens first, and which one you pick decides whether you can lose
a message or duplicate one.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db05_background_work challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Start by naming what the outbox buys you. "Save the order" and "publish the
message" involve two systems and cannot be one transaction — unless the
message is *also* a row in your database, at which point one commit covers
both. Everything after that is delivery.

## Hint 2

The writer is short:

```csharp
await using var tx = await db.Database.BeginTransactionAsync();
db.Orders.Add(order);
db.Outbox.Add(new Outbox { MessageId = Guid.NewGuid(), Payload = … });
await db.SaveChangesAsync();
await tx.CommitAsync();
```

The publisher is the ex8 loop with a network call in the middle.

## Hint 3

Resolve the trap explicitly. Mark-then-send loses a message when the send
fails; send-then-mark duplicates one when the mark fails. Choose send-then-mark
and let the consumer deduplicate — that is why `MessageId` is on the row and
stable across retries. Do not generate a new one on retry, or your
deduplication does nothing.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Build it in three passes: writer only (check the two rows land together);
publisher with no failures; then turn the flakiness on. The failure behaviour
is where all the interesting bugs live and you want the happy path proven
first.

## Hint 2

Think about ordering, because the outbox does not give it to you for free.
Three publishers claiming batches concurrently will publish messages out of
order. If ordering matters, publish single-threaded per partition key —
claim by key, not by row — and accept the throughput cost. If it does not,
say so explicitly somewhere, because the next person will assume it does.

## Hint 3

Name the metric you would alert on. Not the count of unpublished rows — a
burst of writes makes that spike harmlessly. The **age of the oldest
unpublished row** is the signal: it stays near zero when the publisher is
healthy and grows linearly the moment it stops, whatever the write rate is
doing.

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.prompt:
## Review 1 — three ways to stop waiting

Edit `src/Api/V3DB05_BackgroundWork/Review1.cs`. Implement `Wait` so that
`GET /v3db05/wait?ms={n}` is a long-poll that returns as soon as **any** of
these happens:

- the background worker signals — `V3Db05Work.Signal` is a
  `TaskCompletionSource` the worker completes every ~250 ms;
- `n` milliseconds elapse;
- the client disconnects.

Answer **200** with `{"reason":"signalled"}` or `{"reason":"timeout"}`;
**400** when `ms` is outside 1–5000. On a client disconnect nothing is
returned — but the handler must stop waiting immediately and record
`V3Db05Work.Aborted++`, which the gate reads afterwards.

`GET /v3db05/wait/stats` answers **200** with
`{"signalled":n,"timedOut":m,"aborted":k}`.

The mechanism is a linked cancellation token; the interesting part is telling
the three cancellations apart *after* the fact, because the linked token
cannot tell you which source fired.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db05_background_work review1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three independent reasons to stop, one wait. That is what
`CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource` is for: it produces a token
that is cancelled when any of its sources is.

## Hint 2

```csharp
using var timeout = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(ms));
using var linked = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(
    timeout.Token, http.RequestAborted);
```

`HttpContext.RequestAborted` is the client-disconnect source and costs nothing
to honour.

## Hint 3

After the wait ends, ask the *sources*, not the linked token:
`http.RequestAborted.IsCancellationRequested` distinguishes an abort from a
timeout. Check the abort first — a client that disconnected at the same
moment the timeout fired should count as an abort, because there is nobody to
send the timeout to.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Honouring `RequestAborted` is one of the highest-value, lowest-effort things
in a web service and almost nobody does it. Under load, a meaningful fraction
of requests are for clients who have already given up and retried — every one
of those is work you can decline to do, and declining makes the retry storm
smaller rather than larger.

## Hint 2

The linked token deliberately cannot tell you why it fired. That is not an
oversight: it is one token with one meaning, "stop". If you need the reason,
you keep references to the sources — which is a small design lesson about
cancellation generally, since the same question ("why did this stop?") comes
up every time you compose tokens.

## Hint 3

Consider what to await. `Task.WhenAny(signal.Task, Task.Delay(Timeout
.Infinite, linked.Token))` is the idiomatic shape, and the delay task will
throw when the token fires unless you observe it carefully. Decide whether you
catch `OperationCanceledException` or inspect the completed task — one of
those leaves an unobserved exception behind.

lessons.title: V3·DB6 — Configuration, options, secrets and per-environment behaviour
lessons.summary: Eight problems past the provider stack you already know: writing a configuration provider, change tokens and the double-fire, how IOptionsMonitor invalidates its cache, IValidateOptions with several failures, configure and post-configure ordering, awkward binding, secret redaction and per-environment composition.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·DB6 — Configuration, options, secrets and per-environment behaviour

You already know the provider stack: JSON, environment-specific JSON, user
secrets, environment variables, command line, later wins. You know
`services.Configure<T>(section)` and the difference between `IOptions`,
`IOptionsSnapshot` and `IOptionsMonitor`. Sectors `04`, `d08` and `d09` cover
all of that, and this sector assumes it.

What this sector is about is the layer underneath — the part you meet the
first time a requirement does not fit the tutorial. A configuration value that
lives in a database rather than a file. A reload that fires your callback
twice for one save, so your cache rebuilds twice and, once in a while, from a
half-written file. A misconfigured service that starts happily and fails on
the first request that touches the setting. Defaults that need to be layered
by three different components without any of them knowing about the others. A
`TimeSpan` that binds from `"00:00:30"` and a record that silently binds to
nothing. A configuration dump in a support ticket with a database password in
it.

The organising idea: **configuration is a pipeline of providers producing a
flat dictionary, plus a change-notification system, plus a binder.** Almost
every surprising behaviour is one of those three doing exactly what it says.

Everything is under `/v3db06/...`. The options classes, the fake secret store,
the test doubles and the reloadable backing store live in
`src/Api/V3DB06_ConfigSecrets/Model.cs` — given code, read it first. Each
exercise's class implements `IServiceRegistrar` — where the configuration and
options wiring goes — and `IEndpointMapper`.

## Exercise 1 — a provider of your own

Edit `src/Api/V3DB06_ConfigSecrets/Ex1.cs`. Write a configuration source and
provider backed by `V3Db06Store` — an in-memory dictionary with a
`Changed` event — and add it to the configuration root.

- `GET /v3db06/config/{key}` answers **200** with `{"key":…,"value":…}` for a
  key the provider supplies, **404** when no provider has it.
- `POST /v3db06/config` takes `{"key":"dojo:limit","value":"9"}`, writes it to
  the store, and answers **204**. A subsequent `GET` must return the new
  value.

The point is the reload: writing to the store is not enough on its own. A
provider that never signals a change is a provider whose values are read once
and cached forever.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db06_config_secrets ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — the callback that fires twice

Edit `src/Api/V3DB06_ConfigSecrets/Ex2.cs`. Register a change callback on the
configuration that rebuilds an expensive cache
(`await V3Db06Cache.RebuildAsync()`, about 40 ms).

`GET /v3db06/reload` answers **200** with
`{"changes":n,"rebuilds":m,"lastValue":"…"}`.

The gate makes **one** change and requires `rebuilds: 1`. A naive
`ChangeToken.OnChange` registration gives you two — file watchers commonly
raise two events for one save, and `reloadOnChange` propagates both. Debounce
it, and make sure the value you end up caching is the value after the last
event, not the first.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db06_config_secrets ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — how the monitor knows

Edit `src/Api/V3DB06_ConfigSecrets/Ex3.cs`. `GateOptions` is bound from
`Dojo:Gate`, and a second, non-configuration source of truth —
`V3Db06Store.Version` — should also invalidate it.

Register an `IOptionsChangeTokenSource<GateOptions>` so that
`IOptionsMonitor<GateOptions>.CurrentValue` is recomputed when **either** the
configuration section changes or `V3Db06Store` signals.

- `GET /v3db06/gate` answers **200** with
  `{"limit":…,"recomputes":n}` — `recomputes` counts how many times the
  options instance has actually been rebuilt, which the given
  `CountingConfigureOptions` records for you.

The gate changes the section once and the store once, and requires
`recomputes: 3` — the initial build plus one per invalidation.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db06_config_secrets ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — fail at boot, not at 3 a.m.

Edit `src/Api/V3DB06_ConfigSecrets/Ex4.cs`. `MailerOptions` has `Host`,
`Port`, `FromAddress` and `RetryCount`. Wire it up so that a misconfigured
application **refuses to start**, with a message naming every problem at once
rather than the first one.

Requirements:

- bind `Dojo:Mailer`, validate data annotations, and validate on start;
- add an `IValidateOptions<MailerOptions>` that reports **all** failing rules
  in one `ValidateOptionsResult`: port outside 1–65535, `FromAddress` without
  an `@`, `RetryCount` outside 0–10, and `Host` blank;
- `GET /v3db06/mailer/validate` takes a candidate as a query string and
  answers **200** with `{"valid":false,"failures":["…","…"]}` by calling your
  validator directly.

The gate boots the app with three simultaneous mistakes and requires all three
in the startup failure, then calls the endpoint with one mistake.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db06_config_secrets ex4
```

## Exercise 5 — configure, then post-configure

Edit `src/Api/V3DB06_ConfigSecrets/Ex5.cs`. `ClientOptions` must end up with
its `Timeout`, `UserAgent` and `BaseUrl` assembled by three independent
contributors, none of which knows about the others:

1. a library default (`Timeout = 30s`, `UserAgent = "dojo"`);
2. the bound `Dojo:Client` section;
3. a **post-configure** step that appends the environment name to
   `UserAgent` and rewrites `BaseUrl` to `https` if it is `http`.

`GET /v3db06/client` answers **200** with the final options **and** an
`order` array naming each contributor in the order it ran:
`["library-default","configuration","post-configure"]`, recorded via
`V3Db06Trace.Note(name)`.

Getting the order right is the exercise. Two of the three are easy to place
and one of them is not where people expect.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db06_config_secrets ex5
```

## Exercise 6 — the shapes that do not bind

Edit `src/Api/V3DB06_ConfigSecrets/Ex6.cs`. `IngestOptions` has to bind from
`Dojo:Ingest`, which contains an array of endpoints, a dictionary of per-tenant
limits, a `TimeSpan` window, and an enum mode.

`GET /v3db06/ingest` answers **200** with the bound values.
`GET /v3db06/ingest/strict?extra=true` re-binds a fresh instance with
`BinderOptions.ErrorOnUnknownConfiguration` enabled and answers **200** with
`{"bound":false,"error":"…"}` when the section carries a key that has no
matching property, or `{"bound":true}` when it does not.

Two shapes in the given model are deliberately awkward: a positional record
and a property with only an `init` accessor. One of them binds and one does
not. Fix the one that does not **without** changing it to a mutable class, and
say in a comment which rule you relied on.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db06_config_secrets ex6
```

## Exercise 7 — who won, and why

Edit `src/Api/V3DB06_ConfigSecrets/Ex7.cs`.
`GET /v3db06/whence?key={key}` answers **200** with:

```json
{"key":"Dojo:Gate:Limit","value":"50","provider":"EnvironmentVariablesConfigurationProvider","candidates":["JsonConfigurationProvider=25","EnvironmentVariablesConfigurationProvider=50"]}
```

- `value` — what `IConfiguration` actually returns;
- `provider` — the type name of the provider that supplied it;
- `candidates` — every provider that has a value for the key, in provider
  order (earliest first), so a reader can see what was overridden.

**404** when no provider has the key. Walk `IConfigurationRoot.Providers` and
`TryGet`; do not parse `GetDebugView`.

The gate sets the same key in three providers with the container spelling
`Dojo__Gate__Limit` and requires the last one to win.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db06_config_secrets ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — the dump you can paste into a ticket

Edit `src/Api/V3DB06_ConfigSecrets/Ex8.cs`. `GET /v3db06/dump` answers **200**
with every configuration key and value, sorted by key, with secrets
**redacted**:

- a key whose last segment matches any of `password`, `secret`, `token`,
  `key`, `connectionstring` (case-insensitively) → value replaced with
  `"***"`;
- a value that looks like a connection string — contains `Password=` or
  `Pwd=` — → the whole value replaced with `"***"` even if the key looks
  innocent;
- everything else → the real value.

Also report `{"redacted":n}`. The gate plants a secret under an innocuous key
name and a connection string under `Dojo:Storage:Primary`, and fails the
exercise if either value appears anywhere in the response.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db06_config_secrets ex8
```

## Challenge — feature flags that change without a deploy

Edit `src/Api/V3DB06_ConfigSecrets/Challenge.cs`. Build a flag system on the
machinery from the rest of the sector.

`FlagOptions` binds `Dojo:Flags` — a dictionary of flag name to
`{"enabled":bool,"percentage":int,"environments":["Development","Staging"]}`.

`GET /v3db06/flags/{name}?user={id}` answers:

- **404** for an unknown flag;
- **200** with `{"name":…,"on":true,"reason":"percentage"}` otherwise.

Evaluation, in order: if the current environment is not in `environments` the
flag is off with reason `"environment"`; else if `enabled` is false it is off
with reason `"disabled"`; else if `percentage` is 100 it is on with reason
`"enabled"`; else it is on for the stable hash bucket
`V3Db06Hash.Bucket(name, user)` below `percentage`, with reason
`"percentage"`.

Requirements: evaluation reads the **current** configuration, so a flag change
takes effect on the next request with no restart; the options are validated on
start (percentage 0–100, at least one environment); and the same `user`
always gets the same answer for a given flag and percentage.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db06_config_secrets challenge
```

## Review

`review1` is not part of finishing this sector; the scheduler brings it back
later. Edit `src/Api/V3DB06_ConfigSecrets/Review1.cs`: register a different
`IReceiptSender` per environment — a recording fake in Development, a strict
one in Production that refuses to start without a configured endpoint — with
**no** environment check anywhere below `Register`. `GET /v3db06/sender`
reports which implementation is wired and where the decision was made.
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - dotnet/v3db06_config_secrets

## Notes

**A provider is two interfaces and a dictionary.** `IConfigurationSource.Build`
returns an `IConfigurationProvider`; the provider exposes `TryGet`, `Set`,
`GetChildKeys`, `Load` and `GetReloadToken`. `ConfigurationProvider` is a base
class giving you all of it over a `Data` dictionary — so a custom provider is
usually "fill `Data` in `Load`, call `OnReload()` when the source changes".

**Reading a key walks the providers backwards.** `ConfigurationRoot["a:b"]`
iterates `Providers` in reverse and returns the first `TryGet` that succeeds.
That is "later wins", mechanically. It also means the winner is discoverable
at runtime, which is `ex7`.

**Change notification is `IChangeToken`, not events.** A token is single-use:
you register a callback, it fires once, and you must re-register against a
*new* token. `ChangeToken.OnChange(getToken, callback)` does the re-registration
loop for you, and forgetting that pattern is why hand-rolled reload code
usually works exactly once.

**Reloads fire more than once.** A file save is frequently two filesystem
events (truncate then write), and `reloadOnChange` propagates both. Worse, the
first can arrive while the file is half-written, so a naive handler can parse a
truncated file. Debounce — a short delay that resets on each event — and read
the value *after* the delay.

**`IOptionsMonitor` caches, and `IOptionsChangeTokenSource` invalidates.** The
monitor holds a computed `T` per name and drops it when any registered change
token source fires. `services.Configure<T>(section)` registers a
`ConfigurationChangeTokenSource<T>` behind the scenes; registering another one
is how a non-configuration source can invalidate options.

**Validation is opt-in and startup validation is a separate opt-in.**
`AddOptions<T>().Bind(...).ValidateDataAnnotations().ValidateOnStart()`.
Without `ValidateOnStart` the validation runs on first `.Value` access, which
in a web app means "on the unlucky request".

**Post-configure runs after everything else.** The ordering is: all
`IConfigureOptions<T>` in registration order, then all
`IPostConfigureOptions<T>`. `Configure(section)` is itself an
`IConfigureOptions<T>`, so a hard-coded default registered *after* it wins,
which is almost never what anyone intends.

## ex1 - writing a provider

```csharp
public sealed class StoreSource : IConfigurationSource
{
    public IConfigurationProvider Build(IConfigurationBuilder builder) => new StoreProvider();
}

public sealed class StoreProvider : ConfigurationProvider
{
    public StoreProvider() => V3Db06Store.Changed += () => { Load(); OnReload(); };
    public override void Load() => Data = V3Db06Store.Snapshot();
}
```

`OnReload()` is the piece that makes it a *configuration* provider rather than
a dictionary: it fires the reload token, which is what wakes
`IOptionsMonitor`, `IOptionsSnapshot` and every `OnChange` callback in the
process.

The realistic version of this is a provider over a database table or a remote
store, and it comes with an obligation the file providers hide: something has
to poll or subscribe, and that something needs a failure policy. A
configuration provider that throws during `Load` on a transient network error
takes the application down.

## ex2 - debouncing

```csharp
ChangeToken.OnChange(
    () => configuration.GetReloadToken(),
    () => _debounce.Schedule(RebuildAsync));
```

where `Schedule` cancels a pending run and starts a new timer. 200–300 ms is
the usual window: long enough to coalesce the pair of events a save produces,
short enough that nobody notices.

The second-order bug is reading the configuration value *inside* the callback
at the moment it fires rather than after the debounce — you capture the
half-written state and then never look again, because the second event was
coalesced away.

`OnChange` returns an `IDisposable`. Dropping it leaks the registration, which
matters when the thing registering is scoped or transient.

## ex3 - invalidating options from elsewhere

```csharp
services.AddSingleton<IOptionsChangeTokenSource<GateOptions>>(
    new StoreChangeTokenSource<GateOptions>(Options.DefaultName));
```

The monitor subscribes to every registered source for `T`. When any fires, it
evicts the cached instance; the next `CurrentValue` re-runs the whole
configure/post-configure chain.

The `recomputes` count in the exercise makes the caching visible: `CurrentValue`
read a thousand times between changes rebuilds nothing. That is the difference
between `IOptionsMonitor` (cached, invalidated) and `IOptionsSnapshot`
(rebuilt once per request whether anything changed or not).

## ex4 - validation with all the failures

`IValidateOptions<T>.Validate(string? name, T options)` returns
`ValidateOptionsResult`. The important detail is `Fail(IEnumerable<string>)` —
returning on the first problem gives a user one error per restart, which is a
miserable loop when three things are wrong.

`ValidateOnStart` turns validation into a startup failure. The message names
the options type and lists the failures, and the process exits non-zero, which
is exactly what a deployment pipeline needs. Without it, the failure surfaces
as a 500 on whichever request first resolves the options — possibly hours
later, possibly on one pod.

`ValidateDataAnnotations` and a custom validator compose: both run, and both
sets of messages appear.

## ex5 - the ordering people get wrong

`services.Configure<T>(section)` is a registration of `IConfigureOptions<T>`.
So this:

```csharp
services.Configure<ClientOptions>(config.GetSection("Dojo:Client"));
services.Configure<ClientOptions>(o => o.Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30));
```

does not mean "default 30 seconds, overridable by configuration". It means the
opposite: the lambda runs second and overwrites whatever configuration said.
Defaults belong in the class's property initialisers, or in a
`ConfigureOptions` registered *first*, or — for a genuine "always apply this
last" transform — in `PostConfigure`.

Post-configure is the right home for derived and normalised values: appending
the environment to a user agent, forcing `https`, expanding a relative path.
Those are transformations of whatever the final configuration turned out to
be, which is precisely the phase they run in.

## ex6 - binding edge cases

The binder matches configuration keys to **public properties it can write**.
The rules worth memorising:

- Arrays and lists bind from the keys `Items:0`, `Items:1`, … — which is what
  a JSON array becomes in the flat dictionary, and which is why an environment
  variable can add an element.
- `Dictionary<string, T>` binds from child section names as keys.
- `TimeSpan` parses from `"00:00:30"` and `"1.02:03:04"`; it does not parse
  from `30`.
- Enums bind by name, case-insensitively, and by number.
- A property with only an `init` accessor **can** be bound — the binder uses
  the setter's underlying method — but only when the object is constructed by
  the binder, not when you pass it an existing instance.
- A positional record binds through its constructor when the parameter names
  match keys; add a second constructor and it stops.
- `BinderOptions.ErrorOnUnknownConfiguration` turns a typo'd key from silence
  into an exception, which is worth enabling for options you care about.

## ex7 - provider archaeology

```csharp
var root = (IConfigurationRoot)configuration;
foreach (var provider in root.Providers)
    if (provider.TryGet(key, out var value)) { /* candidate */ }
```

Providers are stored in registration order, so the *last* candidate is the
winner. `GetDebugView()` produces the same information as a formatted string
and is excellent for a log line and terrible to parse.

The container spelling is the other half. `Dojo__Gate__Limit` becomes
`Dojo:Gate:Limit` because a colon is not legal in an environment-variable name
on some platforms. The `ASPNETCORE_` and `DOTNET_` prefixes are stripped by the
providers that add them, which is why `ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT` is read as
`ENVIRONMENT` in that provider's data.

## ex8 - redaction

Two rules because one is not enough. A key-name rule catches `Password`,
`ApiKey`, `Token`. A value-shape rule catches the connection string that
somebody stored under `Dojo:Storage:Primary`, which no key-name rule would
flag.

The deeper habit: never log `IConfiguration` wholesale, never put it in an
exception, and treat any endpoint that returns configuration as privileged.
The number of production secrets that have escaped through a diagnostics page
is not small.

## challenge - flags

The flag evaluation itself is a short function. What makes it a challenge is
that it must read *current* configuration — so `IOptionsMonitor<FlagOptions>`
or `IOptionsSnapshot<FlagOptions>`, never `IOptions<FlagOptions>` — and that
the percentage rollout must be **stable**: the same user must get the same
answer every time, or a user watching a page refresh sees the feature flicker.
That is why the bucket is a hash of `(flag, user)` rather than a random
number.

## review1 - composition, not conditionals

The environment decides *what is registered*, in `Register`. Below that,
nothing knows the environment exists. A handler containing
`if (env.IsDevelopment())` is a handler that has never been tested in the
configuration it runs in production.

## Further reading

- [Configuration providers](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/configuration/) — the stack, precedence and custom providers.
- [Implement a custom configuration provider](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/custom-configuration-provider) — `IConfigurationSource`, `ConfigurationProvider` and reload.
- [Options pattern](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/options) — configure, post-configure, named options and the monitor.
- [Options validation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/options#options-validation) — `IValidateOptions<T>`, data annotations and `ValidateOnStart`.
- [Configuration binding](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/configuration#binding) — arrays, dictionaries, records and `BinderOptions`.
- [Safe storage of app secrets](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/app-secrets) — user secrets locally, real stores in production.
lessons.fullReadme:
# V3·DB6 — Configuration, options, secrets and per-environment behaviour

The archive version. Assumes the basics and goes at the machinery.

## The three subsystems

Configuration is not one thing. It is three, and most confusion comes from
attributing a behaviour to the wrong one.

**The provider pipeline** produces a flat `IDictionary<string, string?>` per
provider and reads them in reverse registration order. It knows nothing about
your classes.

**The change system** is `IChangeToken`: a single-use notification with
`HasChanged`, `ActiveChangeCallbacks` and `RegisterChangeCallback`. Providers
expose one via `GetReloadToken()`; the root aggregates them.

**The binder** maps the flat dictionary onto CLR objects by name. It knows
nothing about providers or change tokens.

The options system sits on top of all three and adds caching, validation and
composition.

## Writing a provider

```csharp
public sealed class StoreConfigurationSource : IConfigurationSource
{
    public IConfigurationProvider Build(IConfigurationBuilder builder)
        => new StoreConfigurationProvider();
}

public sealed class StoreConfigurationProvider : ConfigurationProvider, IDisposable
{
    public StoreConfigurationProvider() => V3Db06Store.Changed += OnStoreChanged;

    public override void Load() => Data = V3Db06Store.Snapshot();

    private void OnStoreChanged()
    {
        Load();
        OnReload();          // fires the reload token: everything downstream wakes up
    }

    public void Dispose() => V3Db06Store.Changed -= OnStoreChanged;
}

builder.Configuration.Add(new StoreConfigurationSource());
```

For a remote store, the realistic shape adds: a poll interval, a failure
policy (do **not** throw from `Load` on a transient error — serve the last
good data), an optional-vs-required flag, and a bounded retry. A configuration
provider that can take down the process on a network blip is a liability.

## Change tokens, correctly

```csharp
IDisposable registration = ChangeToken.OnChange(
    () => configuration.GetReloadToken(),   // a NEW token each time
    () => _debounce.Schedule(Rebuild));
```

The first lambda must return a fresh token on each call — that is what makes
the re-registration loop work. Returning a cached token means your callback
fires once, ever.

Debounce implementation, in outline:

```csharp
public void Schedule(Func<Task> work)
{
    _cts?.Cancel();
    var cts = _cts = new CancellationTokenSource();
    _ = Task.Run(async () =>
    {
        try { await Task.Delay(250, cts.Token); } catch (OperationCanceledException) { return; }
        await work();
    });
}
```

## Options composition

```csharp
services.AddOptions<ClientOptions>()
    .Configure(o => { o.Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30); })   // 1: library default
    .Bind(configuration.GetSection("Dojo:Client"))               // 2: configuration
    .PostConfigure(o => { o.UserAgent += $" ({env.EnvironmentName})"; })  // 3: always last
    .ValidateDataAnnotations()
    .ValidateOnStart();
```

Order of execution: every `IConfigureOptions<T>` in registration order, then
every `IPostConfigureOptions<T>`. `Bind` is a configure step, so a `Configure`
registered after it wins over configuration — the commonest ordering bug in
this area.

Named options run the same chain with the name threaded through;
`ConfigureAll` and `PostConfigureAll` apply to every name.

## Validation

```csharp
public sealed class MailerValidator : IValidateOptions<MailerOptions>
{
    public ValidateOptionsResult Validate(string? name, MailerOptions o)
    {
        var failures = new List<string>();
        if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(o.Host)) failures.Add("Host must not be blank.");
        if (o.Port is < 1 or > 65535) failures.Add($"Port {o.Port} is out of range.");
        if (!o.FromAddress.Contains('@')) failures.Add("FromAddress must contain '@'.");
        if (o.RetryCount is < 0 or > 10) failures.Add("RetryCount must be 0-10.");

        return failures.Count == 0
            ? ValidateOptionsResult.Success
            : ValidateOptionsResult.Fail(failures);
    }
}
```

Collect, do not short-circuit. Then `ValidateOnStart()` so the process refuses
to start rather than failing on an unlucky request.

## Binding, the awkward cases

```jsonc
{
  "Dojo": {
    "Ingest": {
      "Endpoints": ["a", "b"],            // Endpoints:0, Endpoints:1
      "Limits": { "acme": 10, "globex": 5 },  // dictionary by child name
      "Window": "00:00:30",               // TimeSpan
      "Mode": "Strict"                    // enum by name
    }
  }
}
```

- `init`-only properties bind when the binder constructs the object.
- A positional record binds through its constructor when parameter names match
  and there is exactly one usable constructor.
- A read-only collection property with no setter is populated in place if it
  is already non-null and the type supports `Add`.
- `ErrorOnUnknownConfiguration` turns a typo into an exception.

## Common mistakes

- **`Configure` after `Bind` for a default.** Configuration is now ignored.
- **Assuming one reload event per change.** Two is normal; one of them may be
  mid-write.
- **Caching a change token.** The callback fires once and never again.
- **`IOptions<T>` for anything reloadable.** Computed once, forever.
- **`IOptionsSnapshot<T>` in a singleton.** Captive dependency, caught at
  startup with scope validation on.
- **Validation without `ValidateOnStart`.** Fails on a request instead of a
  deploy.
- **Returning the first validation failure.** One error per restart.
- **`ToLower()`-style key handling.** Keys are already case-insensitive;
  colons and `__` are the only spellings that matter.
- **Logging `configuration.GetDebugView()`.** Now your secrets are in the log
  aggregator, indexed and retained.
- **`if (env.IsDevelopment())` inside a handler.** Untested code path in
  production.

## Interview answer

> *"How would you make a configuration value change without a redeploy, and
> what would you be careful about?"*

Say: the value has to come from a provider that can reload — a file with
`reloadOnChange`, or a custom provider over a database or key vault that calls
`OnReload` when its source changes — and the consumer has to be
`IOptionsMonitor<T>` or `IOptionsSnapshot<T>`, because `IOptions<T>` is
computed once and cached forever. Then name the care: reload events arrive
more than once per change and sometimes while a file is half-written, so I
debounce and read after the delay; the options should be validated with
`ValidateOnStart` so a bad value fails the deploy, and validated again on
reload so a bad value at runtime does not silently take effect; and the change
should be observable — log the fact that a reload happened and what changed, at
least at the key level, because a value that changed itself is otherwise
invisible during an incident. Finish with the boundary: things that change
behaviour dangerously — a connection string, an authentication mode — should
require a restart, because "no redeploy" also means "no review".

## Check yourself

1. What two interfaces make a configuration provider, and what does the base
   class give you?
2. What exactly does `OnReload()` do?
3. Why must `getToken` in `ChangeToken.OnChange` return a fresh token?
4. Give two reasons a single file save fires two reload events.
5. How does `IOptionsMonitor` decide to recompute, and how would you add your
   own trigger?
6. Contrast `IOptions`, `IOptionsSnapshot` and `IOptionsMonitor` in one line
   each.
7. Why does a `Configure` call after `Bind` defeat configuration?
8. What is `PostConfigure` the right phase for?
9. How does a JSON array appear in the flat configuration dictionary?
10. Which binds: a positional record, an `init`-only property, a read-only
    field?
11. How do you find out which provider supplied a value?
12. Why is a key-name redaction rule insufficient?
13. What does `ValidateOnStart` change about *when* you find out?
14. Name a setting you would deliberately not make hot-reloadable, and why.
15. Where should an environment check live, and where must it not?
lessons.fullReading:
# Reading - dotnet/v3db06_config_secrets

## The design, and why it is shaped like this

The configuration system in .NET is unusually opinionated for a framework
component, and the opinions are worth reading.

The first is that **configuration is flat strings**. Not a typed object, not a
tree, not a schema — a dictionary from colon-separated path to string. That
choice is what lets a JSON file, an INI file, an environment variable, a
command-line argument, a key vault and a database table all be the same kind
of thing. It also means every value is a string until the binder converts it,
which is why `"25"` and `25` are indistinguishable and why an environment
variable can override a JSON number.

The second is that **precedence is positional**. There is no priority field,
no merge strategy, no per-key policy. The last provider that has the key wins.
That is trivially predictable, which matters enormously at 3 a.m., and it is
why `GetDebugView` and the provider walk in `ex7` are so useful: the answer to
"why is this value 50" is always "some provider later in the list said so",
and you can find which.

The third is that **change is a token, not an event**. An `IChangeToken` is
single-use and pull-based: you ask for one, register a callback, and it fires
at most once. This looks awkward next to a C# event and it is deliberate —
it composes. `CompositeChangeToken` combines several; a token can report that
it has no active callbacks so consumers know to poll; and the single-use
contract means there is no ambiguity about ordering between "the value
changed" and "you registered". The cost is that every consumer must
re-register, which is what `ChangeToken.OnChange` exists to hide and what
hand-rolled reload code forgets.

## Reload, honestly

`reloadOnChange: true` uses a `FileSystemWatcher` (or a polling watcher, on
some containers and network filesystems, where the native one does not work
and you will discover this the hard way). Watchers report *filesystem* events,
not logical saves. An editor that writes a temp file and renames produces a
different event sequence from one that truncates and writes; a `kubectl`
ConfigMap update replaces a symlink. Two events for one change is the common
case and three is not rare.

Worse, the events can arrive between the truncate and the write, so a handler
that reads immediately can parse an empty or partial file. The JSON provider
handles a parse failure by throwing, which — inside a reload callback on a
background thread — historically produced a process crash. Modern versions are
more careful, but the general lesson stands: **the reload path is not the
happy path, and it is not covered by your tests.**

Practical guidance. Debounce with a 200–500 ms window that resets on each
event. Read the value after the delay, not when the event arrives. Wrap the
handler in a try/catch that logs and keeps the previous good value, because a
failed reload should never be worse than no reload. And log every reload with
the keys that changed — a value that changed by itself is otherwise invisible
in the timeline of an incident.

The larger question is which settings should be hot-reloadable at all. A
timeout, a page size, a feature flag, a log level: obviously yes, and hot log
levels are one of the genuinely great operational features of this stack. A
connection string, an authentication mode, an encryption key: no. Not because
it is technically impossible but because "changes without a deploy" also means
"changes without a review, a diff, or a rollback", and some changes should
have all three.

## The options system as a small framework

`IOptions<T>` looks trivial and is doing more than it appears.

`IOptionsFactory<T>` builds an instance: construct, run every
`IConfigureOptions<T>` in registration order, run every
`IPostConfigureOptions<T>`, then run every `IValidateOptions<T>` and throw
`OptionsValidationException` on failure. `IOptionsMonitorCache<T>` caches by
name and can be cleared. `IOptionsMonitor<T>` combines the factory and the
cache and subscribes to every `IOptionsChangeTokenSource<T>` to know when to
clear.

That decomposition is why the extension points exist where they do.
`Configure` and `PostConfigure` are two phases because "set a value" and
"derive a value from whatever was set" are different jobs and the second must
happen after all instances of the first. Named options fall out for free
because the whole chain takes a name. And `IOptionsChangeTokenSource` is a
separate interface precisely so that something other than configuration can
invalidate options — a database, a message, an admin endpoint.

The three consumer interfaces map onto the cache. `IOptions<T>` resolves the
value once for the process. `IOptionsSnapshot<T>` is scoped and recomputes per
scope — per request in a web app — whether or not anything changed, so it
costs a rebind per request and cannot be injected into a singleton.
`IOptionsMonitor<T>` is a singleton that returns the cached value and rebuilds
only on invalidation, which makes it both the cheapest and the most current.
The default advice — `IOptions<T>` unless you need reload — is right, but the
monitor is underused: for a singleton service reading a hot-reloadable value,
it is strictly the correct choice.

## Secrets

The provider abstraction is what makes secret handling tractable: code reads
`configuration["Dojo:Db:ConnectionString"]` and does not know whether that
came from a file, an environment variable, or Azure Key Vault. Changing the
source is a startup registration, not a code change.

What the abstraction does not give you is discipline about where secrets end
up once read. The leaks are almost never from the store; they are from the
application. A `GetDebugView()` in a diagnostics endpoint. An options object
serialised into a log line at Debug. An exception message that includes a
connection string. A crash dump. A support engineer pasting a config dump into
a ticket.

So: redact at the boundary, with both a key-name rule and a value-shape rule,
because either alone has a large blind spot. Do not log options objects
wholesale — log the fields you need. Treat any endpoint that returns
configuration as privileged and audited. And prefer secret types that cannot
be stringified by accident where the language lets you.

The other half is rotation. A secret that can be rotated without a deploy
requires a reloadable provider and a consumer that re-reads — which is the
same machinery as this whole sector, applied to the one value where getting it
wrong is worst. Key Vault providers support a reload interval for exactly
this. If your service caches a credential in a singleton at startup, rotation
means a restart, and you should know that before the security team asks.

## Environments, and the shape of good composition

`ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT` selects `appsettings.{Environment}.json` and gates
developer-facing features. It should decide **what is registered** and almost
nothing else.

The failure pattern is easy to recognise once named: `if (env.IsDevelopment())`
inside a handler, a service, or a repository. Every one of those is a code
path that runs in production and has never been executed by a developer, or
vice versa. The alternative is composition — register a fake in Development
and the real thing in Production, behind one interface — which makes the
difference explicit, greppable, and testable by substituting the registration.

A useful discipline: environment checks are allowed in `Program.cs` and in
registration methods, and nowhere else. If a behaviour genuinely needs to vary
below that, it varies on *configuration*, not on environment — because then a
staging environment can be made to behave like production for an afternoon
without a code change, which is a thing you will want.

## When not to use configuration

Two boundaries.

Configuration is not a database. Values that change per user, per tenant or
per request do not belong in `IConfiguration`, however tempting the binding is
— it is a process-wide singleton dictionary with a reload model designed for
occasional change. Per-tenant settings belong in storage, with a cache.

Configuration is also not a feature-management platform. The challenge in this
sector builds a small flag system, and it is honest about its limits: no
audit trail, no targeting rules beyond a percentage, no UI, no gradual
rollout automation. That is fine for a dozen flags. Past that, the reason to
adopt a real feature-management service is not the evaluation logic — which is
twenty lines — but everything around it.
