exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 — a provider of your own

Edit `src/Api/V3DB06_ConfigSecrets/Ex1.cs`. Write an `IConfigurationSource`
and an `IConfigurationProvider` backed by `V3Db06Store`:

```csharp
static IDictionary<string, string?> V3Db06Store.Snapshot();
static void V3Db06Store.Set(string key, string? value);
static event Action V3Db06Store.Changed;   // raised by Set
```

Add the source to the configuration root in `Register`, then implement:

- `GET /v3db06/config/{key}` — **200** with `{"key":"dojo:limit","value":"9"}`
  when any provider has the key, **404** when none does;
- `POST /v3db06/config` — takes `{"key":"dojo:limit","value":"9"}`, writes it
  to the store, answers **204**.

The gate posts a value and immediately reads it back, then reads it a second
time through a freshly resolved `IConfiguration`. Both must show the new
value: a provider that loads once and never signals a change passes the first
check and fails the second.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db06_config_secrets ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`ConfigurationProvider` is a base class that already implements `TryGet`,
`Set`, `GetChildKeys` and `GetReloadToken` over a protected `Data`
dictionary. You are overriding one method and adding one subscription.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public sealed class StoreProvider : ConfigurationProvider
{
    public StoreProvider() => V3Db06Store.Changed += () => { Load(); OnReload(); };
    public override void Load() => Data = V3Db06Store.Snapshot();
}
```

`OnReload()` is protected on the base class and is the whole point.

## Hint 3

The source is three lines and exists only so the builder can construct the
provider at the right time. Register it with
`builder.Configuration.Add(new StoreSource())` — note that `IServiceRegistrar`
gives you the `IConfiguration`, which you can cast to `IConfigurationRoot` and
whose `Providers` you can inspect for the 404.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about what makes this a *configuration* provider rather than a static
dictionary with a getter. Two things: it participates in precedence, so a
later provider can override it; and it participates in change notification, so
`IOptionsMonitor` and every `OnChange` callback in the process wake up when it
changes. `OnReload()` is the second one.

## Hint 2

The realistic version of this class talks to a database or a remote store, and
it needs three things this one does not: a poll interval or subscription, a
failure policy, and an `optional` flag. The failure policy is the one that
matters — throwing from `Load` on a transient network error takes the whole
application down, so the correct behaviour is to log and keep serving the last
good snapshot.

## Hint 3

For the 404, decide whether "no provider has it" is the same as "the value is
null". It is not: a provider can legitimately supply an empty string, and
`configuration[key] is null` conflates the two. Walking the providers with
`TryGet` distinguishes them, which is the same walk you will build properly in
ex7.

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — the callback that fires twice

Edit `src/Api/V3DB06_ConfigSecrets/Ex2.cs`. Register a change callback on the
configuration root that rebuilds an expensive cache:

```csharp
await V3Db06Cache.RebuildAsync(currentValue);   // ~40 ms
```

`GET /v3db06/reload` answers **200** with:

```json
{"changes":2,"rebuilds":1,"lastValue":"nine"}
```

- `changes` — how many times your `OnChange` callback was invoked;
- `rebuilds` — how many times `RebuildAsync` actually ran;
- `lastValue` — the value passed to the last rebuild.

The gate makes **one** logical change to `Dojo:Reload:Value` (which arrives as
two events, as file watchers habitually produce) and requires `rebuilds: 1`
and `lastValue` equal to the *final* value.

Debounce the callback, and make sure you read the configuration value **after**
the debounce window, not when the event arrives.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db06_config_secrets ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two problems in one exercise. The first is that one save produces two events —
so a rebuild per event is two rebuilds. The second is subtler: the first event
can arrive while the source is half-written, so the value you read *at event
time* may not be the value you want to cache.

## Hint 2

The registration pattern re-subscribes for you:

```csharp
ChangeToken.OnChange(
    () => configuration.GetReloadToken(),   // must return a FRESH token each call
    () => _debounce.Schedule(RebuildAsync));
```

Caching that token is the classic bug: the callback then fires exactly once,
ever.

## Hint 3

A debounce is a cancellable delay: cancel the pending one, start a new one,
and do the work only if the delay completes. Read `configuration["…"]` inside
the work, after the delay — that is what makes `lastValue` correct rather than
whatever the first event happened to see.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask why the framework hands you a single-use token instead of an event. It
composes: several tokens combine into one, a token can declare it has no
active callbacks so consumers know to poll, and single-use removes any
ambiguity about whether you registered before or after a change. The cost is
the re-registration loop, and `ChangeToken.OnChange` exists purely to hide it.

## Hint 2

The debounce window is a real trade-off, not a magic number. Too short and you
still double-rebuild on a slow filesystem; too long and a deliberate
configuration change appears not to have worked, so somebody changes it again.
200–500 ms covers the observed event spacing without being perceptible.

## Hint 3

Wrap the rebuild in a try/catch that logs and keeps the previous cache. A
failed reload must never be worse than no reload — and the reload path is
exactly the code path that no test exercises and that runs on a background
thread with nobody to report to.

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — how the monitor knows

Edit `src/Api/V3DB06_ConfigSecrets/Ex3.cs`. `GateOptions` (`int Limit`) binds
from `Dojo:Gate`. A second source of truth — `V3Db06Store`, with a `Changed`
event — must **also** invalidate it.

Register an `IOptionsChangeTokenSource<GateOptions>` whose `GetChangeToken()`
returns a token that fires when the store signals. Use the given
`CountingConfigureOptions`, which increments a counter every time the options
instance is rebuilt.

`GET /v3db06/gate` answers **200** with:

```json
{"limit":50,"recomputes":3}
```

The gate: reads the endpoint (build 1), changes the configuration section
(build 2 on the next read), signals the store (build 3 on the next read), and
requires `recomputes: 3`. Reading the endpoint ten times in a row between
changes must not increase the count.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db06_config_secrets ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`IOptionsMonitor<T>` caches the computed instance and drops it when any
registered `IOptionsChangeTokenSource<T>` fires. `services.Configure<T>(
section)` quietly registers one for the configuration section; you are adding
a second, for a source that is not configuration at all.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public sealed class StoreTokenSource<T> : IOptionsChangeTokenSource<T>
{
    public string? Name => Options.DefaultName;
    public IChangeToken GetChangeToken() => V3Db06Store.Token();   // fresh each call
}

services.AddSingleton<IOptionsChangeTokenSource<GateOptions>, StoreTokenSource<GateOptions>>();
```

## Hint 3

Inject `IOptionsMonitor<GateOptions>` and read `CurrentValue` — not
`IOptions<T>`, which is computed once, and not `IOptionsSnapshot<T>`, which
rebuilds every request and would make `recomputes` climb with every call. The
distinction is exactly what the counter measures.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The counter is the interesting part of this exercise. Read the endpoint ten
times: the count does not move. That is the monitor's cache, and it is why
`IOptionsMonitor` is both the most current and the cheapest of the three
consumer interfaces — it rebuilds on invalidation rather than on a schedule.

## Hint 2

Contrast with `IOptionsSnapshot<T>`, which recomputes once per scope whether
or not anything changed. In a busy service that is a rebind per request of
every options type you inject that way — usually irrelevant, occasionally
measurable, and always more work than the monitor does.

## Hint 3

`GetChangeToken()` must return a **fresh** token each time it is called, for
the same reason as ex2: the monitor registers, the token fires once, and the
monitor re-registers by calling you again. Handing back the same already-fired
token means the options are invalidated once and then frozen forever, which is
a bug that looks exactly like caching working correctly.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — fail at boot, not at 3 a.m.

Edit `src/Api/V3DB06_ConfigSecrets/Ex4.cs`. `MailerOptions` has `Host`
(string), `Port` (int), `FromAddress` (string) and `RetryCount` (int).

Wire it so that a misconfigured application **refuses to start**:

- bind `Dojo:Mailer`;
- `ValidateDataAnnotations()`;
- register an `IValidateOptions<MailerOptions>` reporting **every** failing
  rule in one result:
  - `Host` blank → `"Host must not be blank."`
  - `Port` outside 1–65535 → `"Port {n} is out of range."`
  - `FromAddress` without `@` → `"FromAddress must contain '@'."`
  - `RetryCount` outside 0–10 → `"RetryCount must be between 0 and 10."`
- `ValidateOnStart()`.

`GET /v3db06/mailer/validate?host=&port=99999&from=nobody&retry=3` calls your
validator directly and answers **200** with:

```json
{"valid":false,"failures":["Host must not be blank.","Port 99999 is out of range.","FromAddress must contain '@'."]}
```

The gate boots the app with three simultaneous mistakes and requires all three
names in the startup failure — a validator that returns on the first problem
gives the operator one error per restart.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db06_config_secrets ex4
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Picture the operator. They deploy, it fails, they fix the one error in the
message, deploy again, it fails on the next error. Three round trips through a
pipeline for three typos in one file. Collecting failures is not neatness; it
is the difference between a five-minute fix and an hour.

## Hint 2

`ValidateOnStart` changes *when* you find out, and that is the whole value. Without
it, a bad mail port is discovered by the first customer whose password reset
tries to send — possibly hours after the deploy, possibly on one pod out of
twelve, and the error is a 500 in a log rather than a red pipeline.

## Hint 3

Note that data-annotation validation and your custom validator compose: both
run, and both sets of messages appear in the exception. Use annotations for
the mechanical rules (`[Required]`, `[Range]`) and the custom validator for
anything that needs two fields or real logic — a validator that re-implements
`[Range]` is a validator that will disagree with the attribute one day.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — configure, then post-configure

Edit `src/Api/V3DB06_ConfigSecrets/Ex5.cs`. `ClientOptions` has `Timeout`
(`TimeSpan`), `UserAgent` (string) and `BaseUrl` (string). Three independent
contributors assemble it, none aware of the others:

1. **library default** — `Timeout = 30s`, `UserAgent = "dojo"`;
2. **configuration** — the bound `Dojo:Client` section;
3. **post-configure** — append ` ({EnvironmentName})` to `UserAgent`, and
   rewrite `BaseUrl` from `http://` to `https://` if it starts with `http://`.

Each contributor calls `V3Db06Trace.Note("library-default")`,
`"configuration"` or `"post-configure"` as it runs.

`GET /v3db06/client` answers **200** with:

```json
{"timeout":"00:00:10","userAgent":"dojo-api (Development)","baseUrl":"https://example.test","order":["library-default","configuration","post-configure"]}
```

The gate's configuration sets `Timeout` to 10 seconds and `UserAgent` to
`"dojo-api"`, and requires both to survive — which they will not if you place
the library default in the obvious spot.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db06_config_secrets ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`services.Configure<T>(section)` is not a special kind of registration — it
registers an `IConfigureOptions<T>` like any other. So "configuration" and
"a lambda that sets a default" are the same phase, and they run in
registration order.

## Hint 2

Which means this does the opposite of what it reads like:

```csharp
services.Configure<ClientOptions>(config.GetSection("Dojo:Client"));
services.Configure<ClientOptions>(o => o.Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30));
```

The lambda runs second and overwrites the configured timeout with 30 seconds,
every time.

## Hint 3

The fluent builder makes the order visible:

```csharp
services.AddOptions<ClientOptions>()
    .Configure(o => { /* defaults */ })
    .Bind(configuration.GetSection("Dojo:Client"))
    .PostConfigure(o => { /* derive */ });
```

Post-configure runs after *every* configure step, whatever the registration
order, which is what makes it the right home for a derived value.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Sort the three contributors by what they *are*, not by where they are written.
A default is a starting value. Configuration is an override. Post-configure is
a transformation of whatever the result turned out to be. Those three
descriptions imply the ordering completely, and the framework's phases match
them exactly.

## Hint 2

Note the alternative for defaults that people underuse: property initialisers
on the options class itself. `public TimeSpan Timeout { get; set; } =
TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30);` cannot be ordered wrongly, is visible to anyone
reading the type, and survives every refactor of the registration code. Reach
for `Configure` defaults only when the default has to come from somewhere else.

## Hint 3

Think about why the `https` rewrite belongs in post-configure rather than in
the property or the section. It is a *policy* applied to whatever anybody
configured, including a value that arrives from an environment variable in
production three months from now. Encoding it as a transformation means it
cannot be forgotten; encoding it as a default means it can be overridden by
the exact mistake it exists to prevent.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — the shapes that do not bind

Edit `src/Api/V3DB06_ConfigSecrets/Ex6.cs`. `IngestOptions` binds from
`Dojo:Ingest`:

```jsonc
{
  "Endpoints": ["primary", "secondary"],
  "Limits": { "acme": 10, "globex": 5 },
  "Window": "00:00:30",
  "Mode": "Strict",
  "Retry": { "Attempts": 3, "Backoff": "00:00:02" }
}
```

`Retry` is a positional record and `IngestOptions.Window` has only an `init`
accessor. One of those binds as shipped and one does not.

- `GET /v3db06/ingest` answers **200** with all five values bound:
  `{"endpoints":["primary","secondary"],"limits":{"acme":10,"globex":5},
  "window":"00:00:30","mode":"Strict","retry":{"attempts":3,"backoff":"00:00:02"}}`.
- `GET /v3db06/ingest/strict` binds a **fresh** instance with
  `BinderOptions.ErrorOnUnknownConfiguration = true` and answers **200** with
  `{"bound":false,"error":"…"}` when the section has a key with no matching
  property, or `{"bound":true}` when it does not.

Fix the shape that does not bind **without** turning it into a mutable class,
and name the rule you relied on in a comment.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db06_config_secrets ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The binder writes **public properties it can set**, and constructs objects it
needs to construct. Those are two different mechanisms, and which one applies
decides whether `init` and positional records work.

## Hint 2

`init` is a setter as far as the runtime is concerned — the restriction is a
compiler rule, and the binder uses reflection. So an `init`-only property
binds when the binder is constructing the object. It does **not** bind when
you hand the binder an instance you already made.

## Hint 3

A positional record binds through its constructor when the parameter names
match the keys and there is exactly **one** usable constructor. Adding a
second constructor — including a parameterless one someone added "for
serialisation" — makes the binder ambiguous and it gives up. Check the record
before assuming the problem is elsewhere.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Build the flat dictionary on paper before debugging anything. The JSON above
becomes `Dojo:Ingest:Endpoints:0`, `Dojo:Ingest:Endpoints:1`,
`Dojo:Ingest:Limits:acme`, `Dojo:Ingest:Window`, and so on. Every binding
question becomes obvious once you can see the keys — including why an
environment variable can append to an array.

## Hint 2

`ErrorOnUnknownConfiguration` deserves more use than it gets. A typo in a key
name is currently silent: the property keeps its default and the service
behaves subtly wrong. Turning the typo into a startup exception costs one
option and removes an entire category of "it did not pick up my setting"
tickets. The reason it is off by default is that a shared section legitimately
carries keys one consumer does not know about.

## Hint 3

`TimeSpan` is the type that catches people. It parses from `"00:00:30"` and
`"1.02:03:04"`; it does **not** parse from `30`, and a JSON number there
produces a format exception at bind time with a message that names the
property but not the intent. If your configuration authors keep writing
seconds as integers, bind an `int` and expose a computed `TimeSpan`.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 — who won, and why

Edit `src/Api/V3DB06_ConfigSecrets/Ex7.cs`. Implement `Whence` so that
`GET /v3db06/whence?key={key}` answers **200** with:

```json
{
  "key": "Dojo:Gate:Limit",
  "value": "50",
  "provider": "EnvironmentVariablesConfigurationProvider",
  "candidates": [
    "JsonConfigurationProvider=25",
    "MemoryConfigurationProvider=40",
    "EnvironmentVariablesConfigurationProvider=50"
  ]
}
```

- `value` — what `IConfiguration` actually returns for the key;
- `provider` — the simple type name of the provider that supplied it;
- `candidates` — `"{ProviderTypeName}={value}"` for every provider that has
  the key, in **provider order** (earliest registered first), so a reader can
  see exactly what was overridden by what.

**404** when no provider has the key.

Walk `IConfigurationRoot.Providers` with `TryGet`. Do not parse
`GetDebugView()`. The gate sets the key in three providers, spelling the
environment variable `Dojo__Gate__Limit`, and requires the last-registered
provider to win.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db06_config_secrets ex7
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

This endpoint is worth building once in every service you own. "Why is this
value 50 in production and 25 on my machine" is one of the most common and
most tedious questions in operations, and the answer is always "a later
provider said so" — but finding out which one, without this, means reading
deployment manifests.

## Hint 2

`GetDebugView()` gives you the same information formatted for a human, with
the winning provider annotated per key. It is excellent in a log line at
startup and terrible to parse, which is why the exercise forbids it. Know it
exists; know it will happily print your secrets.

## Hint 3

Consider what to do about the redaction problem this endpoint creates. It is a
configuration reader with no filter, so it will cheerfully return a password
to anyone who guesses the key. Whatever you build in ex8 belongs here too, and
in real code this endpoint would be behind authorisation and audited.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — the dump you can paste into a ticket

Edit `src/Api/V3DB06_ConfigSecrets/Ex8.cs`. Implement `Dump` so that
`GET /v3db06/dump` answers **200** with every configuration key and value,
sorted by key ordinally, secrets redacted:

```json
{
  "redacted": 2,
  "entries": [
    {"key":"Dojo:Gate:Limit","value":"50"},
    {"key":"Dojo:Mailer:ApiKey","value":"***"},
    {"key":"Dojo:Storage:Primary","value":"***"}
  ]
}
```

Redaction rules, both of which must be implemented:

1. **key rule** — the key's **last segment** matches, case-insensitively, any
   of `password`, `secret`, `token`, `key`, `connectionstring`;
2. **value rule** — the value contains `Password=` or `Pwd=`
   (case-insensitively), whatever the key is called.

`configuration.AsEnumerable()` gives you every key; skip entries whose value is
null.

The gate plants a secret under the innocuous key `Dojo:Storage:Primary` and
fails the exercise if either planted value appears anywhere in the response
body.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db06_config_secrets ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two rules because either alone has a large blind spot. A key rule misses a
connection string stored under `Primary`. A value rule misses an API key,
which is just an opaque string with nothing recognisable in it. Together they
cover most of what actually leaks.

## Hint 2

The last segment is what matters, not the whole path:

```csharp
string last = key.Split(':')[^1];
bool sensitive = Sensitive.Any(s => last.Contains(s, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase));
```

Matching the whole path would redact `Dojo:Keyboard:Layout`, which is the kind
of over-redaction that makes people turn the feature off.

## Hint 3

`configuration.AsEnumerable()` yields intermediate section keys with null
values as well as leaves — skip the nulls. Then sort ordinally by key, project
to your DTO, and count the redactions as you go rather than in a second pass.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about how secrets actually escape. Almost never from the secret store —
from the application. A debug endpoint. An options object logged at Debug
level. An exception message carrying a connection string. A crash dump. A
support engineer pasting a config dump into a ticket that is then indexed by
a search system for seven years.

## Hint 2

Note that redaction is defence in depth, not a control. The real controls are:
do not log configuration wholesale, put any endpoint like this behind
authorisation, audit access to it, and keep secrets in a store that can rotate
them. Redaction is what saves you when one of those fails, which it will.

## Hint 3

Consider what your rules would do to a key named `Dojo:Api:PublicKey`. It gets
redacted, and it did not need to be. That is the right side to err on, but it
is worth writing an explicit allow-list escape hatch in real code — otherwise
somebody eventually removes the redaction to see one harmless value and never
puts it back.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — feature flags that change without a deploy

Edit `src/Api/V3DB06_ConfigSecrets/Challenge.cs`. Build a flag system out of
the machinery in this sector.

`FlagOptions` binds `Dojo:Flags` — a dictionary of flag name to:

```jsonc
{ "enabled": true, "percentage": 25, "environments": ["Development", "Staging"] }
```

`GET /v3db06/flags/{name}?user={id}` answers:

- **404** for an unknown flag;
- **400** when `user` is blank;
- **200** with `{"name":"newCheckout","on":true,"reason":"percentage"}`.

Evaluation order, and the `reason` each produces:

1. current environment not listed in `environments` → off, `"environment"`;
2. `enabled` is false → off, `"disabled"`;
3. `percentage` is 100 → on, `"enabled"`;
4. otherwise → on iff `V3Db06Hash.Bucket(name, user) < percentage`,
   `"percentage"`.

Requirements the gate enforces:

- a change to `Dojo:Flags` takes effect on the **next request**, with no
  restart;
- the options are validated on start — `percentage` 0–100 and at least one
  environment, with **all** failures reported together;
- the same `user` gets the same answer for a given flag and percentage, every
  time, across processes.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db06_config_secrets challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three pieces you have already built: a reloadable options consumer (ex3), a
multi-failure validator (ex4), and a bound dictionary (ex6). The evaluation
itself is a four-branch `if`. Assemble rather than invent.

## Hint 2

"Takes effect on the next request with no restart" rules out exactly one of
the three consumer interfaces and permits the other two:

```csharp
IOptionsMonitor<FlagOptions> monitor   // singleton, cached, invalidated
IOptionsSnapshot<FlagOptions> snapshot // scoped, rebuilt per request
```

`IOptions<T>` is computed once for the process and would freeze your flags at
boot.

## Hint 3

The stability requirement is why the bucket is a **hash** of `(name, user)`
rather than a random number. `V3Db06Hash.Bucket` returns 0–99 deterministically.
Including the flag name in the hash matters too — otherwise every 10% flag
targets the same 10% of users, and that cohort experiences every experiment
you ever run.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Get the evaluation order right and write it as a comment before you code it.
Environment first, because a flag not meant for this environment should be off
regardless of anything else. Then the kill switch. Then the shortcut. Then the
rollout. Reordering any two of those changes the semantics in a way that is
easy to ship and hard to notice.

## Hint 2

The stable-bucket requirement is the difference between a rollout and a
flicker. With a random number per request, a user at 25% sees the new checkout
on one page load and the old one on the next — which is worse than either
version, and produces support tickets nobody can reproduce. Determinism is not
an optimisation here; it is the feature.

## Hint 3

Be honest about the limits of what you are building, because that is the
judgement being tested. There is no audit trail of who changed a flag, no
targeting beyond a percentage, no gradual automation, no way to see who is in
the cohort. For a dozen flags that is fine. The reason to adopt a real
feature-management service is everything around the evaluation, not the
evaluation.

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.prompt:
## Review 1 — composition, not conditionals

Edit `src/Api/V3DB06_ConfigSecrets/Review1.cs`. `IReceiptSender` has one
method, `Task<string> SendAsync(string to, string body)`, returning a
transport id.

Register a different implementation per environment, entirely in `Register`:

- **Development** and **Staging** → `RecordingSender`, which stores messages
  in memory and returns `"recorded:{n}"`;
- **Production** → `SmtpSender`, which requires `Dojo:Receipts:Endpoint` to be
  a non-empty URL and must make the application **fail to start** if it is
  missing.

`GET /v3db06/sender` answers **200** with:

```json
{"environment":"Development","implementation":"RecordingSender","decidedIn":"Register"}
```

`POST /v3db06/receipts` sends one and answers **200** with
`{"transportId":"recorded:1"}`.

The constraint the gate checks: the string `IsDevelopment` and the string
`EnvironmentName` may appear **only** inside `Register`. No handler, and
nothing `IReceiptSender` touches, may ask which environment it is in.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3db06_config_secrets review1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The environment decides *what is registered*. Below that, nothing knows it
exists — the handler injects `IReceiptSender` and cannot tell which one it
got, which is exactly the property that makes it testable.

## Hint 2

`IServiceRegistrar` gives you `IConfiguration`, and the environment name is
in it:

```csharp
string env = configuration["ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT"] ?? "Production";
if (env is "Development" or "Staging")
    services.AddSingleton<IReceiptSender, RecordingSender>();
else
    services.AddSingleton<IReceiptSender, SmtpSender>();
```

## Hint 3

The "must fail to start" part is options validation from ex4, applied to
`ReceiptOptions` — but registered **only** on the production branch, so a
developer without an SMTP endpoint can still run the app. That conditional
registration of a *validator* is the piece most people miss.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Name the failure this rule prevents. `if (env.IsDevelopment())` inside a
handler creates two code paths, and each one is only ever executed in the
environment where nobody is looking at it: the development branch is never
exercised in production, and the production branch is never exercised by a
developer. Every bug in either is found by a customer.

## Hint 2

The composition version is greppable, which matters more than it sounds.
"Which implementation runs in staging" is answerable by reading one method,
rather than by searching for environment checks across a codebase and hoping
you found them all.

## Hint 3

Note the escape hatch worth knowing: when a behaviour genuinely must vary
below registration, vary it on **configuration**, not on environment. Then
staging can be made to behave like production for an afternoon by changing a
value, which is a thing you will want during an incident and cannot do with a
compiled-in environment check.
